Command: No Other Gods
Summary: The first commandment: God alone is to be worshipped, and nothing else may rival him.
Commandment: Worship God alone; put nothing else in his place.
Application: Jesus restates this as the first and greatest commandment (Matthew 22:37-38). Idolatry today is not only statues: anything that takes God's rightful first place — wealth, status, pleasure, self — rivals him.
Purpose: God grounds it in his own deliverance of Israel: 'I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt' (Exodus 20:2). Exclusive worship answers who God has shown himself to be.

Command: No Idols
Summary: The second commandment: God's people must not make or worship carved images or any likeness as a god.
Commandment: Do not make or worship an idol or any image as a god.
Application: God cannot be captured in an image made by human hands. The New Testament extends the warning inward: covetousness itself is idolatry (Colossians 3:5).
Purpose: Scripture states the reason in the command itself: God is a jealous God who shows mercy to those who love him and keep his commandments (Exodus 20:5-6). No image may stand in for him.

Command: Do Not Misuse God's Name
Summary: The third commandment: God's name must be treated with reverence, never used emptily, falsely, or as a cover for wrongdoing.
Commandment: Do not use God's name in a worthless, false, or irreverent way.
Application: Bearing God's name is about more than speech: his people carry his name before the world, so their words and conduct must match it.
Purpose: Scripture states the sanction: the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain (Exodus 20:7). His name carries his character, so it must not be used emptily.

Command: Remember the Sabbath
Summary: The fourth commandment: one day in seven is set apart for rest and worship, rooted in creation and in Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
Commandment: Keep one day in seven holy: rest from ordinary work and set it apart for God.
Application: Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath and teaches that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Christians differ on whether seventh-day observance continues literally or is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9-10); both readings are honestly held.
Purpose: Scripture gives two stated grounds: creation rest (Exodus 20:11) and deliverance from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). Debated: some Christians keep a seventh-day Sabbath literally; others see the Sabbath fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9-10). The site does not settle this.

Command: Honor Father and Mother
Summary: The fifth commandment: parents are to be honored in word, care, and provision — the first commandment with a promise attached.
Commandment: Honor your father and mother in how you speak of them, care for them, and provide for them.
Application: Paul quotes this commandment to believers and repeats its promise: that it may go well with you and that you may live long. Honor does not end when a child leaves home; it grows into caring for aging parents.
Purpose: Scripture attaches the stated promise: that thy days may be long upon the land (Exodus 20:12), repeated by Paul to believers (Ephesians 6:2-3).

Command: Do Not Murder
Summary: The sixth commandment: human life, made in God's image, must not be taken unlawfully.
Commandment: Do not take a human life unlawfully.
Application: Jesus presses the commandment to the heart: contempt and hatred already break it in spirit. The commandment forbids murder, not lawful judgment or defense, which Scripture treats separately.
Purpose: To guard human life on the stated ground that man is made in God's image (Genesis 9:6).

Command: Do Not Commit Adultery
Summary: The seventh commandment: marriage is exclusive, and sexual faithfulness guards the covenant between husband and wife.
Commandment: Do not be unfaithful to your marriage; keep sexual union within marriage alone.
Application: Jesus extends the commandment to the heart: lustful intent already breaks it. The positive side is faithfulness that protects both spouse and family.
Purpose: To guard marriage exclusivity; Jesus roots marriage in creation: what God joined, man must not separate (Matthew 19:4-6).

Command: Do Not Steal
Summary: The eighth commandment: what belongs to another must not be taken by force, fraud, or stealth.
Commandment: Do not take what belongs to someone else.
Application: Paul turns the commandment positive: the thief must steal no longer, but work honestly and share with those in need. Theft includes fraud and withheld wages, not only burglary.
Purpose: To protect what belongs to another; Paul turns it positive: work honestly and share with those in need (Ephesians 4:28).

Command: Do Not Bear False Witness
Summary: The ninth commandment: truth must be told, especially where another person's name and standing are at stake.
Commandment: Do not testify falsely against another person.
Application: False witness destroys a neighbor's reputation and corrupts justice. Jesus contrasts truth-telling with the devil, whom he calls the father of lies.
Purpose: To protect a neighbor's name and the integrity of justice; false testimony corrupts both.

Command: Do Not Covet
Summary: The tenth commandment: desire itself is addressed — not only acts, but the grasping heart that wants what belongs to another.
Commandment: Do not set your heart on possessing what belongs to your neighbor.
Application: This is the commandment that reaches inward, which is why Paul calls covetousness idolatry. It exposes that sin begins in desire before it becomes action.
Purpose: To reach desire itself, not only acts; Paul calls covetousness idolatry (Colossians 3:5).

Command: Honor the Aged
Summary: The respect law: rise before gray hair and honor the aged, treating age itself as worthy of deference.
Commandment: Stand up in the presence of gray hair and honor the aged.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Paul applies the same posture inside the church: treat older men as fathers and older women as mothers, correcting with gentleness.
Purpose: Leviticus 19:32 commands rising before gray hair as reverence for age itself; Paul applies the posture inside the church (1 Timothy 5:1-2).

Command: Be fruitful and multiply
Summary: The creation mandate, restated to Noah after the flood: humanity is to multiply and fill the earth.
Commandment: Be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth.
Application: Given first in Eden and repeated as the first word of the post-flood world, this is a standing mandate, not a moment's task. The Genesis 1 and Genesis 9 utterances are one command restated, not two commands.
Purpose: To fill the earth with image-bearers who carry God's blessing outward; Genesis 1:28 joins it to dominion, and Genesis 9:1-7 restates it as the foundation of the renewed world.

Command: Circumcise every male child
Summary: God's covenant command to Abraham: every man child among you shall be circumcised on the eighth day, as the token of the covenant between God and Abraham's seed (Genesis 17:10-12). The sign was cut into the flesh of the household — sons, servants, and all — marking them as covenant people.
Commandment: Circumcise every male child, as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham.
Application: The sign marked Abraham's household as God's own, and the uncircumcised male was cut off from his people (Genesis 17:14). Debated: Jews continue circumcision as the covenant sign; the New Testament holds it is not required for Gentile believers (Galatians 5:2-6; Acts 15), with circumcision of the heart as the fulfilment. This row does not settle that difference.
Purpose: To mark Abraham's seed with the sign of the everlasting covenant in their flesh (Genesis 17:11-13); the sign's ongoing force is the debated point, not its original purpose.

Command: Believe God exists
Summary: Exodus 20:2 opens the Ten Words with God's self-declaration: 'I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.' In the traditional enumeration this verse is counted as a positive command — the first mitzvah — even though it reads as a statement rather than an imperative, because it grounds every command that follows in who God is.
Commandment: Believe that God exists, and that he is the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt.
Application: Every other command rests on this one: obedience follows from knowing who commands. The New Testament carries the same ground forward — without faith it is impossible to please God, for he that cometh to God must believe that he is (Hebrews 11:6).
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground is the Exodus itself: the God who redeemed Israel is the God who commands Israel (Exodus 20:2).

Command: Offer the Passover lamb
Summary: On the fourteenth day of the first month, at evening, Israel offers the Passover lamb as the LORD commanded.
Commandment: On the fourteenth day of the first month at even, offer the Passover lamb to the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The lamb's blood on the doorposts marked the houses God passed over in Egypt; the New Testament reads the lamb as fulfilled in Christ, our Passover sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Eat the Passover lamb roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs
Summary: The Passover lamb is eaten roasted with fire, together with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Commandment: Eat the Passover lamb roast with fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The bitter herbs recalled the bitterness of slavery in Egypt, and the unleavened bread the haste of departure. The New Testament reads the Passover lamb as fulfilled in Christ, our Passover sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not eat the Passover lamb raw or boiled
Summary: The Passover lamb may not be eaten raw or boiled in water; it must be roasted with fire.
Commandment: Do not eat the Passover lamb raw, nor boiled in water, but roast with fire.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The roasting was part of the haste and wholeness of the meal on the night of deliverance. The ritual form belongs to Israel's covenant calendar, not to Christian observance.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not leave any of the Passover lamb until morning
Summary: No part of the Passover lamb may remain uneaten until morning; what is left must be burned with fire.
Commandment: Leave none of the Passover lamb until the morning; whatever remains until morning, burn with fire.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament reads the Passover lamb as fulfilled in Christ, our Passover sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7). The ritual meal form belongs to Israel's covenant calendar, not to Christian observance.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not break a bone of the Passover lamb
Summary: No bone of the Passover lamb may be broken when it is eaten.
Commandment: Do not break any bone of the Passover lamb.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. John 19:36 applies the unbroken-bone detail to Jesus, whose bones were not broken at his death. The ritual detail belongs to Israel's covenant calendar, not to Christian observance.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not carry Passover flesh outside the house
Summary: The flesh of the Passover lamb must be eaten in the one house where the meal is kept, not carried outside.
Commandment: Do not carry any of the Passover flesh out of the house; eat it in the one house.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule kept the household meal whole on the night of deliverance. The New Testament reads the Passover lamb as fulfilled in Christ, our Passover sacrificed for us (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: No foreigner or hired servant shall eat the Passover
Summary: A foreigner merely passing through, and a hired servant, may not eat the Passover unless brought into the covenant household.
Commandment: No foreigner or hired servant shall eat the Passover.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule guarded the covenant character of the meal; the stranger who joined the household by circumcision could eat (Exodus 12:48).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: No uncircumcised person shall eat the Passover
Summary: No uncircumcised male may eat the Passover; circumcision was the entry into the covenant meal.
Commandment: No uncircumcised person shall eat the Passover.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Circumcision marked belonging to the covenant people, and the Passover meal belonged to that people.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Eat unleavened bread on Passover
Summary: Unleavened bread is eaten through the Passover feast, recalling the haste of the departure from Egypt.
Commandment: Eat unleavened bread throughout the Passover feast.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Unleavened bread recalled bread baked in haste, without time to rise, on the night Israel left Egypt. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not eat leaven during Passover
Summary: No leavened bread may be eaten during the Passover feast; only unleavened bread is eaten.
Commandment: Eat no leavened bread during the feast; eat unleavened bread instead.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The prohibition is the negative side of the unleavened-bread memorial of the hasty departure from Egypt. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Leaven shall not be seen in your borders during Passover
Summary: During Unleavened Bread, no leaven may be seen anywhere within Israel's borders, not only in the house.
Commandment: Let no leaven be seen in all your borders during the seven days.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The wider boundary extended the clean break from leaven beyond the house to the whole land's feast observance. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Leaven shall not be found in your houses during Passover
Summary: During the seven days of Unleavened Bread, no leaven may be found in any Israelite house.
Commandment: For seven days, let no leaven be found in your houses.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The empty house pictured a people wholly separated from Egypt's leaven for the whole feast week. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Sanctify every firstborn male to the LORD
Summary: The command: Sanctify every firstborn male to the LORD (Exodus 13:2). The firstborn male, of both man and beast, belonged to the LORD from birth, set apart in memory of the Exodus.
Commandment: Sanctify every firstborn male to the LORD, as prescribed in Exodus 13:2.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: because the LORD slew all the firstborn in Egypt and spared Israel's, therefore the firstborn are his (Exodus 13:14-15).

Command: Redeem the firstborn son
Summary: The command: Redeem the firstborn son (Exodus 13:13). Every firstborn son was redeemed with a price paid to the priest, recalling that God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt.
Commandment: Redeem the firstborn son, as prescribed in Exodus 13:13.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Redemption of the firstborn remembered that God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt. The New Testament speaks of Jesus as the firstborn and of believers as redeemed, but does not continue the redemption payment as a Christian rite (Colossians 1:15-18; 1 Peter 1:18-19).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: because the LORD slew all the firstborn in Egypt and spared Israel's, therefore the firstborn are his (Exodus 13:14-15).

Command: Redeem the firstborn donkey
Summary: The command: Redeem the firstborn donkey (Exodus 13:13). The firstling donkey was redeemed with a lamb given to the priest, because the donkey itself, as an unclean animal, could not be sacrificed.
Commandment: Redeem the firstborn donkey, as prescribed in Exodus 13:13.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Redemption of the firstborn remembered that God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt. The New Testament speaks of Jesus as the firstborn and of believers as redeemed, but does not continue the redemption payment as a Christian rite (Colossians 1:15-18; 1 Peter 1:18-19).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: because the LORD slew all the firstborn in Egypt and spared Israel's, therefore the firstborn are his (Exodus 13:14-15).

Command: Rest on the first day of Unleavened Bread
Summary: The first day of Unleavened Bread is a holy convocation of rest, opening the seven days of unleavened bread.
Commandment: Keep the first day of Unleavened Bread as a holy convocation and rest on it.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The opening rest tied the feast week to the haste of the departure from Egypt. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Do no servile work on the first day of Unleavened Bread
Summary: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, no servile work may be done; the day is a holy convocation.
Commandment: On the first day of Unleavened Bread, do no servile work.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The work ban set the feast's opening day apart from ordinary labor. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Rest on the seventh day of Unleavened Bread
Summary: The seventh day of Unleavened Bread is a holy convocation of rest, closing the seven days of unleavened bread.
Commandment: Keep the seventh day of Unleavened Bread as a holy convocation and rest on it.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The closing rest ended the feast week as it began, in worship rather than work. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Do no servile work on the seventh day of Unleavened Bread
Summary: On the seventh day of Unleavened Bread, no servile work may be done; the day is a holy convocation.
Commandment: On the seventh day of Unleavened Bread, do no servile work.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The closing work ban matched the opening one, framing the whole feast week. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Keep the second Passover if unclean or on a journey
Summary: A man unclean by a dead body, or on a journey far off, at the first Passover, shall keep the Passover in the second month, on the fourteenth day at even.
Commandment: If unclean by a dead body or on a journey at Passover, keep the Passover in the second month on the fourteenth day at even.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The second Passover is mercy built into the calendar: uncleanness or a journey did not mean a year of exclusion. The defiled are not kept from the table for a month but are cleansed and welcomed (1 John 1:7-9).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the men defiled by a dead body asked why they should be kept back from offering the LORD's offering — and God answered with a second date, not a refusal (Numbers 9:6-11).

Command: Build a sanctuary for God
Summary: The command: Build a sanctuary for God (Exodus 25:8). Israel was to make a sanctuary patterned on what Moses was shown on the mountain, so that God might dwell among them.
Commandment: Build a sanctuary for God, as prescribed in Exodus 25:8.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Set the Bread of the Presence before God continually
Summary: The command: Set the Bread of the Presence before God continually (Exodus 25:30). Twelve loaves stood continually before the LORD on the table in the holy place, renewed every Sabbath.
Commandment: Set the Bread of the Presence before God continually, as prescribed in Exodus 25:30.

Summary: The command: Keep the lamps burning continually (Exodus 27:20). Pure olive oil kept the lampstand burning continually before the LORD in the holy place.

Summary: The command: Priests shall wear the sacred garments for service (Exodus 28:2). Aaron and his sons ministered in garments made for glory and for beauty, each piece prescribed in Exodus 28.

Summary: The command: The breastplate shall not be loosened from the ephod (Exodus 28:28). The breastplate of judgment was bound to the ephod with blue lace so it would not come loose during service.

Command: The robe's hem shall not be torn
Summary: The command: The robe's hem shall not be torn (Exodus 28:32). The ephod's robe was woven whole, with its opening bound so that it would not tear.
Commandment: The robe's hem shall not be torn.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. Command: Do not curse a ruler of your people
Summary: The ruler of the people — the one set in authority over them — is not to be cursed.
Commandment: Do not curse a ruler of your people.
Application: The New Testament repeats the respect: honour the king (1 Peter 2:17), and be subject to governing authorities (Romans 13:1-7). Respect does not mean silent approval of wrongdoing — the prophets rebuked kings — but it forbids contemptuous cursing of the ruler's person and office.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the ruler bears God-given authority, so cursing him dishonours the order God set. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 22:28).

Command: Do not afflict a widow or fatherless child
Summary: One of the protections for the vulnerable in Exodus 22: do not afflict a widow or fatherless child.
Commandment: Do not afflict a widow or fatherless child
Application: God's care for those without a defender is carried by James into the church as pure religion: visiting orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27).

Command: Lend without interest to a poor brother
Summary: When a poor brother is in need, lend to him without interest, giving him what his need requires.
Commandment: Lend without interest to a poor brother.
Application: The positive side of the interest ban is open-handed lending: help is given freely, not sold. Generous lending to the needy remains a mark of a community that treats money as a means of mercy.
Purpose: To protect the poor: lending to a needy brother is help freely given, not an opportunity for gain.

Command: Do not charge interest to a brother
Summary: A lender must not charge interest — usury — to a fellow Israelite, above all to the poor man who borrows out of need.
Commandment: Do not charge interest to a brother.
Application: Lending to a brother in need was help, not business: profit from a brother's poverty was forbidden. The enduring principle is that need must not be turned into a revenue stream, even where modern commercial lending raises questions the ancient law did not directly address.
Purpose: To make wrongs right and to protect the poor: a brother's need was not an occasion for profit.

Command: Do not pervert justice for the poor
Summary: Do not wrest the judgment of the poor in his cause: poverty must not lose a man his case.
Commandment: Do not pervert justice for the poor.
Application: The poor man has no patron and no bribe to offer, which is exactly why the Law guards his cause expressly. A court that bends against the poor because they are poor has perverted judgment itself.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the poor are the most exposed to bent judgment, so the Law names their cause expressly; God is no respecter of persons in judgment.

Command: Do not follow a multitude to do evil in judgment
Summary: Do not follow a multitude to do evil, and do not slant your testimony in a cause to follow a crowd and wrest judgment.
Commandment: Do not follow a multitude to do evil in judgment.
Application: A crowd is not evidence, and a cause is not decided by how many voices shout for it. The New Testament repeats the impartiality: show no partiality (James 2:9), and judge with right judgment, not by appearances (John 7:24).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the multitude can carry a court away from the truth, and the law guards the lone witness and the unpopular party against that pressure. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 23:2).

Command: Do not show favour to the poor in judgment either
Summary: In judgment, do not favour the poor either: pity for a poor litigant must not bend the verdict any more than respect for a rich one.
Commandment: Do not show favour to the poor in judgment either.
Application: Impartiality cuts both ways. Favouring the poor in court feels merciful, but it is still partiality — and it wrongs the other party while patronising the poor man, whose cause should win on its merits.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: justice is blind to wealth and poverty alike, so favour shown to the poor in judgment is partiality no less than favour shown to the rich.

Command: Keep far from a false matter in judgment
Summary: Keep far from a false matter: a judge must not lend his court to a charge he knows to be false, nor condemn the innocent or justify the wicked on false evidence.
Commandment: Keep far from a false matter in judgment.
Application: 'Keep far' is stronger than 'do not do': the judge is to keep his distance from falsehood altogether, not merely avoid its worst forms. Innocent blood is the price when courts traffic in false matters.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: falsehood in judgment sheds innocent blood, so the judge must keep far from a false matter, not merely refrain from its grossest form.

Command: Do not take a bribe
Summary: A judge must not take a gift — a bribe — for the bribe blinds the wise and perverts the words of the righteous.
Commandment: Do not take a bribe.
Application: Scripture gives the reason with the command: a bribe blinds even the wise. No judge is so clear-sighted that a gift leaves his judgment untouched, which is why the ban is absolute rather than limited to proven corruption.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous (Exodus 23:8).

Command: Return lost property to its owner
Summary: If you meet your enemy's ox or ass going astray, you shall surely bring it back to him; lost property is returned to its owner, even an enemy's.
Commandment: Return lost property to its owner.
Application: Lost property is not finders-keepers; it belongs to its owner, and you are its keeper until he comes for it. The command pointedly includes an enemy's animal: neighbourliness is not reserved for friends.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the lost thing belongs to your brother, and you are its keeper until he comes for it (Deuteronomy 22:1-3).

Command: Help your neighbour's fallen animal
Summary: If you see your neighbour's ass or ox fallen under its burden, do not hide yourself: help him lift it — and the same for the animal of one who hates you.
Commandment: Help your neighbour's fallen animal.
Application: Jesus appeals to the same instinct: which of you, having an ox fallen into a pit, will not straightway pull him out on the Sabbath day (Luke 14:5)? Mercy to a neighbour's animal, even an enemy's, is commanded help, not optional kindness.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the animal is under a burden it cannot bear, and the owner's need — even an enemy owner's need — obliges help (Exodus 23:5; Deuteronomy 22:4).

Command: Pay a hired servant his wages on time
Summary: The wages of a hired servant are given him on his day, before the sun goes down: the day's pay is not held past the day it was earned.
Commandment: Pay a hired servant his wages on time.
Application: Prompt pay is the positive form of the labour law: the wage arrives when it is needed, at the day's end, because the labourer is poor and sets his heart upon it. Employers today owe the same promptness, whatever the pay period's form.
Purpose: Deuteronomy states the ground: the laborer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15); James warns withheld wages cry out (James 5:4). Here that ground requires paying wages on time.

Command: Do not oppress a hired servant
Summary: Do not oppress a hired servant, whether he is a brother or a stranger within your gates: the labourer must not be squeezed by his employer.
Commandment: Do not oppress a hired servant.
Application: Oppression of a hired servant takes many forms — withheld pay, crushing hours, threats — and the Law forbids them all together. The labourer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15), and James warns that withheld wages cry out (James 5:4).
Purpose: Deuteronomy states the ground: the laborer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15); James warns withheld wages cry out (James 5:4). Here that ground forbids oppressing a hired servant.

Command: Do not keep a hired servant's wages overnight
Summary: The wages of a hired servant must not remain with the employer all night until morning; the day's pay is paid on the day.
Commandment: Do not keep a hired servant's wages overnight.
Application: A day labourer lives on the day's wage: keeping it overnight is keeping his supper and his family's bread. Prompt pay is not generosity but justice, and delayed pay is a quiet form of oppression.
Purpose: Deuteronomy states the ground: the laborer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15); James warns withheld wages cry out (James 5:4). Here that ground forbids keeping wages overnight.

Command: Judge your neighbour righteously
Summary: Judge your neighbour in righteousness: the verdict follows the truth of the cause, not the standing of the parties.
Commandment: Judge your neighbour righteously.
Application: Righteous judgment is the positive side of impartiality — not merely refusing bribes and favour, but actively weighing the cause aright. A righteous verdict is the aim; impartiality is the guardrail that gets the judge there.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: righteous judgment weighs the cause itself, with neither fear nor favour toward the parties.

Command: Do not show partiality in judgment
Summary: In judgment, do not respect persons: neither the great nor the small may bend the verdict by who they are.
Commandment: Do not show partiality in judgment.
Application: Partiality is the judge's besetting sin, and it wears two faces — deference to the great and pity for the small. Both are forbidden, because judgment belongs to God, who is no respecter of persons.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: judgment is God's, and he shows no partiality; a judge who respects persons has taken God's seat for his own favour.

Command: Reprove your neighbour rather than bearing sin for him
Summary: One of the neighbour-laws of Leviticus 19:17-18: reprove your neighbour rather than bearing sin for him, part of the passage that ends in 'thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.'
Commandment: Reprove your neighbour rather than bearing sin for him
Application: Jesus joins this neighbour rule to love of God as the hinge of the Law (Matthew 22:39-40); love of neighbour is the measure of love of God in practice.
Purpose: Leviticus 19:18 states the neighbor rule; Jesus joins it to love of God as the hinge of the Law (Matthew 22:39-40).

Command: Do not curse the deaf
Summary: One half of the Leviticus 19:14 pair: do not curse the deaf. The verse forbids cruelty that its victim cannot detect or avoid.
Commandment: Do not curse the deaf
Application: Scripture's ground is the fear of God: he sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see. The same duty covers every advantage taken over someone who cannot defend themselves.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: but shalt fear thy God (Leviticus 19:14) — God sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see.

Command: Do not put a stumbling block before the blind
Summary: One half of the Leviticus 19:14 pair: do not put a stumbling block before the blind. The verse forbids cruelty that its victim cannot detect or avoid.
Commandment: Do not put a stumbling block before the blind
Application: Scripture's ground is the fear of God: he sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see. The same duty covers every advantage taken over someone who cannot defend themselves.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: but shalt fear thy God (Leviticus 19:14) — God sees what the deaf cannot hear and the blind cannot see.

Command: Love the stranger as yourself
Summary: Leviticus 19:34 extends neighbour-love to the stranger dwelling among Israel: 'thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.' Israel's own memory of Egypt is the ground of the duty.
Commandment: Love the stranger who dwells with you as yourself.
Application: The church hears the same ground: those who were once strangers and aliens have been brought near (Ephesians 2:19), and love for the stranger is neighbour-love in its widest honest form.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt (Leviticus 19:34).

Command: Use just balances, weights and measures
Summary: Keep just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin: every measure used in trade must be true.
Commandment: Use just balances, weights and measures.
Application: The positive form of honest trade: the merchant's measures are themselves just, not merely free of proven fraud. Honest measures still mark honest trade today, wherever goods are weighed, counted, or priced.
Purpose: Proverbs states the reason as God's own delight and abomination: a false balance is an abomination, but a just weight is his delight (Proverbs 11:1).

Command: Do not use false weights or measures
Summary: Scales, weights, and measures in trade must be true: no false balance, no double standard, one weight for buying and another for selling.
Commandment: Do not use false weights or measures.
Application: Fraud in trade is theft disguised as business, and the false balance is its oldest instrument. A just weight is God's delight precisely because the marketplace runs on trust, and a rigged measure steals from every customer who cannot check it.
Purpose: Proverbs states the reason as God's own delight and abomination: a false balance is an abomination, but a just weight is his delight (Proverbs 11:1).

Command: Do not keep diverse weights in your bag
Summary: You shall not have in your bag diverse weights, a great and a small: one standard for buying and one for selling is fraud.
Commandment: Do not keep diverse weights in your bag.
Application: Diverse weights are fraud kept ready: the heavy weight for buying, the light for selling, carried together in the same bag. The ban strikes at the instrument of fraud, not only at its use — the merchant must not even keep the means of cheating.
Purpose: Proverbs states the reason as God's own delight and abomination: a false balance is an abomination, but a just weight is his delight (Proverbs 11:1). Here that reason forbids even keeping diverse weights.

Command: Do not round the corners of your head
Summary: One of the appearance laws of Leviticus 19:27: do not round the corners of your head.
Commandment: Do not round the corners of your head
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the corners marked Israel's consecration and separated its mourning and appearance from neighbouring pagan customs. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the corners marked Israel's consecration and separated its mourning and appearance from neighbouring pagan customs. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Leviticus 19:27).

Command: Do not make cuttings for the dead
Summary: One of the mourning marks forbidden in Leviticus 19:28: do not make cuttings for the dead.
Commandment: Do not make cuttings for the dead
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: cuttings and marks were the visible rites of pagan mourning and idolatrous devotion; Israel's grief was not to take those forms. Debated: whether the prohibition covers all permanent marks today, or only marks made for the dead and for idolatry, is a genuine difference of reading — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: cuttings and marks were the visible rites of pagan mourning and idolatrous devotion; Israel's grief was not to take those forms. Scripture states the prohibition with the qualifier 'for the dead' (Leviticus 19:28).

Command: Do not breed cattle with a diverse kind
Summary: One of the mixture laws of Leviticus 19:19: do not breed cattle with a diverse kind. Scripture states the prohibition without a stated reason.
Commandment: Do not breed cattle with a diverse kind
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the mixture law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason Scripture does not state; the priestly garments, which mixed materials by God's own command (Exodus 28), are the noted exception.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture; the mixture law is classed among the chukim. The one scriptural exception noted by tradition is the priestly garments themselves, which mixed materials by God's own command (Exodus 28).

Command: Do not sow your field with mixed seed
Summary: Do not sow your field with mingled seed, nor your vineyard with divers seeds: each kind is sown by itself.
Commandment: Do not sow your field with mixed seed.
Application: The agricultural mixture law draws a boundary in the field itself: kinds are kept distinct in sowing. These are chukim — statutes whose reason Scripture does not explain, and which tradition has long read as teaching that God may set boundaries whose wisdom is his own.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture; the law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason is not given. Deuteronomy 22:9 adds a consequence — the fruit is forfeited — but not a reason.

Command: Do not wear a garment of mixed wool and linen
Summary: One of the mixture laws of Leviticus 19:19: do not wear a garment of mixed wool and linen. Scripture states the prohibition without a stated reason.
Commandment: Do not wear a garment of mixed wool and linen
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the mixture law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason Scripture does not state; the priestly garments, which mixed materials by God's own command (Exodus 28), are the noted exception.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture; the mixture law is classed among the chukim. The one scriptural exception noted by tradition is the priestly garments themselves, which mixed materials by God's own command (Exodus 28).

Command: A man shall not wear a woman's garment
Summary: One half of the Deuteronomy 22:5 distinction: a man shall not wear a woman's garment.
Commandment: A man shall not wear a woman's garment
Application: Scripture's stated ground: for all that do so are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 22:5). Debated: whether the verse binds specific garments today or the broader distinction it expresses is a genuine difference of reading — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: for all that do so are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 22:5).

Command: Send away the mother bird before taking the young
Summary: One half of the mother-bird law of Deuteronomy 22:6-7: send away the mother bird before taking the young. Even in taking from nature, mercy was to limit what could be taken.
Commandment: Send away the mother bird before taking the young
Application: Scripture's stated reason, in the form of a promise: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days (Deuteronomy 22:7). Mercy to the creature is joined to blessing on the keeper.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason, in the form of a promise: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days (Deuteronomy 22:7).

Command: Do not take a widow's garment in pledge
Summary: Do not take a widow's garment in pledge: her raiment is not security for a loan.
Commandment: Do not take a widow's garment in pledge.
Application: A widow's garment is her warmth and her dignity, and the Law removes it entirely from the creditor's reach — not merely to be returned by sunset, but never to be taken at all. The defenceless are protected by prohibition, not only by procedure.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care forbids taking a widow's garment in pledge.

Command: Do not enter a debtor's house to take his pledge
Summary: When you lend your brother anything, you shall not go into his house to fetch his pledge: you stand outside, and he brings the pledge out to you.
Commandment: Do not enter a debtor's house to take his pledge.
Application: Dignity is part of justice: the lender may not invade the borrower's house to seize the pledge. The threshold is a boundary the creditor does not cross, however good his claim.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee (Deuteronomy 24:13). Here that dignity forbids entering the debtor's house for the pledge.

Command: Return the pledge by sunset
Summary: In any case, you shall deliver the pledge again by sunset, that the debtor may sleep in his own raiment and bless you.
Commandment: Return the pledge by sunset.
Application: Sunset is the deadline mercy sets: the pledge returns before night, so the borrower sleeps warm and the lender's righteousness is counted before the LORD. The procedure belonged to Israel's civil law; the dignity it protects is the same mercy that still binds a creditor today.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee (Deuteronomy 24:13).

Command: Offer a burnt offering as prescribed
Summary: The command: Offer a burnt offering as prescribed (Leviticus 1:3). The burnt offering, wholly consumed on the altar, was offered of the herd, the flock, or fowl, as Leviticus 1 prescribes.
Commandment: Offer a burnt offering as prescribed, as prescribed in Leviticus 1:3.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Commandment: Do not offer a blemished animal.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: it shall not be accepted for you (Leviticus 22:21).

Command: Do not offer an animal under eight days old
Summary: The command: Do not offer an animal under eight days old (Leviticus 22:27). A bullock, sheep, or goat had to remain seven days with its dam and might be offered only from the eighth day.

Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the newborn remained seven days with its dam before it could be given, honouring the natural order God made.

Summary: A man with a running issue counts seven days for his cleansing after the discharge stops, washes his clothes, bathes in running water, and on the eighth day brings two turtledoves or pigeons to the priest.
Commandment: A man with a discharge shall count seven days for cleansing, wash, bathe, and bring his offering on the eighth day.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The counting and washing gave the unclean man a definite road back to worship. Jesus' touch restored those the purity laws isolated (Luke 8:43-48).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Burn the red heifer and use its ashes for purification
Summary: A red heifer without spot or blemish, never yoked, is slaughtered and burned outside the camp with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet, and its ashes are kept for the water of purification.
Commandment: Burn a red heifer without spot or blemish, never yoked, outside the camp, and keep its ashes for the water of purification.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews makes the contrast explicit: if the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ purge the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the ashes are for a purification for sin — the water of separation (Numbers 19:9). No further reason is given; tradition classes it among the chukim, statutes whose reason is not explained.

Command: Prepare and sprinkle the water of purification
Summary: Ashes of the red heifer are put in a vessel with running water, and a clean man sprinkles the water of purification on the unclean person on the third and seventh days.
Commandment: Prepare the water of purification from the heifer's ashes and running water, and sprinkle it on the unclean on the third and seventh days.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews makes the contrast explicit: if the ashes of an heifer sprinkling the unclean sanctified to the purifying of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ purge the conscience (Hebrews 9:13-14).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the ashes are for a purification for sin — the water of separation (Numbers 19:9). No further reason is given; tradition classes it among the chukim, statutes whose reason is not explained.

Command: Immerse in water for purification from impurity
Summary: One made unclean by an emission shall wash all his flesh in water and be unclean until the evening, when washing restores him.
Commandment: He that is unclean by an emission shall wash all his flesh in water and be unclean until the even.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The evening washing marked the boundary of a day's uncleanness: water and sunset together restored the person. Jesus' touch restored those the purity laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Do not enter the sanctuary while unclean
Summary: Israel must keep separate from uncleanness when approaching the sanctuary, so that the unclean do not defile God's tabernacle among them.
Commandment: Do not come near the sanctuary while unclean, lest you defile God's tabernacle.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The warning guarded the holy place from defilement and taught Israel that approach to God required cleansing. Jesus' touch restored those the purity laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: A Nazirite shall not drink wine or strong drink
Summary: Throughout the vow, the Nazirite drinks no wine or strong drink, and takes no vinegar of wine or of strong drink.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall drink no wine or strong drink for all the days of his separation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration.

Command: A Nazirite shall not eat grapes
Summary: Throughout the vow, the Nazirite eats no grapes, moist or dried, and nothing made of the vine.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall eat no grapes, moist or dried, for all the days of his separation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, extended to the whole fruit of the vine.

Command: A Nazirite shall not eat grape kernels
Summary: Throughout the vow, the Nazirite eats nothing of the vine, not even the kernels or husks of grapes.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall eat no grape kernels or husks for all the days of his separation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, extended even to kernels and husks.

Command: A Nazirite shall not cut his hair
Summary: Throughout the vow, no razor comes upon the Nazirite's head; the locks of his hair grow until the days of separation are fulfilled.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall let no razor come upon his head for all the days of his separation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — hair uncut as the visible sign of the vow.

Command: A Nazirite shall not defile himself for the dead
Summary: Throughout the vow, the Nazirite comes at no dead body, not even for father, mother, brother, or sister, lest his consecration be defiled.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall not come at any dead body for all the days of his separation.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — corpse-avoidance as the priest-like holiness of the vow.

Command: A Nazirite shall shave and bring offerings when the vow ends
Summary: When the days of the Nazirite vow are fulfilled, the Nazirite shaves the head of his separation at the door of the tabernacle and brings a burnt offering, a sin offering, and a peace offering.
Commandment: When the vow is fulfilled, the Nazirite shall shave his head at the door of the tabernacle and bring the offerings of completion.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Acts 21:23-26 shows Paul joining men under a vow in Jerusalem, which shows the practice continued among Jewish believers, not that it is imposed on Christians.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, hair uncut as the visible sign, and corpse-avoidance as the priest-like holiness of the vow; the closing shaving and offerings return the separated one to ordinary life.

Command: Do not eat animals that do not chew the cud or lack split hooves
Summary: A land animal is clean only if it both chews the cud and divides the hoof; an animal lacking either sign is unclean and may not be eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat any land animal that does not both chew the cud and divide the hoof.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The two-sign test gave Israel a plain rule for the herds and wild animals. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Do not eat fish without fins and scales
Summary: Water creatures without fins and scales are unclean and may not be eaten; only fish with both fins and scales are clean.
Commandment: Do not eat any water creature that lacks fins and scales.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The fins-and-scales test gave Israel a plain rule for the waters. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Do not eat unclean birds
Summary: The birds listed in Leviticus 11 — birds of prey and scavengers such as the eagle, vulture, raven, and owl — are unclean and may not be eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat the unclean birds listed in Leviticus 11.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The list names carrion and predatory birds as unclean. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Do not eat creeping things
Summary: Creeping things that creep upon the earth — worms, snails, moles, and the like — are unclean and may not be eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat any creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The creeping kinds were wholly excluded from Israel's table. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Do not eat an animal found dead
Summary: An animal that dies of itself, not slaughtered, may not be eaten by Israel; it may be given to the stranger, but Israel, as a holy people, shall not eat it.
Commandment: Do not eat any animal found dead of itself.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule kept Israel from eating carrion, whose blood was not properly shed and whose death was unwitnessed. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Slaughter animals for food as prescribed
Summary: Animals slaughtered for food away from the sanctuary must be killed as the LORD commanded, so that ordinary meat-eating stays within God's order.
Commandment: Slaughter animals for food as the LORD has commanded, when you eat meat away from the sanctuary.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Deuteronomy 12 allowed slaughter at home in the land, once Israel lived too far from the sanctuary for every meal to come from it — freedom within God's prescribed order, not lawlessness.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the prescribed slaughter kept even ordinary meat-eating holy and distinct, with the blood duly dealt with (Deuteronomy 12:23-24).

Command: Cover the blood of a slaughtered beast or bird
Summary: When a beast or bird that may be eaten is hunted and killed, its blood must be poured out and covered with dust.
Commandment: When you hunt a beast or bird that may be eaten, pour out its blood and cover it with dust.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Covering the blood honored the life it carried, even outside the sanctuary: the blood was not treated as common. The life-in-the-blood principle is repeated at Jerusalem for Gentile believers (Acts 15:29).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the life of all flesh is the blood thereof (Leviticus 17:14).

Command: Do not eat flesh torn by beasts
Summary: Flesh torn by beasts in the field may not be eaten; as holy men, Israel shall cast it to the dogs instead.
Commandment: Do not eat flesh torn of beasts in the field; cast it to the dogs.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule kept Israel from eating an animal killed and mauled rather than slaughtered, and it is classed here with the food laws rather than with the civil restitution laws of its parent row. The New Testament records the food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: ye shall be holy men unto me, and shall not eat flesh torn of beasts (Exodus 22:31).

Command: Do not uncover the nakedness of your mother
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not uncover the nakedness of your mother. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not uncover the nakedness of your mother
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Know that God is one
Summary: Deuteronomy 6:4 declares the Shema's foundation: 'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD.' The oneness of God is the ground of the whole-person love that follows.
Commandment: Know that the LORD our God is one LORD.
Application: Jesus quotes this as the first and greatest commandment's ground, joining it to love of neighbour as the summary of the whole Law and the Prophets (Mark 12:29-31).

Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The booths turned memory into dwelling: for a week each year Israel lived again as the wilderness generation lived. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Take the four species on Tabernacles
Summary: On the first day of Tabernacles, Israel takes the fruit of goodly trees, palm branches, boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook, and rejoices before the LORD.
Commandment: On the first day of Tabernacles, take the four species — goodly fruit, palm branches, thick boughs, and brook willows — and rejoice before the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The branches in hand made the harvest joy visible and tangible through the feast week. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Count fifty days from the sheaf offering
Summary: From the day the sheaf is waved, Israel counts seven Sabbaths complete — fifty days — to the Feast of Weeks.
Commandment: Count from the morrow after the Sabbath, from the day the sheaf is waved, seven Sabbaths complete, even fifty days.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The counting bound Weeks to Firstfruits and made the harvest season one long act of thanksgiving. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Wave the sheaf of firstfruits
Summary: On the day after the Sabbath in Passover week, the priest waves a sheaf of the firstfruits of the harvest before the LORD, and Israel's harvest may then be eaten.
Commandment: On the morrow after the Sabbath, wave the sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest before the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The waved sheaf gave the whole harvest to God first. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20). Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Offer two loaves of new grain on Weeks
Summary: On the Feast of Weeks, two wave loaves baked with leaven from the new grain are offered as firstfruits to the LORD.
Commandment: On the Feast of Weeks, offer two wave loaves of fine flour baked with leaven, the firstfruits unto the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The leavened loaves are the feast's one exception: the harvest offering itself, unlike the Passover bread, could be leavened. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: To rehearse God's saving acts at appointed seasons (Leviticus 23); Paul calls Christ our Passover (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Command: Offer the Passover festival offerings
Summary: During the seven days of Unleavened Bread, the appointed burnt offerings are brought each day as the festival offering of Passover.
Commandment: Offer the appointed burnt offerings of the Passover festival each day of Unleavened Bread.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Offer the Weeks festival offerings
Summary: On the Feast of Weeks, the appointed burnt offerings, grain offering, and sin offering are brought as the festival offering.
Commandment: Offer the appointed offerings of the Feast of Weeks.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Offer the Trumpets festival offerings
Summary: On the Day of Trumpets, the appointed burnt offerings and sin offering are brought in addition to the monthly offering.

Command: Offer the Atonement festival offerings
Summary: On the Day of Atonement, the appointed burnt offerings and sin offering are brought in addition to the sin offering of atonement.
Commandment: Offer the appointed offerings of the Day of Atonement.

Command: Offer the Tabernacles festival offerings
Summary: During the seven days of Tabernacles, the appointed burnt offerings are brought each day, decreasing in number through the week, with a sin offering daily.
Commandment: Offer the appointed offerings of the Feast of Tabernacles each day of the feast.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
