Command: Appear before the LORD three times a year
Summary: Three times a year — at Unleavened Bread, at Weeks, and at Tabernacles — every male in Israel appears before the LORD in the place he chooses.
Commandment: Three times in a year shall all your males appear before the LORD your God in the place which he shall choose.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The thrice-yearly pilgrimage gathered the whole nation to one sanctuary and one calendar, so no tribe kept its own feasts alone.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the pilgrimage feasts gather Israel to the one place God chooses (Deuteronomy 16:16).

Command: Do not appear before the LORD empty-handed
Summary: No one appears before the LORD at the pilgrimage feasts empty-handed; every man gives as he is able, according to the blessing God has given him.
Commandment: Do not appear before the LORD empty; every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The gift measured gratitude, not wealth: each gave as he was able, according to the blessing he had received.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: giving at the feasts answers the blessing God has given (Deuteronomy 16:17).

Command: Do not offer Passover blood with leaven
Summary: The blood of the Passover sacrifice may not be offered while leaven is present; the sacrifice and leaven do not mix.
Commandment: Do not offer the blood of the Passover sacrifice with leavened bread.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule joins the Passover sacrifice to the unleavened-bread memorial: deliverance and the removal of leaven go together.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not leave the Passover fat until morning
Summary: The fat of the Passover sacrifice may not be left until morning; the sacrifice must be completed within its appointed time.
Commandment: Do not leave the fat of the Passover sacrifice until the morning.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Like the flesh, the fat belonged to the night's offering and could not be left over to the next day.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the sacrifice is offered at its appointed season, and its parts are dealt with within that time (Exodus 23:18).

Command: Do not boil a kid in its mother's milk
Summary: A kid may not be boiled in its own mother's milk; the young animal and the milk that nourished it must not be mixed in the pot.
Commandment: Do not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The threefold form — not to cook, not to eat, not to benefit — closes every use of the mixture. The New Testament records the food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the prohibition keeps what gives life (milk) from being mixed with what takes life (meat) in cooking and eating, and keeps Israel's table distinct; Scripture states no reason for this rule.

Command: Let the land rest in the sabbatical year
Summary: The land itself keeps a sabbath in the seventh year: a sabbath of rest unto the LORD, in which the ground is not worked as in other years.
Commandment: Let the land rest in the sabbatical year.
Application: The land's sabbath mirrors the people's: one year in seven, work stops and the ground rests. The calendar system belonged to Israel's land order, but the pattern — rest built into the rhythm of labour — still instructs any people tempted to work without ceasing.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the sabbatical year, that purpose takes the form of the land itself resting.

Command: Do not sow in the sabbatical year
Summary: In the seventh year the field is not sown: the land rests through the sabbatical year.
Commandment: Do not sow in the sabbatical year.
Application: An unsown year is a year of trust: no seed goes in, yet the people are promised enough from the sixth year's harvest and the land's own growth. The command makes dependence on God a matter of farming practice, not only of prayer.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the sabbatical year, that purpose takes the form of an unsown field.

Command: Do not reap the aftergrowth in the sabbatical year
Summary: In the sabbatical year, the aftergrowth — what grows of itself — is not to be reaped as a harvest.
Commandment: Do not reap the aftergrowth in the sabbatical year.
Application: Aftergrowth in the sabbatical year is free food, not a crop: it may be eaten by the household, the servant, the stranger, and the beasts, but not reaped as a harvest. The distinction between eating and harvesting protects the year's rest.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the sabbatical year, that purpose takes the form of leaving the aftergrowth unreaped.

Command: Do not gather grapes of the untrimmed vine in the sabbatical year
Summary: In the sabbatical year, the grapes of the untrimmed vine are not to be gathered as a harvest.
Commandment: Do not gather grapes of the untrimmed vine in the sabbatical year.
Application: As in Jubilee, the sabbatical vine is left untrimmed and its fruit unharvested: the year's growth is free for the poor and the beasts, not gathered as a crop. The mirror between sabbatical and Jubilee rules guards both years' character as release.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the sabbatical year, that purpose takes the form of leaving the untrimmed vine ungathered.

Command: Release debts in the sabbatical year
Summary: Every seventh year is a year of release: the LORD's release is proclaimed, and debts among brothers are released.
Commandment: Release debts in the sabbatical year.
Application: The sabbatical release stopped debt from becoming a life sentence: every seven years the slate among brothers was wiped. The calendar system belonged to Israel's land order, but the warning against permanent debt still speaks to any age of easy credit.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of debts released every seventh year.

Command: Do not demand payment of a released debt
Summary: In the sabbatical year of release, a creditor must not demand payment of a debt from his neighbour or brother whose debt has been released.
Commandment: Do not demand payment of a released debt.
Application: Release means release: once the sabbatical year has cancelled the debt, pursuing it again undoes the year's mercy. The creditor's loss is real, and the Law asks him to bear it as his share of the community's reset.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of debts no longer demanded once released.

Command: Sanctify the fiftieth year as Jubilee
Summary: The fiftieth year is sanctified as Jubilee: liberty is proclaimed throughout the land, and each man returns to his possession and his family.
Commandment: Sanctify the fiftieth year as Jubilee.
Application: Jubilee was the great reset: after seven sabbaths of years, land returned and debts of bondage ended. Jesus takes up Jubilee language for his mission (Luke 4:18-19), but the calendar system belonged to Israel's land order and is not reinstated as law.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Jesus takes up Jubilee language for his mission (Luke 4:18-19), but the calendar system belonged to Israel's land order and is not reinstated as law.

Command: Sound the shofar on the Day of Atonement of the Jubilee year
Summary: On the Day of Atonement in the Jubilee year, the trumpet of the jubilee is sounded throughout the land, proclaiming liberty.
Commandment: Sound the shofar on the Day of Atonement of the Jubilee year.
Application: Atonement and release sound together: on the day Israel's sins are covered, the trumpet proclaims liberty to every inhabitant. The pairing teaches that release from debt and release from sin belong to the same God of mercy.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). The shofar on the Day of Atonement proclaims that liberty publicly, throughout the land.

Command: Return every man to his possession in the Jubilee
Summary: In the Jubilee, every man returns to his possession: land sold under pressure reverts to its family, and the family's footing in the land is restored.
Commandment: Return every man to his possession in the Jubilee.
Application: No family's loss was final. Jubilee capped the damage of debt and bad years by restoring the land itself — the one asset a farming family could not do without. The calendar system has ended, but the warning against permanent destitution still speaks.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the Jubilee, that purpose takes the form of every man returning to his possession.

Command: Do not sow in the Jubilee year
Summary: In the Jubilee year the field is not sown: the land rests, as in the sabbatical year, and the people live on what it gives of itself.
Commandment: Do not sow in the Jubilee year.
Application: Two fallow years could run together — sabbatical and Jubilee — and the people were promised provision enough to carry them (Leviticus 25:20-22). The command tests trust: release is practised, not merely proclaimed.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the Jubilee year, that purpose takes the form of an unsown field.

Command: Do not reap the aftergrowth in the Jubilee year
Summary: In the Jubilee year, the aftergrowth — what springs up of itself without sowing — is not to be reaped as a crop.
Commandment: Do not reap the aftergrowth in the Jubilee year.
Application: Aftergrowth is the land's own gift, not the farmer's crop, and in Jubilee it stays free for whoever needs it. Reaping it as a harvest would turn release back into ordinary farming.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the Jubilee year, that purpose takes the form of leaving the aftergrowth unreaped.

Command: Do not gather grapes of the untrimmed vine in the Jubilee year
Summary: In the Jubilee year, the grapes of the untrimmed vine are not to be gathered as a harvest.
Commandment: Do not gather grapes of the untrimmed vine in the Jubilee year.
Application: Jubilee, like the sabbatical year, leaves the vine untrimmed and its fruit unharvested: the year's produce is free, not farmed. The prohibition guards the year's character as release rather than ordinary agriculture.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the Jubilee year, that purpose takes the form of leaving the untrimmed vine ungathered.

Command: A kinsman shall redeem sold land
Summary: If a brother sells part of his possession and becomes poor, his kinsman — the redeemer — comes and redeems what his brother sold.
Commandment: A kinsman shall redeem sold land.
Application: Redemption is family responsibility in action: the kinsman buys back the land so the family keeps its footing. Boaz's redemption of Naomi's land (Ruth 4) is the picture of this law lived out, and the greater Redeemer it foreshadows is its deepest meaning.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of the kinsman-redeemer restoring sold land.

Command: Redeem a house in a walled city within a year
Summary: A house sold in a walled city may be redeemed within a whole year after it is sold; after the year, if unredeemed, it passes to the buyer permanently.
Commandment: Redeem a house in a walled city within a year.
Application: City houses followed a different rule from country land: the one-year window balanced the seller's chance to recover against the buyer's need for certainty. The distinction shows the Law's care for the different economics of town and country.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). For walled-city houses, that purpose takes the form of a one-year redemption window.

Command: Levite houses are always redeemable
Summary: The houses of the Levites in their cities are always redeemable, and return in the Jubilee: the tribe without a land inheritance kept its homes secure.
Commandment: Levite houses are always redeemable.
Application: The Levites had no tribal territory, so their city houses were their footing — and the Law protected them more strongly than other houses. A tribe set apart for God's service was not to be left homeless by the market.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). For the Levites, who had no tribal land, that purpose takes the form of houses always redeemable.

Command: Do not sell Levite pastureland
Summary: The field of the suburbs of the Levite cities — their pastureland — must not be sold, for it is their perpetual possession.
Commandment: Do not sell Levite pastureland.
Application: Levite pastureland was common land for the cities' flocks, and its sale would have stripped the Levites' towns of their livelihood. The ban keeps a permanent possession permanent.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). For Levite cities, that purpose takes the form of pastureland that may never be sold.

Command: Give the Levites cities to dwell in
Summary: The children of Israel give to the Levites, from their inheritance, cities to dwell in, with suburbs for their cattle.
Commandment: Give the Levites cities to dwell in.
Application: The tribe without a land inheritance received cities instead: forty-eight cities scattered through the tribes, so that Levites lived among all Israel rather than apart from it. The arrangement belonged to Israel's tribal land system.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the Levites, who had no tribal territory, were provided for by cities throughout the tribes, so that ministry lived among the people rather than apart from them.

Command: Give the great heave offering to the priests
Summary: The command: Give the great heave offering to the priests (Numbers 18:8). The heave offerings of Israel, the best of oil, wine, wheat, and firstfruits, belonged to Aaron and his sons.
Commandment: Give the great heave offering to the priests, as prescribed in Numbers 18:8.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the heave offerings were the priests' portion for their service at the altar (Numbers 18:8-19).

Command: Bring the firstfruits to the house of the LORD
Summary: The command: Bring the firstfruits to the house of the LORD (Exodus 23:19). The first of the firstfruits of the land was brought into the house of the LORD, with the confession of deliverance in Deuteronomy 26.
Commandment: Bring the firstfruits to the house of the LORD, as prescribed in Exodus 23:19.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament keeps the principle in a new key: Christ is the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20), and Christians are urged to give first and cheerfully, not by the old basket rite (2 Corinthians 9:7). The rite belongs to the land and the sanctuary; the first-giving heart it taught does not expire with it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the confession itself gives the reason — 'a Syrian ready to perish was my father,' and God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them this land (Deuteronomy 26:5-10).

Command: Recite the firstfruits confession
Summary: The command: Recite the firstfruits confession (Deuteronomy 26:5). Bringing the basket of firstfruits, Israel confessed: a Syrian ready to perish was my father, and the LORD brought us out of Egypt into this land.

Command: Give the foreleg, cheeks, and maw to the priest
Summary: The command: Give the foreleg, cheeks, and maw to the priest (Deuteronomy 18:3). From every animal slaughtered for food, the shoulder, the two cheeks, and the maw belonged to the priest.
Commandment: Give the foreleg, cheeks, and maw to the priest, as prescribed in Deuteronomy 18:3.

Command: Give the first of your dough as an offering
Summary: The command: Give the first of your dough as an offering (Numbers 15:20). The first of the dough was lifted up as a heave offering to the LORD, as the firstfruits of the threshingfloor.
Commandment: Give the first of your dough as an offering, as prescribed in Numbers 15:20.

Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: as the firstfruits of the threshingfloor, so the first of the dough was lifted up to the LORD (Numbers 15:20).

Command: Give a tithe of the herd and flock
Summary: The command: Give a tithe of the herd and flock (Leviticus 27:32). Every tenth animal passing under the rod belonged to the LORD as a tithe of herd and flock.
Commandment: Give a tithe of the herd and flock, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:32.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament shifts the frame from a fixed percentage to cheerful, generous giving — God loves a cheerful giver — while keeping the duty to support ministry and the poor. Debated: some hold the fixed tenth continues as the giving standard; others hold the New Testament replaces the percentage with cheerful, generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7) while keeping support for ministry and the poor.
Purpose: To support the Levites, the poor, and worship (Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 14). Debated: some hold the fixed tenth continues as the giving standard; others hold the New Testament replaces the percentage with cheerful, generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7) while keeping support for ministry and the poor. Summary: The command: Do not eat the firstborn outside Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:17). The firstling, the tithe, and the heave offering were to be eaten before the LORD in the place he chose, not in one's own gates.
Commandment: Do not eat the firstborn outside Jerusalem.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: holy things were eaten before the LORD in the place he chose, not in one's own gates (Deuteronomy 12:17-18).

Command: Do not eat vow and freewill offerings outside Jerusalem
Summary: The command: Do not eat vow and freewill offerings outside Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:17). Vows and freewill offerings were brought to the place God chose and eaten there, not wherever one pleased.
Commandment: Do not eat vow and freewill offerings outside Jerusalem.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: vows and freewill offerings were brought to the place the LORD chose (Deuteronomy 12:17-18).

Command: Do not eat the heave offering outside Jerusalem
Summary: The command: Do not eat the heave offering outside Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:17). Heave offerings belonged to the place God chose and might not be eaten in one's own towns.
Commandment: Do not eat the heave offering outside Jerusalem.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the heave offering was eaten before the LORD in the place he chose (Deuteronomy 12:17-18).

Command: Do not delay giving firstfruits
Summary: The command: Do not delay giving firstfruits (Exodus 22:29). The first of the harvest was not to be held back while other produce was enjoyed.
Commandment: Do not delay giving firstfruits.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Zacchaeus shows the spirit of restitution alive in the gospel: he repaid fourfold those he had defrauded. Justice restores, not merely punishes.
Purpose: The enduring duty behind this row is prompt giving: firstfruits were not to be held back. The firstfruits rite itself belonged to the land-and-temple system, while prompt, first-giving generosity endures.

Command: Do not work the firstborn ox
Summary: The command: Do not work the firstborn ox (Deuteronomy 15:19). The firstling ox might not be put to work, since it was sanctified to the LORD.
Commandment: Do not work the firstborn ox.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the firstling was sanctified unto the LORD and might not be put to common work (Deuteronomy 15:19).

Command: Recite the tithe confession
Summary: The command: Recite the tithe confession (Deuteronomy 26:13). After giving the third-year tithe, Israel confessed before the LORD that the hallowed things had been brought out of the house and given as commanded.
Commandment: Recite the tithe confession, as prescribed in Deuteronomy 26:13.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the confession made giving public and accountable before the LORD, closing the tithe cycle with an honest declaration.

Command: Give the poor tithe in the third year
Summary: At the end of three years, the tithe of that year's increase is brought forth and laid up within the gates, for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.
Commandment: Give the poor tithe in the third year.
Application: The third-year tithe fed those without land or defender, stored within the gates where they could reach it. Views differ today on whether tithing as a fixed percentage continues or whether the New Testament's cheerful, generous giving replaces the percentage while keeping the duty to support ministry and the poor; this row states the third-year tithe in its own form.
Purpose: To support the Levites, the poor, and worship (Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 14). Debated: whether the fixed tithe continues today or whether generous giving fulfils its purpose.

Command: Leave the corners of your field for the poor
Summary: The corners of the field are left for the poor, standing unreaped for those who have no field of their own.
Commandment: Leave the corners of your field for the poor.
Application: The unreaped corner is the poor man's field within the rich man's field — a share of the harvest set aside by law, not by the owner's mood. It dignifies the gleaner, who harvests rather than begs.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the field, that care takes the form of leaving the corners for the poor.

Command: Leave gleanings of your harvest for the poor
Summary: The gleanings of the harvest are left for the poor, who may gather them from the field.
Commandment: Leave gleanings of your harvest for the poor.
Application: The positive form of the harvest gleaning law: what falls in the reaping belongs, by law, to the poor who follow the reapers. Ruth's gleaning in Boaz's field is the living picture of this law at work.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the harvest, that care takes the form of leaving the gleanings for the poor.

Command: Leave the forgotten sheaf in the field
Summary: The forgotten sheaf is left in the field for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, that the LORD may bless you in all the work of your hands.
Commandment: Leave the forgotten sheaf in the field.
Application: The positive form of the forgotten-sheaf law: what was forgotten is deliberately left, and the blessing is tied to the leaving. Provision for the defenceless is built into the harvest's accidents, not only its plans.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care takes the form of leaving the forgotten sheaf for the defenceless.

Command: Leave grape gleanings for the poor and stranger
Summary: The gleanings of the vineyard are left for the poor and the stranger, who may gather them for themselves.
Commandment: Leave grape gleanings for the poor and stranger.
Application: The positive form of the gleaning law: the vineyard's remainder is not waste but provision, deliberately left where the landless can gather it with dignity, by their own hands.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the vineyard, that care takes the form of leaving the gleanings for the poor and stranger.

Command: Open your hand to your poor brother
Summary: To a poor brother you shall open your hand wide, and surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wants.
Commandment: Open your hand to your poor brother.
Application: Open-handed lending is measured by the need, not by the lender's comfort: 'sufficient for his need' is the standard. The sabbatical setting does not confine the duty — generous help for a brother in need endures in any age.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of an open hand, sufficient for the brother's need.

Command: Do not harden your heart toward your poor brother
Summary: When a poor brother is among you, do not harden your heart or shut your hand against him.
Commandment: Do not harden your heart toward your poor brother.
Application: Hardness of heart is the inward root of every refusal to help: the Law forbids the closing itself, not only the closed hand. Generosity begins before the purse opens, in a heart that stays soft toward a brother's need.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of a heart not hardened toward a poor brother.

Command: Support a poor brother or stranger living with you
Summary: If a brother or a stranger living with you becomes poor and falls into decay, you shall relieve him, that he may live with you.
Commandment: Support a poor brother or stranger living with you.
Application: Relief here is personal and practical: the poor man is kept living beside you, not shipped elsewhere or left to sink. The duty to sustain a needy neighbour outlives the land system it was first given in — it is pure religion in any age (James 1:27).
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care takes the form of relieving a poor brother or stranger so he may live with you.

Command: Give a half-shekel as atonement money
Summary: The command: Give a half-shekel as atonement money (Exodus 30:13). Every numbered Israelite, rich and poor alike, gave half a shekel as atonement money for the service of the tabernacle.
Commandment: Give a half-shekel as atonement money, as prescribed in Exodus 30:13.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Appoint judges and officers in all your gates
Summary: In all your gates you shall appoint judges and officers, by tribe, to judge the people with just judgment.
Commandment: Appoint judges and officers in all your gates.
Application: Justice was local before it was national: every town had its judges, so that no one had to travel far or wait long for a hearing. The gate-court system belonged to Israel's polity, but the principle — justice accessible, local, and impartial — remains the measure of any court system.
Purpose: To secure impartial justice: no bribes, no partiality, no conviction on one witness. Here that purpose takes the form of judges and officers appointed in every town.

Command: Obey the ruling of the high court
Summary: When a matter is too hard for the local court, it goes up to the central court at the place God chooses, and its ruling is obeyed.
Commandment: Obey the ruling of the high court.
Application: Hard cases had a final court, so that disputes did not fester or turn to feud. The central court belonged to Israel's polity; the enduring wisdom is that hard cases need a settled, lawful resolution rather than private force.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: hard cases need a final, lawful resolution, so the central court's ruling binds — lest every dispute end in feud or private force.

Command: Do not deviate from the high court's ruling right or left
Summary: From the high court's sentence you shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left: its ruling is followed as given.
Commandment: Do not deviate from the high court's ruling right or left.
Application: Deviation, even in a direction that looks wiser, unravels a common law: if every party follows only the rulings he likes, there is no court at all. The court system belonged to Israel's polity; respect for lawful judgment, rather than picking rulings à la carte, is the lasting principle.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: a common law holds only if its final rulings are followed as given, not turned from to the right or to the left.

Command: Do not fear any man in judgment
Summary: In judgment, do not fear any man: neither the great man's face nor the small man's anger may bend the verdict, for the judgment is God's.
Commandment: Do not fear any man in judgment.
Application: Fear is partiality's quiet form: the judge who dreads a powerful litigant has already surrendered his court. 'The judgment is God's' frees the judge from every human audience — his verdict answers to God alone.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: judgment belongs to God, so fear of any man in judgment is a surrender of the court; the judge answers to God alone.

Command: Do not spread a false report
Summary: No one shall raise or spread a false report — neither inventing a lie nor carrying on a rumour he has not verified.
Commandment: Do not spread a false report.
Application: A false report wounds before it is checked, and in court it can condemn the innocent. The command binds both the inventor and the repeater: do not lend your mouth to what you do not know to be true.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: truth is the foundation of just judgment, so a false report — invented or merely repeated — corrupts justice at its root.

Command: A matter is established by two or three witnesses; one witness alone is insufficient
Summary: At the mouth of two witnesses, or three, shall a matter be established; one witness alone is insufficient to convict.
Commandment: A matter is established by two or three witnesses; one witness alone is insufficient.
Application: One voice, however confident, cannot carry a conviction: the two-witness rule guards against the single accuser, the mistaken memory, and the malicious charge. The rule carried into the church's own discipline (Matthew 18:16; 1 Timothy 5:19).
Purpose: To secure impartial justice: no bribes, no partiality, no conviction on one witness. Here that purpose takes the form of two or three witnesses establishing a matter.

Command: Judges shall make diligent inquisition of witnesses
Summary: The judges must make diligent inquisition: when a witness is accused of falsehood, the court investigates carefully before it judges.
Commandment: Judges shall make diligent inquisition of witnesses.
Application: A court that takes testimony at face value invites false witnesses to prosper. Diligent inquisition — careful, sceptical investigation — is the court's duty, and it remains the standard of any fair hearing today.
Purpose: To secure impartial justice: no bribes, no partiality, no conviction on one witness. Here that purpose takes the form of diligent inquisition before judgment.

Command: Do to a false witness as he intended to do to his brother
Summary: If a witness is found to be false, the court does to him as he intended to do to his brother: the penalty he sought becomes his own.
Commandment: Do to a false witness as he intended to do to his brother.
Application: False witness is punished by its own design: the perjurer aimed a penalty at his brother, and that penalty falls on him. The symmetry deters the gravest courtroom crime, and the deterrent principle endures even where the penalty procedure belonged to Israel's courts.
Purpose: To secure impartial justice: no bribes, no partiality, no conviction on one witness. Here that purpose takes the form of the false witness bearing the penalty he sought.

Command: Execute by stoning where the Law decrees stoning
Summary: Where the Law decrees death by stoning — as for the stubborn and rebellious son and other capital offences — the court was to carry out that sentence by stoning.
Commandment: Execute by stoning where the Law decrees stoning.
Application: Stoning is one of the four modes of execution the Law assigns to the court, and the community itself took part in it. The mode belonged to Israel's court system, which no longer functions; the offences it marked still teach the gravity of rebellion against God's order.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: each mode of execution matched the offence as the Law assigned it, so that punishment was measured rather than arbitrary.

Command: Execute by burning where the Law decrees burning
Summary: Where the Law decrees death by burning — as for a man who marries both a woman and her mother — the court was to carry out that sentence by burning.
Commandment: Execute by burning where the Law decrees burning.
Application: Burning is one of the four modes of execution the Law assigns to the court. The mode belonged to Israel's court system, which no longer functions; the offence it marked — sexual corruption within the family — still teaches how seriously the Law guarded the household.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: each mode of execution matched the offence as the Law assigned it, so that punishment was measured rather than arbitrary.

Command: Execute by the sword where the Law decrees the sword
Summary: Where the Law decrees death by the sword for a capital offence, the court was to carry out that sentence by the sword, and not by another mode of execution.
Commandment: The court shall execute by the sword where the Law decrees the sword.
Application: Capital punishment in Israel belonged to the court, never to private vengeance. The mode mattered because the sentence was the Law's, not the executioner's invention; today the life-for-life principle behind it endures as a warning about the gravity of murder, while the execution itself belonged to Israel's court system.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: each mode of execution matched the gravity and nature of the offence as the Law assigned it, so that punishment was measured rather than arbitrary.

Command: Execute by strangling where the Law decrees strangling
Summary: Where the Law decrees death by strangling — as for adultery under Leviticus 20:10 — the court was to carry out that sentence by strangling.
Commandment: Execute by strangling where the Law decrees strangling.
Application: Strangling is one of the four modes of execution the Law assigns to the court. The mode belonged to Israel's court system, which no longer functions; the gravity of the offences it marked — above all adultery — still teaches the seriousness of covenant-breaking.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: each mode of execution matched the offence as the Law assigned it, so that punishment was measured rather than arbitrary.

Command: Hang the executed on a tree and bury him the same day
Summary: When a man has committed a sin worthy of death and is put to death, and is hanged on a tree, his body is taken down and buried the same day.
Commandment: Hang the executed on a tree and bury him the same day.
Application: Hanging displayed the sentence, and same-day burial limited it: the body was not left as a lingering spectacle. The procedure belonged to Israel's court system; the dignity it guarded — even the executed are buried, not exposed — still speaks.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the sentence is displayed and then ended by burial the same day, so that punishment does not become desecration.

Command: Do not leave a hanged body on the tree overnight
Summary: The body of one hanged on a tree must not remain all night upon the tree; he is buried the same day, for he that is hanged is accursed of God, and the land must not be defiled.
Commandment: Do not leave a hanged body on the tree overnight.
Application: Overnight exposure defiled the land and degraded the dead beyond the sentence. The Law draws a line even here: punishment ends at death, and the body is given to the ground the same day.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the land must not be defiled by a body left hanging, so burial the same day ends the sentence rather than prolonging it.

Command: Flog the guilty as the court decrees
Summary: If there is a controversy and the wicked man is worthy to be beaten, the judge causes him to be beaten before his face, according to his fault, by a certain number.
Commandment: Flog the guilty as the court decrees.
Application: Flogging in Israel was a court sentence, measured by fault and administered before the judge — not a private beating. The procedure belonged to Israel's courts; the limit it embodies — punishment proportionate and bounded — is its lasting lesson. Paul received this punishment five times (2 Corinthians 11:24).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lest, if thou shouldest exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee (Deuteronomy 25:3). Here that reason bounds the flogging the court decrees.

Command: Do not exceed forty stripes in flogging
Summary: Forty stripes the judge may give him, and not exceed: forty is the cap, and the court must not go beyond it.
Commandment: Do not exceed forty stripes in flogging.
Application: The cap exists because punishment without limit becomes cruelty: even a man judged worthy of stripes must remain a brother in the court's eyes, not a degraded thing. Forty stripes is the outer bound, and the court stops there.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lest, if thou shouldest exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee (Deuteronomy 25:3).

Command: Do not strike your father or mother
Summary: A child who strikes his father or mother commits a capital offence under the Law of Moses, striking at the honour and authority God gave parents.
Commandment: Do not strike your father or mother.
Application: Honour for parents is not mere politeness; in Israel's law, violent assault on a parent was treated as an attack on God's own ordering of the family. The command still teaches that parental honour is owed in deed as well as word.
Purpose: To guard the honour and authority of parents, whose place in the family God himself established; the scaled penalties were civil detail, while the duty to honour parents is the enduring substance.

Command: Do not curse your father or mother
Summary: A child who curses his father or his mother is not to do so: the Law treats cursing a parent as a grave offence against parental honour.
Commandment: Do not curse your father or mother.
Application: Cursing is more than rudeness: it is the spoken rejection of the honour owed to parents. The death penalty belonged to Israel's court, but the prohibition itself — honour parents in word as well as deed — endures wherever the fifth commandment is honoured.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: parents bear God-given authority in the family, so cursing them strikes at the order God set; honour for parents is owed in speech as well as in deed.

Command: Restore what was taken by robbery or fraud
Summary: One who has taken by robbery, or defrauded, or kept a deposit, or found a lost thing and denied it, must restore the principal in full and add a fifth part, and bring his trespass offering.
Commandment: Restore what was taken by robbery or fraud.
Application: Restoration goes beyond return: principal plus a fifth marks the wrong, and confession before God accompanies repayment to man. Zacchaeus shows the same spirit in the gospel (Luke 19:8) — restitution is repentance made tangible.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: what was taken by robbery or fraud is restored in full, with a fifth added, because justice restores and does not merely punish.

Command: Repay five oxen for an ox stolen and slaughtered, four sheep for a sheep
Summary: A thief who steals an ox and slaughters or sells it repays five oxen for the ox; for a sheep stolen and slaughtered or sold, four sheep.
Commandment: Repay five oxen for an ox stolen and slaughtered, and four sheep for a sheep.
Application: Theft that destroys the evidence or converts it to profit costs more than theft caught with the goods in hand. Zacchaeus shows restitution alive in the gospel (Luke 19:8): justice restores, and restoration is scaled to the wrong.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: theft repaid, with a heavier scale where the stolen animal was slaughtered or sold.

Command: Repay double when stolen goods are found alive in his hand
Summary: A thief caught with the stolen ox, ass, or sheep still alive in his hand repays double.
Commandment: Repay double when stolen goods are found alive in his hand.
Application: Double repayment where the goods survive, four- or fivefold where they were slaughtered or sold: the scale tracks both the wrong and the damage. Justice restores the victim and penalises the thief in measure.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: theft repaid double where the stolen thing is found alive in the thief's hand.

Command: Do not rob your neighbour
Summary: Do not rob your neighbour: do not take his property by force or by oppression.
Commandment: Do not rob your neighbour.
Application: Robbery differs from stealthy theft by its openness, but not by its guilt: taking what is another's, whether by force or by pressure, is forbidden. The neighbour's goods are under God's protection, not the strong man's reach.
Purpose: Deuteronomy states the ground: the laborer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15); James warns withheld wages cry out (James 5:4). Here that ground forbids robbing a neighbour of what is his.

Command: Do not defraud your neighbour
Summary: Do not defraud your neighbour: no taking by deceit what honest dealing would not give.
Commandment: Do not defraud your neighbour.
Application: Fraud is theft with a plausible face — the short measure, the false account, the withheld due. The labourer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15), and defrauding him is not sharp business but oppression.
Purpose: Deuteronomy states the ground: the laborer depends on the day's pay (Deuteronomy 24:15); James warns withheld wages cry out (James 5:4). Here that ground forbids defrauding a neighbour.

Command: Do not lie to one another
Summary: Do not lie to one another: speech between neighbours must be truthful.
Commandment: Do not lie to one another.
Application: Lying breaks the shared ground on which neighbours settle disputes, trade, and trust. The command is general — it binds every neighbourly word, not only testimony in court.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: truthful speech is the ground of neighbourly trust; a community of lies cannot judge, trade, or live together justly.

Command: Do not deal falsely with one another
Summary: Dealings between neighbours must be honest: no false dealing, no sharp practice dressed up as trade.
Commandment: Do not deal falsely with one another.
Application: False dealing is fraud before it is theft — the rigged scale, the hidden defect, the misleading word. Honest trade is a moral duty, not merely a commercial convention.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: false dealing corrupts the trust on which neighbourly life and trade depend, so it is forbidden alongside lying and stealing (Leviticus 19:11).

Command: Do not swear falsely by God's name
Summary: Do not swear falsely by God's name: an oath in his name must be true, for a false oath profanes the name it invokes.
Commandment: Do not swear falsely by God's name.
Application: Views differ on Jesus' words 'swear not at all' (Matthew 5:33-37): some read them as forbidding all oaths, others as forbidding false and casual oaths, noting that Paul himself swears oaths (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23). What is not debated is the core: a false oath profanes God's name.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: swearing falsely profanes the name of God (Leviticus 19:12).

Command: Do not wrong one another in trade
Summary: In buying and selling, one man must not wrong another — no overreaching in price, no exploiting a neighbour's ignorance or need in trade.
Commandment: Do not wrong one another in trade.
Application: Trade wronging is fraud's quiet cousin: the price that exploits, the bargain struck on a neighbour's ignorance. The Jubilee setting does not confine the principle — honest dealing in trade endures wherever neighbours buy and sell.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here the same care for a neighbour's standing takes the enduring form of honest dealing in trade.

Command: Do not wrong one another with words
Summary: One man must not wrong another with words — no speech that grieves, shames, or puts a neighbour down, including reminding him of a past he has left behind.
Commandment: Do not wrong one another with words.
Application: Words can wrong as surely as prices can: the taunt, the reminder of a convert's past, the remark meant to sting. The command guards the neighbour's dignity in speech, a duty that outlives the Jubilee calendar entirely.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: words that wound a neighbour wrong him as truly as a bad bargain does, so the Law forbids wronging with words alongside wronging in trade (Leviticus 25:17).

Command: Do not hide yourself from lost property
Summary: Do not hide yourself from your brother's lost thing — his ox, sheep, ass, or garment gone astray: you must not look away and pass by.
Commandment: Do not hide yourself from lost property.
Application: Hiding oneself is the negative form of the return law: looking away is itself the offence. The Good Samaritan story makes the same point in the New Testament — passing by is not neutrality but neglect.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the lost thing belongs to your brother, and you are its keeper until he comes for it (Deuteronomy 22:1-3).

Command: Do not hide yourself from your brother's fallen animal
Summary: Do not hide yourself from your brother's ass or ox fallen by the way: you must not look away from the animal under its burden.
Commandment: Do not hide yourself from your brother's fallen animal.
Application: As with lost property, looking away is the offence: the fallen animal's owner needs help, and the passer-by who hides himself has refused it. The negative form guards the positive duty to lift.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the animal is under a burden it cannot bear, and the owner's need — even an enemy owner's need — obliges help (Exodus 23:5; Deuteronomy 22:4).

Command: Pay for damage caused by an open pit
Summary: If a man opens a pit or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or ass falls in, the pit's owner pays for the animal, though the dead animal becomes his.
Commandment: Pay for damage caused by an open pit you have left uncovered.
Application: Negligence has a price: leaving a hazard open on your ground makes you liable for what falls into it. The rule still teaches that those who create a danger must bear the cost of it.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the one who left a hazard uncovered repays the loss it caused.

Command: Pay for damage caused by an ox goring another ox
Summary: If one man's ox gores another man's ox so that it dies, the living ox is sold and the price divided, and the dead ox divided as well; if the ox was known to gore, the owner pays ox for ox.
Commandment: Pay for damage caused by an ox goring another ox, as the Law scales it to the owner's knowledge.
Application: Even animal against animal has its measure: shared loss where no fault was known, full repayment where danger was known and ignored. The distinction between accident and culpable negligence runs through the whole law of damages.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: damage between neighbours' animals is shared or repaid according to what the owner knew.

Command: Pay for damage caused by grazing
Summary: If a man lets his beast loose into another man's field or vineyard so that it grazes there, he repays from the best of his own field and vineyard.
Commandment: Pay for damage caused by grazing on another's land.
Application: Careless pasturing is not a trifle: the owner whose beast ate his neighbour's crop pays from his best, not his leftovers. The measure teaches that damage is repaid at full value, not at a discount.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: grazing damage repaid from the best of the offender's own field.

Command: Pay for damage caused by fire
Summary: If fire breaks out and catches thorns and consumes stacked grain or standing corn or the field, the one who kindled the fire makes restitution.
Commandment: Pay for damage caused by fire you kindled.
Application: Fire spreads beyond the hand that lit it, and so does liability: the one who kindled it answers for all it consumes. The rule still teaches care with any risk that can run beyond one's own boundary.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the kindler of a fire repays the damage the fire causes.

Command: Pay a ransom if a warned ox kills a person
Summary: If an ox known to gore has been warned about and its owner failed to keep it in, and it kills a person, the owner pays a ransom for his life as the court lays upon him.
Commandment: Pay a ransom if a warned ox kills a person, as the court determines.
Application: Known danger ignored becomes personal responsibility: the owner who was warned and did nothing cannot plead accident. The ransom marks both the value of the life lost and the owner's culpable negligence.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: a warned owner who failed to restrain a dangerous animal answers with a ransom for the life lost.

Command: Appoint cities of refuge
Summary: Three cities of refuge are set apart in the land, with roads prepared, so that a manslayer may flee there and live.
Commandment: Appoint cities of refuge.
Application: Refuge was prepared in advance, not improvised after a killing: cities set apart and roads maintained, so that flight was possible in the hour of danger. The cities belonged to Israel's land system and no longer function; the foresight they embody — protection prepared before it is needed — remains instructive.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance takes the form of cities appointed in advance.

Command: Do not accept ransom for a manslayer's life
Summary: No ransom may be taken for the life of a murderer who is guilty of death: he shall surely be put to death, and money cannot buy back a life deliberately taken.
Commandment: Do not accept ransom for a manslayer's life.
Application: Life deliberately taken is not a debt that money can settle. The ban on ransom marks murder as different in kind from property wrongs, where repayment can make things right.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance forbids ransoming a murderer's life.

Command: Do not accept ransom to shorten a manslayer's exile
Summary: No ransom may be taken to let a manslayer in a city of refuge return early to his own land before the high priest's death.
Commandment: Do not accept ransom to shorten a manslayer's exile.
Application: Exile in the city was the sentence, and money could not shorten it: the high priest's death, not a payment, set the term. Justice that can be bought is not justice, and the Law guards even this sentence from purchase.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance forbids ransoming an early return.

Command: Give the firstborn a double portion
Summary: The firstborn receives a double portion of all that his father has: the right of the firstborn is his, whatever the father's affections.
Commandment: Give the firstborn a double portion.
Application: The double portion recognised the firstborn's standing and his future responsibility for the household. The inheritance system belonged to Israel's tribal order, but the principle — family provision by fixed right, not by favour — still rebukes partiality.
Purpose: To keep family land within the tribe and provide for daughters where there was no son (Numbers 27; 36). Here that purpose takes the form of the firstborn's double portion.

Command: Do not prefer the loved wife's son over the firstborn
Summary: A father with two wives must not prefer the loved wife's son over the firstborn son of the hated wife when he divides the inheritance.
Commandment: Do not prefer the loved wife's son over the firstborn.
Application: Favouritism in the household must not rewrite inheritance: birthright is not a prize for being loved. The rule protected the unloved wife's son from a father's affection becoming another child's disinheritance.
Purpose: To keep family land within the tribe and provide for daughters where there was no son (Numbers 27; 36). Here that purpose takes the form of birthright protected from household favouritism.

Command: Daughters inherit when there is no son
Summary: If a man dies and has no son, his inheritance passes to his daughter: daughters inherit where there is no son.
Commandment: Daughters inherit when there is no son.
Application: The daughters of Zelophehad set the precedent: their appeal changed the law itself, showing God's law making room for justice within its own framework. Inheritance law protected the family's footing, and a daughter without brothers was not to be left landless.
Purpose: To keep family land within the tribe and provide for daughters where there was no son (Numbers 27; 36). Here that purpose takes the form of daughters inheriting where there is no son.

Command: An heiress shall marry within her father's tribe
Summary: An heiress — a daughter who inherits because there is no son — marries within the family of her father's tribe, so that the inheritance stays in the tribe.
Commandment: An heiress shall marry within her father's tribe.
Application: The heiress's marriage rule is the complement of her inheritance right: she inherits, and her marriage keeps the inheritance where it belongs. The daughters of Zelophehad married within Manasseh, and the law was kept.
Purpose: To keep family land within the tribe and provide for daughters where there was no son (Numbers 27; 36). Here that purpose takes the form of an heiress marrying within her father's tribe.

Command: Release a Hebrew servant in the seventh year
Summary: A Hebrew servant was to serve six years and go free in the seventh, so that servitude in Israel could never become permanent bondage for a fellow Hebrew.
Commandment: Release a Hebrew servant in the seventh year, after six years of service.
Application: The six-year limit restrained an ancient institution rather than endorsing it. Paul later points past regulation to brotherhood (Philemon 16); the institution these laws governed has ended, but the restraint they taught — no permanent grip on another person's liberty — remains instructive.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). The laws regulated servanthood, not endorsed it, and the institution they governed has ended.

Command: Furnish a departing servant liberally
Summary: A departing servant is furnished liberally out of the flock, the threshingfloor, and the winepress, as the LORD has blessed the master.
Commandment: Furnish a departing servant liberally.
Application: Liberality is measured by the master's blessing: the servant shares in the prosperity his labour helped to make. Release with provision, not bare release, is the Law's pattern — and generosity at parting remains a mark of just dealing.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint takes the form of liberal furnishing at departure.

Command: Do not sell a Hebrew servant as a slave is sold
Summary: A Hebrew servant must not be sold as a slave is sold — no slave-market transaction for a brother.
Commandment: Do not sell a Hebrew servant as a slave is sold.
Application: The manner of sale marked the man's standing: a Hebrew in service was not merchandise, and his transfer could not follow the slave market's ways. The restraint honours the brother even in his poverty.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint forbids selling a Hebrew as a slave is sold.

Command: Do not rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour
Summary: A master must not rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour — with harsh, crushing severity.
Commandment: Do not rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour.
Application: Rigour is rule meant to break rather than to employ: driving a servant beyond endurance. The Law forbids it outright, because the servant is a brother, and fear of God — 'thou shalt fear thy God' — stands behind the prohibition.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint forbids ruling with rigour.

Command: Do not return an escaped servant to his master
Summary: A servant who has escaped from his master to you must not be delivered back to his master: Israel is his refuge.
Commandment: Do not return an escaped servant to his master.
Application: The runaway was not a thief to be returned but a person seeking refuge, and the law made Israel his refuge. Paul's letter to Philemon moves in the same direction for a later age: Onesimus returns no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother. The institution has ended; the refuge principle — do not hand the fleeing back to their oppressor — remains a moral warning.
Purpose: Scripture states the command without a separate reason beyond the servant's refuge itself (Deuteronomy 23:15-16); TRADITIONAL reading: the escaped servant is treated as a person seeking protection, not property to be restored.

Command: Do not sell a maidservant to a foreign people
Summary: A maidservant sold into service was not to be dealt with deceitfully by selling her on to a foreign people; her master owed her the protections of the Law.
Commandment: Do not sell a maidservant to a foreign people.
Application: The prohibition restrained a traffic in vulnerable girls, keeping them within the Law's protections rather than beyond them. The institution has ended, but the restraint — the vulnerable must not be traded away from protection — still convicts.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: a maidservant was not merchandise to be sold on outside the covenant's protections.

Command: Redeem a Hebrew servant sold to a stranger
Summary: If a Hebrew servant has sold himself to a stranger or sojourner, redemption belongs to him: his kin may redeem him, or he may redeem himself as he prospers.
Commandment: Redeem a Hebrew servant sold to a stranger.
Application: Even sold outside the community, a Hebrew was not abandoned: kin or his own earnings could buy him back, at a price reckoned by the years remaining to Jubilee. Redemption kept a door open where debt had shut one.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint takes the form of redemption for a servant sold to a stranger.

Command: Give a bill of divorce when sending a wife away
Summary: Deuteronomy 24:1 requires a written bill of divorcement when a man sends his wife away: 'then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house.' The document protects the woman's standing to remarry.
Commandment: When sending a wife away, give her a bill of divorce in her hand.
Application: Debated: how far these divorce provisions carry into the church is genuinely disputed, with Jesus' teaching on divorce (Matthew 19:3-9) central — this row does not settle it. The protection aimed at — a dismissed wife with a document, not a word — is plain.
Purpose: To protect the weaker party at each family step (Deuteronomy 21-25). Debated: the divorce certificate is read by Jesus as concession to hardness of heart, not God's design (Matthew 19:8), and levirate marriage ended, while creation marriage itself is reaffirmed. The site does not settle a single duration for this cluster because its parts do not share one fate.

Command: A divorced woman who remarried shall not return to her first husband

Commandment: A divorced woman who has remarried shall not return to her first husband.

Application: These civil provisions belonged to ancient Israel's family law and have passed with it; the protection of the weaker party they aimed at remains the lesson.
Purpose: To preserve the dead brother's name and inheritance in Israel: the child of the union carries the dead man's name (Deuteronomy 25:5-6).

Command: Perform chalitzah if the brother refuses levirate marriage
Summary: One of the family laws of Deuteronomy 21–25: perform chalitzah if the brother refuses levirate marriage. These laws protected the weaker party at each family step.

Command: Perform the sotah law for a wife suspected of adultery
Summary: Numbers 5:30 gives the law of jealousies: when the spirit of jealousy comes upon a husband, he shall set his wife before the LORD, and the priest shall execute upon her all this law. Where no witness existed, the matter was put before God.
Commandment: Perform the sotah law for a wife suspected of adultery, setting her before the LORD.
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the procedure gave a suspected wife a public, God-decided vindication instead of a husband's private vengeance. The procedure belonged to the tabernacle system and has passed with it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the procedure gave a suspected wife a public, God-decided vindication instead of a husband's private vengeance. Scripture states the procedure without a stated reason beyond the spirit of jealousy coming upon the husband (Numbers 5:14,30).

Command: A seducer shall marry the maiden he seduced
Summary: Exodus 22:16 requires a man who entices an unbetrothed maiden to marry her: 'he shall surely endow her to be his wife.' If her father refuses, he still pays the bride-price (Exodus 22:17).
Commandment: A man who seduces an unbetrothed maiden shall marry her, or pay her bride-price if her father refuses.
Application: The wrong is not left with the maiden alone: the seducer bears its cost and its responsibility. The scaled civil remedy was for ancient Israel; the repay-and-restore duty — making a wrong right at the wrongdoer's cost — is the enduring substance.
Purpose: To make the wrong right for the maiden and her household: the seducer bears the cost and the responsibility of marriage, or pays the bride-price if her father refuses (Exodus 22:16-17).

Commandment: Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother.

Command: There shall be no cult prostitute among Israel
Summary: One of the Deuteronomy 23:17-18 laws: there shall be no cult prostitute among Israel. Fertility worship of the surrounding nations was to have no place in Israel, and its profits no place in God's house.
Commandment: There shall be no cult prostitute among Israel
Application: Scripture's stated ground: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 23:18).
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 23:18).

Command: Offer terms of peace before besieging a city
Summary: Deuteronomy 20:10 requires peace to be offered before a siege: 'When thou comest nigh unto a city to fight against it, then proclaim peace unto it.' Only a city that refuses peace is besieged.
Commandment: Offer terms of peace before besieging a city.
Application: Even in war the Law set restraints — a striking limit for the ancient world, where siege warfare usually spared nothing. Peace offered first is the pattern; destruction was never the first word.
Purpose: To restrain war even in conquest: offer peace, exempt the newly married and fearful, spare fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20). These laws bounded Israel's wars and do not govern any modern army as Mosaic law.

Command: Do not fear the enemy in battle
Summary: Deuteronomy 20:3 addresses Israel's army before battle: 'Let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them.' The priest's charge grounds courage in God's presence with the army.
Commandment: Do not fear the enemy in battle; the LORD your God goes with you.
Application: The battle setting belonged to ancient Israel's wars, which these laws bounded but do not govern today. The courage itself — fear answered by God's presence — is the enduring lesson for every fear God's people face.
Purpose: To restrain war even in conquest: offer peace, exempt the newly married and fearful, spare fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20). These laws bounded Israel's wars and do not govern any modern army as Mosaic law.

Command: Do not destroy fruit trees in a siege
Summary: Deuteronomy 20:19 forbids cutting down a city's fruit trees for siege works: 'for the tree of the field is man's life, to employ them in the siege?' Food-bearing trees were not weapons of war.
Commandment: Do not destroy fruit trees in a siege.
Application: The restraint is memorable because it is so concrete: even besieging armies must leave the means of life standing. Wanton destruction, even of an enemy's livelihood, is refused.
Purpose: To restrain war even in conquest: offer peace, exempt the newly married and fearful, spare fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20). These laws bounded Israel's wars and do not govern any modern army as Mosaic law.

Command: Keep the war camp holy

Commandment: Keep the war camp holy
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee (Deuteronomy 23:14). The camp itself has passed; the principle that God's presence calls for cleanliness and order remains.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee (Deuteronomy 23:14).

Command: Utterly destroy the seven nations of Canaan
Summary: Deuteronomy 20:17 commands the utter destruction of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites — the seven nations of the land — as the LORD commanded.
Commandment: Utterly destroy the seven nations of Canaan, as the LORD commanded.
Application: Scripture states the purpose plainly: that they teach you not to do after all their abominations, which they have done unto their gods (Deuteronomy 20:18). The campaign belonged to the conquest generation; it does not govern any modern army.
Purpose: To restrain war even in conquest: offer peace, exempt the newly married and fearful, spare fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20). These laws bounded Israel's wars and do not govern any modern army as Mosaic law.

Command: Save alive nothing that breathes of the Canaanite cities
Summary: Deuteronomy 20:16 gives the conquest exception to the offer of peace: of the cities of the seven nations, 'thou shalt save alive nothing that breatheth.' The command is limited to those named cities in that campaign.
Commandment: Of the Canaanite cities, save alive nothing that breathes.
Application: This is the hardest of the war laws, and it is also the most bounded: a specific campaign, named nations, a stated purpose — that they teach Israel not their abominations (Deuteronomy 20:18). It does not license any modern war, and it is not to be generalised beyond its stated bounds.
Purpose: To restrain war even in conquest: offer peace, exempt the newly married and fearful, spare fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20). These laws bounded Israel's wars and do not govern any modern army as Mosaic law.

Command: Remember what Amalek did to you
Summary: Deuteronomy 25:17 commands remembrance: 'Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt.' Amalek attacked the faint and weary at the rear of the march.
Commandment: Remember what Amalek did to you on the way out of Egypt.
Application: Scripture's stated context: Amalek met Israel by the way and smote the hindmost of thee (Deuteronomy 25:18). Debated: whether remembrance today is a historical duty, a warning against cruelty to the weak, or both, is genuinely disputed — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: Amalek met Israel by the way and smote the hindmost, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:18).

Command: Blot out the remembrance of Amalek
Summary: Deuteronomy 25:19 commands blotting out Amalek's remembrance from under heaven, once Israel has rest in the land. The attacker of the weak was not to be left standing as a power.

Commandment: Appoint as king over Israel the man whom the LORD your God chooses, from among your brethren.
Application: Scripture's stated context: Israel's desire for a king like the nations is answered by God's choice, not by the people's preference alone (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). The Israelite monarchy has passed.

Command: Perform the law of the heifer for an unsolved murder

Commandment: Perform the law of the heifer for an unsolved murder.
Application: The rite answered two needs at once: a community stained by an unsolved killing needed atonement, and a community tempted to shrug at an unknown victim needed to say publicly, 'our hands have not shed this blood.' The New Testament answers the same guilt differently — in Christ, who bears it — and the rite itself has ceased.
Purpose: Scripture's stated purpose: so shall the guilt of innocent blood be put away from among you (Deuteronomy 21:9, in the form of the elders' declaration and the atonement prayer, 21:7-8).

Command: Fulfil what you have vowed
Summary: What has gone out of your lips you shall keep and perform: a freewill offering vowed to the LORD is fulfilled as vowed.
Commandment: Fulfil what you have vowed.
Application: The positive form of vow-keeping: the word given to God is performed, fully and as spoken. The New Testament sharpens the duty into plain truthfulness — let your Yes be Yes (Matthew 5:37) — so that vows themselves become rarer and words truer.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee (Deuteronomy 23:21).

Command: Do not delay paying a vow

Commandment: Do not delay paying a vow.
Application: Delay turns a vow into a debt dodged: God requires what was promised, and slackness in paying is itself sin. Ecclesiastes agrees — do not be slow to keep what you promised God (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee (Deuteronomy 23:21).

Commandment: Do not break your word in a vow.
Application: A vow is a word given to God, not a bargaining chip. The New Testament sharpens the duty further: let your Yes be Yes and your No be No (Matthew 5:37; James 5:12) — plain truthfulness that needs no oath to prop it up.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee (Deuteronomy 23:21).

Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).
