Summary: A woman with a discharge beyond her monthly course counts seven days from when it stops, and on the eighth day brings two turtles or young pigeons to the priest for atonement.
Commandment: A woman with a discharge shall count seven days for cleansing and bring her offering on the eighth day.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The counting and offering gave the afflicted woman a definite road back to worship. The bleeding woman who touched Jesus was healed and told her faith had made her whole (Luke 8:43-48).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Do not eat a limb torn from a living animal
Summary: A limb torn from a living animal may not be eaten; the animal's life must be duly taken and its blood shed before its flesh is eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat a limb torn from a living animal, for the blood is the life.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule is bound to the blood itself: flesh eaten while the creature still lives treats its life as food. The Jerusalem council likewise told Gentile believers to abstain from things strangled and from blood (Acts 15:29).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: only be sure that thou eat not the blood, for the blood is the life (Deuteronomy 12:23).

Command: Do not eat winged swarming things
Summary: Winged creeping things that swarm and walk on all fours, apart from the clean leaping kinds, are unclean and may not be eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat winged swarming things that are unclean.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The general ban covers the swarming kinds, with only the leaping locust kinds excepted. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Rejoice before the LORD on the festivals
Summary: At the appointed feasts, Israel rejoices before the LORD — sons, daughters, servants, Levites, strangers, fatherless, and widows together — in the place God chooses.
Commandment: Rejoice before the LORD your God at the appointed feasts, you and your household with the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The feasts were not private fasts but shared joy, with the vulnerable deliberately included in the rejoicing. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the feasts rehearse God's saving acts and his gift of the harvest and the land (Deuteronomy 16:13-15).

Command: Sanctify the priest
Summary: The command: Sanctify the priest (Leviticus 21:8). Israel was to sanctify the priest, who offered the bread of God, treating him as holy because the LORD who sanctifies is holy.
Commandment: Sanctify the priest, as prescribed in Leviticus 21:8.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The marriage rules guarded the priesthood's public holiness in a world where priests were public figures; they are not Christian marriage law, which is governed by creation and by the New Testament household commands (Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:22-33). The high priest's stricter rule — a virgin of his own people — is included here as the second half of the same law.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8).

Command: Eat the firstborn animals before the LORD in Jerusalem
Summary: The command: Eat the firstborn animals before the LORD in Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 15:20). The firstling of herd and flock, if without blemish, was eaten year by year before the LORD in the place he chose.
Commandment: Eat the firstborn animals before the LORD in Jerusalem, as prescribed in Deuteronomy 15:20.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the firstling without blemish was eaten before the LORD year by year in the place he chose (Deuteronomy 15:20).

Command: Fear your mother and father
Summary: Leviticus 19:3 opens the holiness chapter with two duties side by side: 'Ye shall fear every man his mother, and his father, and keep my sabbaths: I am the LORD.' Fear here is reverent honour, paired with keeping the Sabbath as the mark of a household ordered by God.
Commandment: Fear — that is, reverently honour — your mother and your father.
Application: Honour for parents is the first school of honour for God: a household where parents are feared in this reverent sense is a household learning to fear the LORD. The fifth commandment carries the same duty (Exodus 20:12).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the duty stands beside Sabbath-keeping under the seal 'I am the LORD' (Leviticus 19:3).

Command: Levites shall do the service of the Tent of Meeting
Summary: The command: Levites shall do the service of the Tent of Meeting (Numbers 18:23). The Levites bore the iniquity of the sanctuary's service and did the work of the tent of meeting.
Commandment: Levites shall do the service of the Tent of Meeting, as prescribed in Numbers 18:23.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah: the Levites did the work of the tent of meeting and bore the charge of the sanctuary. It cannot be practised as written without the standing tabernacle/temple; its enduring lesson is ordered, God-appointed service in worship.
Purpose: Adapted from the tithes parent: the Levites' service was sustained by the tithe because they had no land inheritance among Israel (Numbers 18:23-24); the service itself belonged to the tent of meeting.

Command: Sanctify the new moon and the months
Summary: The month of the Exodus is made the first month of Israel's year, so the sacred calendar counts from deliverance.
Commandment: Sanctify the new moon: let the month of the Exodus be the first month of the year to you.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The calendar itself was reset around redemption: Israel's year began with the month God brought them out of Egypt.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the month of the Exodus becomes the beginning of months for Israel (Exodus 12:2).

Command: Redeem a tithe by adding a fifth to its value
Summary: The command: Redeem a tithe by adding a fifth to its value (Leviticus 27:31). A tithe of seed or fruit redeemed by its owner was paid at its value plus a fifth part.
Commandment: Redeem a tithe by adding a fifth to its value, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:31.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament shifts the frame from a fixed percentage to cheerful, generous giving — God loves a cheerful giver — while keeping the duty to support ministry and the poor. Debated: some hold the fixed tenth continues as the giving standard; others hold the New Testament replaces the percentage with cheerful, generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7) while keeping support for ministry and the poor.
Purpose: To support the Levites, the poor, and worship (Numbers 18; Deuteronomy 14). Debated: some hold the fixed tenth continues as the giving standard; others hold the New Testament replaces the percentage with cheerful, generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:7) while keeping support for ministry and the poor. The site does not settle the percentage.

Command: Redeem a dedicated house by adding a fifth
Summary: The command: Redeem a dedicated house by adding a fifth (Leviticus 27:15). One who redeemed a sanctified house paid the priest's valuation plus a fifth part.
Commandment: Redeem a dedicated house by adding a fifth, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:15.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: Observe the law of a dedicated field
Summary: The command: Observe the law of a dedicated field (Leviticus 27:16). A field sanctified to the LORD was valued by the seed sown in it, fifty shekels of silver to a homer of barley seed, reckoned by the years to the jubile.
Commandment: Observe the law of a dedicated field, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:16.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: The priest who offers a burnt offering shall have its hide
Summary: The command: The priest who offers a burnt offering shall have its hide (Leviticus 7:8). The skin of the burnt offering belonged to the priest who offered it.
Commandment: The priest who offers a burnt offering shall have its hide, as prescribed in Leviticus 7:8.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: A priest's daughter married to a stranger shall not eat holy food
Summary: The command: A priest's daughter married to a stranger shall not eat holy food (Leviticus 22:12). A priest's daughter married to a stranger lost the right to eat of her father's holy things, unless widowed or divorced and childless and returned home.
Commandment: A priest's daughter married to a stranger shall not eat holy food.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament replaces the whole system of holy food: all who are in Christ are a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5,9), and the meal that marks God's people is the Lord's Supper, not the priestly portions. The boundary itself — holy things are not common things — is fulfilled, not continued.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the holy things are the LORD's, set apart for the priesthood (Leviticus 22:3-16).

Command: Do not go beyond the Sabbath boundary
Summary: On the Sabbath, each person is to remain in his place and not go out beyond the appointed boundary for gathering or travel.
Commandment: On the Sabbath day, abide in your place; do not go out beyond the Sabbath boundary.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The manna rule taught Israel to rest in God's provision rather than go out gathering on the Sabbath. Debated: some Christians keep the Sabbath day as a binding command; others see its rest fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 4; Colossians 2:16-17). The site does not settle the question.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Sabbath is the LORD's day of rest, kept holy in remembrance of creation and of deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15).

Command: Do not kindle fire on the Sabbath day
Summary: No fire may be kindled in Israel's dwellings on the Sabbath day, setting the day apart from ordinary work.
Commandment: Kindle no fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The fire ban made the Sabbath rest visible in every home: even the day's ordinary preparations stopped. Debated: some Christians keep the Sabbath day as a binding command; others see its rest fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 4; Colossians 2:16-17). The site does not settle the question.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Sabbath is the LORD's day of rest, kept holy in remembrance of creation and of deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15).

Command: Do not go up to the altar by steps
Summary: The command: Do not go up to the altar by steps (Exodus 20:26). A ramp rather than steps kept the priest's nakedness from being exposed as he ascended to the altar.
Commandment: Do not go up to the altar by steps.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lest nakedness be discovered on the altar (Exodus 20:26).

Command: Do not walk in the ordinances of Egypt or Canaan
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not walk in the ordinances of Egypt or Canaan. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not walk in the ordinances of Egypt or Canaan
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Do not eat flesh with its blood
Summary: Flesh may not be eaten with its blood in it; the blood must be drained, for the life is in the blood.
Commandment: Do not eat flesh with the blood.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Leviticus 19:26 forbids eating with the blood in the context of pagan practices, but the blood rule itself rests on the life in the blood (Leviticus 17:11) and is repeated for Gentile believers at Jerusalem (Acts 15:29).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the life of the flesh is in the blood, and it is given upon the altar to make atonement (Leviticus 17:11).

Command: Do not eat bread from the new crop before the sheaf offering
Summary: No bread made from the new grain harvest may be eaten until the sheaf of firstfruits has been waved before the LORD.
Commandment: Eat no bread from the new crop until the day the sheaf offering is brought.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The first sheaf went to God before Israel ate of the harvest: firstfruits first, then the table. The New Testament keeps the principle in a new key — Christ is the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the confession itself gives the reason — 'a Syrian ready to perish was my father,' and God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them this land (Deuteronomy 26:5-10).

Command: Do not follow the thoughts of your heart or the sight of your eyes into idolatry
Summary: Numbers 15:39 joins the fringe to its warning: Israel was not to seek after its own heart and its own eyes, after which it used to go a whoring. The wandering heart and eye are the road to idolatry.
Commandment: Do not follow the thoughts of your heart or the sight of your eyes into idolatry.
Application: The fringe reminded; the warning endures without the fringe. Hearts and eyes still lead astray, and God's word still answers them.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that ye may look upon the fringe and remember all the commandments of the LORD and do them, and not follow your own heart and eyes (Numbers 15:39).

Command: Do not castrate any animal
Summary: The command: Do not castrate any animal (Leviticus 22:24). No beast was to be bruised, crushed, broken, or cut, whether for offering or otherwise, in the land.
Commandment: Do not castrate any animal.
Application: This prohibition is stated generally, not only for the altar, and so it binds beyond the temple system.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: mutilating an animal marred God's creation and disqualified it from the altar; the prohibition is stated generally, not only for sacrifices.

Command: Do not offer a deformed animal as a vow
Summary: The command: Do not offer a deformed animal as a vow (Leviticus 22:23). An animal with a superfluous or lacking part might be given only as a freewill offering, never as a vow.
Commandment: Do not offer a deformed animal as a vow.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: a vow bound the offerer to his word, so only a whole animal could discharge it; a deformed animal sufficed only as a freewill gift.

Command: Levites shall not perform priestly service
Summary: The command: Levites shall not perform priestly service (Numbers 18:3). The Levites kept the charge of the tabernacle but might not come near the vessels of the sanctuary or the altar, lest they die.
Commandment: Levites shall not perform priestly service.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the priesthood was given to Aaron and his sons; the Levites kept the charge of the tabernacle but might not approach the altar, lest they die (Numbers 18:3).

Command: A stranger shall not come near the sanctuary
Summary: The command: A stranger shall not come near the sanctuary (Numbers 18:4). No stranger might come near the sanctuary's service, which belonged to Aaron and his sons.
Commandment: A stranger shall not come near the sanctuary.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the charge of the sanctuary was Aaron's, and a stranger who came near was put to death (Numbers 18:4, 7).

Command: Do not offer strange incense on the altar
Summary: The command: Do not offer strange incense on the altar (Exodus 30:9). Only the prescribed incense might be burned on the golden altar; no other offering, burnt offering, or drink offering belonged there.
Commandment: Do not offer strange incense on the altar.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Aaron shall not enter the holy place at all times
Summary: The command: Aaron shall not enter the holy place at all times (Leviticus 16:2). After the deaths of Nadab and Abihu, Aaron might not enter the most holy place whenever he chose, but only as appointed, lest he die.
Commandment: Aaron shall not enter the holy place at all times.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews reads the Day as a shadow: Christ entered the true Most Holy Place with his own blood, securing an eternal redemption the yearly rite could only picture. (Distinct from the Jewish Cultural Backgrounds entry on the Day of Atonement as a feast; this entry covers the commanded rite as law.)
Purpose: Annual cleansing for the people's sins (Leviticus 16). Hebrews reads it as shadow of Christ's entry with his own blood (Hebrews 9:11-14).

Command: A priest's daughter shall not profane herself by prostitution
Summary: Leviticus 21:9 addresses the priest's daughter who profanes herself by playing the harlot: she profanes her father, and the sentence is burning. The priest's household shared the priesthood's holiness.
Commandment: A priest's daughter shall not profane herself by prostitution.
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8). The priestly system has passed; the call to a household above reproach, and the protection of daughters from exploitation, remains.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8).

Command: Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute
Summary: Leviticus 19:29 forbids a father from profaning his daughter by making her a harlot, 'lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness.' The daughter's body is not her father's to trade.
Commandment: Do not profane your daughter by making her a prostitute.
Application: The command protects daughters from being used by their own households, and warns that private exploitation corrupts the whole land. Parents guard their children's honour; they do not sell it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lest the land fall to whoredom, and the land become full of wickedness (Leviticus 19:29).

Command: Do not shave a bald patch for the dead in a leprous scall
Summary: In examining a scall, the priest must not have the bald patch shaved away: the scall is left so its spreading or healing can be judged after seven days.
Commandment: Do not shave the bald patch in a leprous scall; let the priest examine it unshaved.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The unshaved patch preserved the evidence the priest needed to judge the disease. Jesus' touch restored those the purity laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Do not make baldness for the dead
Summary: Deuteronomy 14:1 forbids making baldness between the eyes for the dead: 'Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead.' Israel's grief was not to take the mourning rites of the nations.
Commandment: Do not make baldness for the dead.
Application: Grief is real and permitted; pagan mourning rites are not the shape it must take. God's children mourn as those who belong to a living Father, not as those who cut themselves for the dead. Debated: whether the prohibition covers all ritual mourning marks today, or only those tied to pagan rites for the dead, is a genuine difference of reading — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: ye are the children of the LORD your God (Deuteronomy 14:1).

Command: Do not let idolaters dwell in your land
Summary: Exodus 23:33 forbids letting the idolatrous nations remain in the land, 'lest they make thee sin against me: for if thou serve their gods, it will surely be a snare unto thee.' The danger named is not the neighbours as such but their worship, which would snare Israel.
Commandment: Do not let idolaters dwell in your land, lest their worship become a snare to you.
Application: This was a conquest-era land policy for ancient Israel, not a rule for the church's neighbours today. Its enduring lesson is the snare principle: tolerated idolatry spreads, and God's people guard their worship accordingly.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lest they make thee sin against me, for if thou serve their gods, it will surely be a snare unto thee (Exodus 23:33).

Command: Do not show mercy to idolaters
Summary: Deuteronomy 7:2, in the conquest commands, forbids showing mercy to the seven nations devoted to destruction: 'thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them.' The verse belongs to a specific, unrepeatable campaign against entrenched idolatry in the land.
Commandment: In the conquest campaign, show no mercy to the idolatrous nations devoted to destruction.
Application: This command in its stated form governed ancient Israel's conquest, not the church's treatment of unbelievers today — the gospel commands mercy to all. Its enduring point is separation from idolatry itself, which is never to be spared a place in God's people's worship.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: in the conquest setting, sparing the idolatrous nations would leave their idolatry standing in the land (Deuteronomy 7:4-5); the separation from idolatry is the enduring point, not mercy as such.

Command: Do not forsake the Levite
Summary: The command: Do not forsake the Levite (Deuteronomy 12:19). The Levite, having no portion or inheritance with Israel, was not to be forsaken as long as Israel lived in the land.
Commandment: Do not forsake the Levite.
Application: Debated: some hold the Levite's support continues as support for those who minister, while others hold the Levitical order itself has ceased and giving is now governed by New Testament generosity. The site does not settle the form; the duty not to abandon those who serve is the enduring point.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the Levite had no part nor inheritance with Israel, and depended on the people's gifts (Deuteronomy 12:19; Deuteronomy 14:27).

Command: Do not sell a captive woman
Summary: One of the family laws of Deuteronomy 21–25: do not sell a captive woman. These laws protected the weaker party at each family step.
Commandment: Do not sell a captive woman
Application: These civil provisions belonged to ancient Israel's family law and have passed with it; the protection of the weaker party they aimed at remains the lesson.
Purpose: To protect a captive woman once married: she is not merchandise to be sold for gain after being humbled (Deuteronomy 21:14).

Command: An unclean man shall not enter the war camp until evening
Summary: One of the war-camp holiness laws of Deuteronomy 23: an unclean man shall not enter the war camp until evening. The camp was to be kept clean because God walked in its midst.
Commandment: An unclean man shall not enter the war camp until evening
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee (Deuteronomy 23:14). The camp itself has passed; the principle that God's presence calls for cleanliness and order remains.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee; therefore shall thy camp be holy: that he see no unclean thing in thee, and turn away from thee (Deuteronomy 23:14).

Command: Do not offer burnt offerings in any place you choose
Summary: The command: Do not offer burnt offerings in any place you choose (Deuteronomy 12:13). Burnt offerings might be offered only in the place the LORD chose, not in every place that seemed right.
Commandment: Do not offer burnt offerings in any place you choose.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: offerings belonged in the place the LORD chose to put his name, lest worship fragment into every high place (Deuteronomy 12:13-14).

Command: Do not make molten gods
Summary: Exodus 34:17, given with the renewed covenant, forbids molten gods outright: 'Thou shalt make thee no molten gods.' The command answers the golden calf directly — cast metal, however sacred the occasion, cannot be God.
Commandment: Do not make molten gods.
Application: The calf was made in the very shadow of Sinai, which is the point: proximity to revelation does not excuse idolatry. No cast image, however costly, may receive worship.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the prohibition stands in the covenant renewed after the golden calf (Exodus 32; 34:17).

Command: Do not turn to idols
Summary: Leviticus 19:4 forbids even turning toward idols: 'Turn ye not unto idols, nor make to yourselves molten gods: I am the LORD your God.' The sin begins before the idol is made, in the turning of attention and trust.
Commandment: Do not turn to idols, nor make molten gods for yourselves.
Application: Idolatry starts with a glance, not a statue. Guarding the turn of heart and eye is the first defence of exclusive worship.
Purpose: Scripture's stated seal: I am the LORD your God (Leviticus 19:4).

Command: Do not worship the sun, moon, or host of heaven
Summary: Deuteronomy 4:19 warns Israel, when it lifts its eyes to heaven, not to be driven to worship the sun, the moon, or the host of heaven, 'which the LORD thy God hath divided unto all nations under the whole heaven.' The heavenly bodies are creatures given to all peoples, not gods for any people.
Commandment: Do not worship the sun, the moon, or the host of heaven.
Application: The lights of heaven declare God's glory; they do not receive his worship. Whatever beauty or order creation shows, praise passes through it to the Creator.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the heavenly bodies are divided unto all nations as creatures, not given to Israel as gods (Deuteronomy 4:19).

Command: Do not sacrifice to any god except the LORD
Summary: Exodus 22:20 sentences sacrifice to any god other than the LORD: 'He that sacrificeth unto any god, save unto the LORD only, he shall be utterly destroyed.' The verse guards exclusive worship at its most concrete point — the altar.
Commandment: Sacrifice to no god except the LORD alone.
Application: Sacrifice is worship in its costliest form, and it belongs to one altar and one God. The civil penalty belonged to ancient Israel; the exclusivity of worship endures undiminished.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the LORD alone is God, and sacrifice belongs to him alone (Exodus 22:20; Deuteronomy 6:4).

Command: Do not pass a child through fire to Molech
Summary: One of the occult practices forbidden in Deuteronomy 18 and Leviticus 19: do not pass a child through fire to Molech. Israel was not to seek guidance from the dead or from hidden powers as the nations did.
Commandment: Do not pass a child through fire to Molech
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:12). God's people seek him alone for guidance, through his word and his prophets.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:12).

Command: Do not remove the staves from the ark
Summary: The command: Do not remove the staves from the ark (Exodus 25:15). The carrying poles stayed in the rings of the ark so it could be moved without being touched.
Commandment: Do not remove the staves from the ark.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Do not sell land permanently
Summary: The land must not be sold permanently, for the land is God's: sales were leases until Jubilee, not alienations for ever.
Commandment: Do not sell land permanently.
Application: Because the land belonged to God and was apportioned to families, no sale could cut a family off from it for ever. The rule capped debt's damage: a family might lease its land in hardship, but Jubilee always brought it home.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). Here that purpose takes the form of the land itself: it is God's, and no sale alienates it for ever.

Command: Do not eat the tithe in mourning, in uncleanness, or for the dead
Summary: The command: Do not eat the tithe in mourning, in uncleanness, or for the dead (Deuteronomy 26:14). The tithe confession declared that none of it had been eaten in mourning, in uncleanness, or given for the dead.
Commandment: Do not eat the tithe in mourning, in uncleanness, or for the dead.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: holy gifts were not to be spent in mourning rites or for the dead, keeping worship of the LORD distinct from death customs.

Command: Do not observe times
Summary: One of the occult practices forbidden in Deuteronomy 18 and Leviticus 19: do not observe times. Israel was not to seek guidance from the dead or from hidden powers as the nations did.
Commandment: Do not observe times
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:12). God's people seek him alone for guidance, through his word and his prophets.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for all that do these things are an abomination unto the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:12).

Command: Do not build an altar of hewn stones
Summary: The command: Do not build an altar of hewn stones (Exodus 20:25). An altar of earth or unhewn stone kept human tool-work off the place of sacrifice.
Commandment: Do not build an altar of hewn stones.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: lifting a tool upon the altar pollutes it (Exodus 20:25).

Command: Do not seek the peace of Ammon or Moab
Summary: Deuteronomy 23:6 forbids seeking the peace or prosperity of Ammon or Moab for ever, because they refused Israel bread and water and hired Balaam to curse them.
Commandment: Do not seek the peace or prosperity of Ammon or Moab.
Application: This foreign-policy stance belonged to ancient Israel's relations with two specific nations, now gone as nations; it does not govern the church's relations with any people today. Its ground — remembered hostility to God's people on their journey — is the stated reason.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: Ammon and Moab refused Israel bread and water on the way and hired Balaam to curse them (Deuteronomy 23:4-5).

Command: Do not harvest a neighbour's grain with a sickle
Summary: When you go into your neighbour's standing corn, you may pluck ears with your hand, but you must not move a sickle over his grain: eating in passing is allowed, harvesting is not.
Commandment: Do not harvest a neighbour's grain with a sickle.
Application: The traveller's hunger is met from the field's edge, but the sickle would turn a snack into a harvest. The line between eating and harvesting protected the neighbour's crop while feeding the passer-by — a distinction tied to Israel's agrarian field law.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the neighbour's field feeds the passing traveller by hand, but the sickle marks a harvest, and a harvest belongs to the field's owner.

Command: Do not let an inheritance move from tribe to tribe
Summary: The inheritance of the children of Israel must not move from tribe to tribe: each tribe keeps the inheritance of its fathers.
Commandment: Do not let an inheritance move from tribe to tribe.
Application: Tribal allotments were a permanent trust, not a market: marriage and inheritance law together kept each tribe's land within the tribe. The tribal land system ended with Israel's polity, but the care for a family's footing in the land is the law's lasting lesson.
Purpose: To keep family land within the tribe and provide for daughters where there was no son (Numbers 27; 36). Here that purpose takes the form of inheritance that does not move between tribes.

Command: Compensate for loss and healing after injury
Summary: When one person injures another in a quarrel and the victim is confined but recovers, the one who struck him must pay for the lost time and for the healing.
Commandment: Compensate the injured person for his loss of time and for his healing.
Application: Justice here is restorative, not merely punitive: the offender bears the real costs his violence caused. The same duty lives on wherever injury is done — make the victim whole as far as payment can.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the injured party is repaid for what the injury actually cost him, in lost time and in healing.

Command: Compensate eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and other injury measures
Summary: Injury was to be measured by injury: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
Commandment: Compensate injury by the measures the Law sets: eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and the other measures likewise.
Application: This was a court's rule of proportion, capping retaliation at the harm done — never a licence for personal revenge. Jesus later forbids turning it into private vengeance (Matthew 5:38-39), while the principle of proportionate, court-administered justice endures.
Purpose: To make wrongs right in proportion: punishment must match the injury, neither falling short of it nor exceeding it.

Command: Free a servant for an eye or tooth injury
Summary: If a master strikes his servant and destroys an eye or knocks out a tooth, the servant goes free for the eye's sake or the tooth's sake.
Commandment: Free a servant whom you have injured by destroying an eye or knocking out a tooth.
Application: Even within servanthood, the servant's body was not the master's property to maim with impunity; grave injury broke the bond. The institution this law governed has ended, but it still teaches that power over another person never licences cruelty.
Purpose: To restrain a master: permanent injury to a servant ended the servant's service, so that cruelty cost the master his labour.

Command: Leave olive gleanings for the poor, stranger, fatherless, and widow
Summary: When you beat your olive tree, do not go over the boughs again: the remaining olives are for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow.
Commandment: Leave olive gleanings for the poor, stranger, fatherless, and widow.
Application: One beating, not a second gleaning pass: the olives left after the first beating belong to those without trees of their own. The olive yard, like the field and the vineyard, carries provision for the defenceless in its remainder.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care takes the form of olive gleanings left for the defenceless.

Command: Keep the law of an unpaid bailee
Summary: An unpaid bailee — one keeping a neighbour's money or goods for nothing — swears before God if the thing is stolen, and pays double only if he himself is found to be the thief.
Commandment: Keep the law of an unpaid bailee.
Application: Unpaid keeping is neighbourly help, so the keeper's liability is lighter than the paid keeper's: oath clears him where theft came from outside. But if the keeper himself stole, he pays double like any thief.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: an unpaid keeper answers by oath, and pays double only if he himself took the thing.

Command: Keep the law of a paid bailee
Summary: A paid bailee — one hired to keep another's animal or goods — answers by the Law's distinctions: he is liable where his own fault lost it, and cleared by oath where loss came without his fault.
Commandment: Keep the law of a paid bailee.
Application: Trusteeship is graded by reward: one paid to keep a thing bears more responsibility than one who keeps it for free. The rule still guides any paid custody — the keeper's duty matches the trust and payment he accepted.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: a paid keeper answers for goods entrusted to him, by the Law's distinctions between fault and misfortune.

Command: Keep the law of a borrower
Summary: A borrower who borrows an animal or article and it is hurt or dies while the owner is absent must make it good; if the owner was present, or it was hired, the terms differ.
Commandment: Keep the law of a borrower.
Application: Borrowing is not a gift: the borrower enjoys the use, so he bears the risk of loss while it is in his hands. The rule still teaches that borrowed things are held in trust and must be made good if lost.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the borrower who had the use of a thing answers for its loss or hurt.

Command: Do not destroy objects associated with God's name
Summary: Deuteronomy 12:4 forbids treating the LORD as the nations treated their gods: 'Ye shall not do so unto the LORD your God.' The nations destroyed and desecrated in worship; Israel was not to handle God's name, his sanctuary, or his worship with the same violence.
Commandment: Do not destroy or desecrate what is associated with God's name, as the nations did to their gods.
Application: Reverence for God's name covers his sanctuary, his word, and his worship: what bears his name is handled with honour, not smashed, defaced, or treated as common.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the verse answers the destruction of pagan altars in the preceding verses — that destruction is for idols, never for the LORD (Deuteronomy 12:2-4).

Command: Redeem a disqualified consecrated animal and eat it as common meat
Summary: The command: Redeem a disqualified consecrated animal and eat it as common meat (Deuteronomy 12:15). A consecrated animal that developed a blemish was redeemed and eaten as common meat, like the roebuck and the hart, but its blood was not eaten.
Commandment: Redeem a disqualified consecrated animal and eat it as common meat, as prescribed in Deuteronomy 12:15.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: a blemished consecrated animal lost its altar fitness but not its value; redemption kept the vow honest without wasting the beast.

Command: Examine the signs of fowl to distinguish clean from unclean
Summary: Clean fowl are known by the signs Scripture gives: the unclean birds are listed by name, and all other fowl may be eaten.
Commandment: Examine the signs of fowl: eat only what is not among the unclean birds listed in Scripture.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Deuteronomy 14 repeats the Leviticus list for a new generation entering the land. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Do not send a freed servant away empty-handed
Summary: When a Hebrew servant is sent out free in the seventh year, he must not be sent away empty-handed.
Commandment: Do not send a freed servant away empty-handed.
Application: Freedom without provision is a door into fresh destitution: the freed servant leaves with something to start on. The negative form guards the positive gift — liberation must not be hollow.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint forbids sending a freed servant away empty.

Command: Do not eat leavened bread with the Passover on the afternoon of the fourteenth day
Summary: On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, when the Passover lamb is sacrificed, no leavened bread may be eaten with it.
Commandment: On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, eat no leavened bread with the Passover sacrifice.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule ties the leaven ban directly to the Passover sacrifice itself, not only to the seven-day feast. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not leave the meat of the festival offering until the morning
Summary: The meat of the festival sacrifice offered at Passover must be eaten the same night and none left until morning.
Commandment: Do not leave any of the meat of the festival sacrifice until the morning.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The same-night rule kept the festival meal within its appointed night, as with the Passover lamb itself.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the festival sacrifice is eaten at its appointed feast (Deuteronomy 16:4).

Command: Do not offer an animal with a temporary blemish
Summary: The command: Do not offer an animal with a temporary blemish (Deuteronomy 17:1). Even a temporary blemish, a passing defect, made an animal an abomination to the LORD as a sacrifice.
Commandment: Do not offer an animal with a temporary blemish.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: any blemish, even a passing one, was an abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 17:1).

Command: The Levites shall have no inheritance portion in the land
Summary: The command: The Levites shall have no inheritance portion in the land (Deuteronomy 18:2). The LORD himself was the Levites' inheritance; they received no portion of land among their brethren.
Commandment: The Levites shall have no inheritance portion in the land.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the LORD is their inheritance, as he said unto them (Deuteronomy 18:2).

Command: Do not prophesy in the name of other gods
Summary: Deuteronomy 18:20 sentences the prophet who speaks in the name of other gods: 'even that prophet shall die.' Prophecy in another god's name imports another god's worship with it.
Commandment: Do not prophesy in the name of other gods.
Application: Scripture's stated test: when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken (Deuteronomy 18:22). A message from another god is false prophecy whatever its form.
Purpose: Scripture's stated test: when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Command: Do not prophesy falsely in God's name
Summary: Deuteronomy 18:20 sentences the prophet who presumes to speak a word in God's name which God has not commanded: 'even that prophet shall die.' The sentence guards God's name from human invention.
Commandment: Do not prophesy falsely in God's name.
Application: Scripture's stated test: when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken (Deuteronomy 18:22). The civil penalty belonged to ancient Israel; the test of truth endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated test: when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Command: Do not be afraid of killing the false prophet
Summary: When a prophet's word does not come to pass, it is a word the LORD has not spoken: do not be afraid of him, and do not let his threats bind your conscience.
Commandment: Do not be afraid of killing the false prophet.
Application: The title follows the traditional mitzvah's form, which pairs the test of fulfilment with the false prophet's sentence; its substance is freedom from fear of a prophet whose word failed. The New Testament repeats the test in church form: try the spirits whether they are of God (1 John 4:1). The death sentence belonged to Israel's court; the testing of prophets endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated test: when a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken (Deuteronomy 18:22).

Command: A judge shall not pity a murderer at trial
Summary: At the trial of a murderer, the judge's eye must not pity him so as to spare a guilty verdict: pity must not bend the finding of guilt.
Commandment: A judge shall not pity a murderer at trial.
Application: Pity has its place, but not in the finding of fact: a judge who spares a murderer out of pity has perverted judgment and left innocent blood unanswered. The cities' court procedure belonged to Israel's land system; impartiality in judging guilt endures as justice wisdom.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance forbids pity bending a murder trial.

Command: Do not oppress a servant who has fled to you for refuge
Summary: An escaped servant who dwells with you, in the place he chooses within your gates, must not be oppressed.
Commandment: Do not oppress a servant who has fled to you for refuge.
Application: Refuge that oppresses is no refuge: the escaped servant dwells where it pleases him best, and is not vexed for having fled. Protection without oppression is the whole of the law's demand toward him.
Purpose: Scripture states the command without a separate reason beyond the servant's refuge itself (Deuteronomy 23:15-16); TRADITIONAL reading: the escaped servant is treated as a person seeking protection, not property to be restored.

Command: Do not punish a person who was forced to commit a crime
Summary: A person forced to commit a crime is not punished for it: where there was no willing act, there is no guilt to punish.
Commandment: Do not punish a person who was forced to commit a crime.
Application: Guilt requires willingness: the betrothed damsel taken by force in the field is the Law's example — she cried out, none heard, and no guilt attaches to her. The principle endures wherever coercion is pleaded: the forced act is not the forced person's crime.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: guilt requires a willing act, so one forced to commit a crime bears no punishment for it; the Law's example is the damsel taken by force, to whom no guilt attaches.

Command: Do not remove the signs of skin disease
Summary: In a case of skin disease, Israel must take heed and observe diligently all that the Levitical priests teach, and not remove or tamper with the signs the priest must judge.
Commandment: Take heed in the plague of leprosy: observe diligently and do according to all that the priests the Levites teach you; do not remove the signs of the disease.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Debated: the priestly examination procedure belonged to the temple order that has ended, while the underlying duty to heed God's word and to protect neighbors from disease is read by some as enduring wisdom. The site does not settle a single duration for this verse's procedure.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the signs were preserved so the priest could judge rightly whether the disease spread or healed, protecting both the afflicted and the camp.

Command: Do not delay returning a pledge needed by the debtor
Summary: If the debtor is poor, you shall not sleep with his pledge: the garment taken in pledge is not kept overnight from a man who needs it.
Commandment: Do not delay returning a pledge needed by the debtor.
Application: A poor man's cloak is his blanket for the night: keeping it overnight takes his sleep, not only his garment. The delay itself is the offence, and the pledge must be back before dark.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that he may sleep in his own raiment, and bless thee (Deuteronomy 24:13). Here that reason forbids sleeping with a poor man's pledge.

Command: Relatives of litigants shall not testify
Summary: Fathers are not put to death for the children, nor children for the fathers: every man is put to death for his own sin, and no relative bears another's guilt in testimony or sentence.
Commandment: Relatives of litigants shall not testify.
Application: The title follows the traditional mitzvah's form, which bars relatives from testifying in one another's cases; its ground is Deuteronomy 24:16 — guilt is individual, not inherited. A relative's testimony for or against kin is barred because affection and interest bend it, and because no man answers for another's sin.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: guilt is individual — every man for his own sin — so relatives, whose affection and interest bend testimony, do not testify in one another's cases (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Command: Do not pity the enticer to idolatry
Summary: One of the Deuteronomy 13 safeguards against idolatry: do not pity the enticer to idolatry. The chapter treats enticement to idolatry as a public danger to the whole community, not a private opinion.
Commandment: Do not pity the enticer to idolatry
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3). These civil penalties belonged to ancient Israel's theocracy; the refusal to follow idolatrous leading endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Command: Do not cease hating the enticer to idolatry
Summary: One of the Deuteronomy 13 safeguards against idolatry: do not cease hating the enticer to idolatry. The chapter treats enticement to idolatry as a public danger to the whole community, not a private opinion.
Commandment: Do not cease hating the enticer to idolatry
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3). These civil penalties belonged to ancient Israel's theocracy; the refusal to follow idolatrous leading endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Command: Do not plead in defence of the enticer to idolatry
Summary: One of the Deuteronomy 13 safeguards against idolatry: do not plead in defence of the enticer to idolatry. The chapter treats enticement to idolatry as a public danger to the whole community, not a private opinion.
Commandment: Do not plead in defence of the enticer to idolatry
Application: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3). These civil penalties belonged to ancient Israel's theocracy; the refusal to follow idolatrous leading endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for the LORD your God proveth you, to know whether ye love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deuteronomy 13:3).

Command: Do not shear the firstborn sheep
Summary: The command: Do not shear the firstborn sheep (Deuteronomy 15:19). The firstling sheep might not be shorn, nor might the firstling ox be worked; both were holy to the LORD.
Commandment: Do not shear the firstborn sheep.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the firstling was holy unto the LORD and might not be used for common profit (Deuteronomy 15:19).

Command: Do not set a foreigner as king over Israel
Summary: Deuteronomy 17:15 forbids setting a stranger as king: 'thou mayest not set a stranger over thee, which is not thy brother.' The king was to be one of the covenant people, sharing their history and law.
Commandment: Do not set a foreigner as king over Israel.
Application: Scripture's stated context: Israel's desire for a king like the nations is answered by God's choice, not by the people's preference alone (Deuteronomy 17:14-15). The king from outside the covenant would bring outside gods with him.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: Israel's desire for a king like the nations is answered by God's choice, not by the people's preference alone (Deuteronomy 17:14-15).

Command: Do not return to Egypt to dwell there permanently
Summary: One of the restraints on Israel's king in Deuteronomy 17:16-17: do not return to Egypt to dwell there permanently. The king was to be kept from the usual machinery of ancient power.
Commandment: Do not return to Egypt to dwell there permanently
Application: Scripture's stated reasons: that his heart turn not away (wives, Deuteronomy 17:17), and that the people not be returned to Egypt (the horses restraint, Deuteronomy 17:16). Power was to rest on God's law, not on armies, wealth, or alliances.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reasons: that his heart turn not away (wives, Deuteronomy 17:17), and that the people not be returned to Egypt (horses, Deuteronomy 17:16).

Command: Do not work or sow the valley of the heifer
Summary: In the rite for an unsolved murder, the valley where the heifer's neck is broken is neither worked nor sown: no farming use is made of it.
Commandment: Do not work or sow the valley of the heifer.
Application: The rough valley, neither eared nor sown, is set apart for the rite alone: ordinary use would profane the place where the community answers for innocent blood. The rite belonged to Israel's land system and no longer functions.
Purpose: Scripture's stated purpose: so shall the guilt of innocent blood be put away from among you (Deuteronomy 21:9, in the form of the elders' declaration and the atonement prayer, 21:7-8).

Command: Help lift up your brother's fallen animal
Summary: If your brother's ass or ox is fallen down by the way, you shall surely help him lift it up again.
Commandment: Help lift up your brother's fallen animal.
Application: The positive form of the fallen-animal law: help is not offered from a distance but given with one's own hands, lifting what the animal cannot lift alone. Even an enemy's animal is covered by the parallel account (Exodus 23:5).
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the animal is under a burden it cannot bear, and the owner's need — even an enemy owner's need — obliges help (Exodus 23:5; Deuteronomy 22:4).

Command: A woman shall not wear a man's garment
Summary: One half of the Deuteronomy 22:5 distinction: a woman shall not wear a man's garment.
Commandment: A woman shall not wear a man's garment
Application: Scripture's stated ground: for all that do so are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 22:5). Debated: whether the verse binds specific garments today or the broader distinction it expresses is a genuine difference of reading — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: for all that do so are abomination unto the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 22:5).

Command: Do not take the mother bird with her young
Summary: One half of the mother-bird law of Deuteronomy 22:6-7: do not take the mother bird with her young. Even in taking from nature, mercy was to limit what could be taken.
Commandment: Do not take the mother bird with her young
Application: Scripture's stated reason, in the form of a promise: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days (Deuteronomy 22:7). Mercy to the creature is joined to blessing on the keeper.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason, in the form of a promise: that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days (Deuteronomy 22:7).

Command: Do not eat the produce of a vineyard sown with diverse seed
Summary: The produce of a vineyard sown with diverse seed is forfeited: it must not be eaten, for the whole is defiled by the mixture.
Commandment: Do not eat the produce of a vineyard sown with diverse seed.
Application: Deuteronomy adds a consequence to the mixture law: the fruit of a vineyard sown with diverse seed is forfeited, not eaten. The law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason Scripture does not explain; it is not restated in the New Testament and is not Christian obligation.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture; the law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason is not given. Deuteronomy 22:9 adds a consequence — the fruit is forfeited — but not a reason.

Command: Do not retrieve the forgotten sheaf
Summary: When you reap your harvest and forget a sheaf in the field, do not go back to fetch it: the forgotten sheaf stays where it fell.
Commandment: Do not retrieve the forgotten sheaf.
Application: Forgetfulness becomes provision: the sheaf left behind by accident is not recovered by the owner but left for the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow. The law turns a mistake into charity without the owner having to decide to be generous.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care takes the form of a forgotten sheaf left in the field.

Command: A newly married man shall be free at home for a year
Summary: Deuteronomy 24:5 frees a newly married man from public business for a year: 'he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.' The new household takes precedence over the state's claims.
Commandment: A newly married man shall be free at home for one year, to cheer his wife.
Application: Debated: how far these civil provisions carry into the church is genuinely disputed — this row does not settle it. What is not debated is the protection the law aimed at: a new marriage given its first year intact.
Purpose: To protect the weaker party at each family step (Deuteronomy 21-25). Debated: the divorce certificate is read by Jesus as concession to hardness of heart, not God's design (Matthew 19:8), and levirate marriage ended, while creation marriage itself is reaffirmed. The site does not settle a single duration for this cluster because its parts do not share one fate.

Command: Anybody who knows evidence must testify in court
Summary: If a person hears the voice of swearing — is called as a witness — and knows evidence but does not utter it, he bears his iniquity: one who knows evidence must testify.
Commandment: Anybody who knows evidence must testify in court.
Application: Silence is not neutrality when a court needs the truth: the witness who withholds what he knows lets a false case stand. The duty to testify endures wherever justice depends on witnesses willing to speak.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: justice depends on witnesses who speak what they know; withholding evidence lets a false case stand, so the witness who stays silent bears the guilt.

Command: Bring an ascending and descending offering according to means
Summary: The command: Bring an ascending and descending offering according to means (Leviticus 5:7). The offering slid with the sinner's means: lamb or goat, two birds, or fine flour for the very poor, so no one was shut out from atonement.
Commandment: Bring an ascending and descending offering according to means, as prescribed in Leviticus 5:7.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Do not sever the head of a fowl brought as a sin offering
Summary: The command: Do not sever the head of a fowl brought as a sin offering (Leviticus 5:8). The priest wrung off the bird's head for the sin offering without severing it from the body.
Commandment: Do not sever the head of a fowl brought as a sin offering.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Burn sacrifices left over past their eating time
Summary: The command: Burn sacrifices left over past their eating time (Leviticus 7:17). Flesh of a peace offering remaining on the third day was burned with fire.
Commandment: Burn sacrifices left over past their eating time, as prescribed in Leviticus 7:17.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah.
