Command: Examine the signs of locusts to distinguish clean from unclean
Summary: Among winged creeping things, only those with jointed legs above their feet for leaping — locusts, crickets, and grasshoppers after their kinds — are clean.
Commandment: Examine the signs of locusts and like insects: only those with legs for leaping are clean to eat.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The leaping-leg sign separated a few clean insects from the rest of the swarming kinds. The New Testament records these food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: To mark Israel's table as distinct (Leviticus 11). The New Testament records the distinctions set aside: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and Peter's vision confirms it (Acts 10).

Command: Observe the laws of menstrual impurity
Summary: A woman in her monthly separation is unclean seven days, and whoever touches her or what she lies or sits upon is unclean until the evening and must wash.
Commandment: Observe the laws of menstrual impurity: seven days of separation, with washing for any contact.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The seven-day separation ordered household life around the rhythm of uncleanness and return. Jesus' touch restored those the purity laws isolated (Luke 8:43-48).
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Do not make pleasurable contact with a forbidden woman
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not make pleasurable contact with a forbidden woman. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not make pleasurable contact with a forbidden woman
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Do not eat flesh left over from a sacrifice
Summary: The command: Do not eat flesh left over from a sacrifice (Leviticus 19:8). A peace offering eaten on the third day was an abomination and was not accepted; what remained was to be burned.
Commandment: Do not eat flesh left over from a sacrifice.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: flesh eaten on the third day is an abomination and is not accepted (Leviticus 19:7-8).

Command: Do not eat fruit of a tree during its first three years
Summary: Fruit of a newly planted tree is not to be eaten during its first three years; it is counted as uncircumcised, set apart and not for use.
Commandment: Do not eat fruit of a tree during its first three years.
Application: The three-year wait taught patience and restraint: the planter does not snatch the first fruit but lets the tree establish itself. The rule belonged to Israel's land law; whether and how it binds outside the land is a matter of the land system's scope, and it is drafted here in its stated form.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture for the three-year bar; it is classed among the statutes whose wisdom is God's own, teaching restraint with firstfruits.

Command: The fourth-year crops must be holy
Summary: In the fourth year, all the fruit of the tree is holy, to praise the LORD with; only from the fifth year is it eaten as ordinary food.
Commandment: The fourth-year crops must be holy.
Application: The fourth year's fruit is consecrated in praise before any of it is eaten as common food. The sequence — three years untouched, one year holy, then ordinary use — orders the planter's claim on his own tree behind God's claim.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the fourth year's fruit is holy to the LORD, so that the planter's use of his tree begins with consecration, not consumption.

Command: Bring a guilt offering for relations with a betrothed bondwoman
Summary: The command: Bring a guilt offering for relations with a betrothed bondwoman (Leviticus 19:22). A man who lay with a bondwoman betrothed to another brought a ram as a trespass offering, and the woman was scourged rather than put to death.
Commandment: Bring a guilt offering for relations with a betrothed bondwoman, as prescribed in Leviticus 19:22.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the offering made atonement where the death penalty did not apply, because the woman was not free; guilt still required blood and restitution.

Command: The high priest shall not have relations with a widow even outside marriage
Summary: The command: The high priest shall not have relations with a widow even outside marriage (Leviticus 21:15). The prohibition reached beyond marriage itself: the high priest was not to profane his seed by relations with a widow.
Commandment: The high priest shall not have relations with a widow even outside marriage.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The marriage rules guarded the priesthood's public holiness in a world where priests were public figures; they are not Christian marriage law, which is governed by creation and by the New Testament household commands (Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:22-33). The high priest's stricter rule — a virgin of his own people — is included here as the second half of the same law.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8).

Command: An impure priest shall not serve in the sanctuary
Summary: The command: An impure priest shall not serve in the sanctuary (Leviticus 22:2). A priest in a state of uncleanness was to be separated from the holy things and not approach them in his uncleanness.
Commandment: An impure priest shall not serve in the sanctuary.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the holy things are the LORD's, and uncleanness profanes them (Leviticus 22:2-3).

Command: An impure priest after immersion shall not serve until sundown
Summary: The command: An impure priest after immersion shall not serve until sundown (Leviticus 22:7). A priest who washed for uncleanness remained unclean until evening, and only then might eat of the holy things.
Commandment: An impure priest after immersion shall not serve until sundown.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament replaces the whole system of holy food: all who are in Christ are a holy priesthood (1 Peter 2:5,9), and the meal that marks God's people is the Lord's Supper, not the priestly portions. The boundary itself — holy things are not common things — is fulfilled, not continued.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the holy things are the LORD's, set apart for the priesthood (Leviticus 22:3-16).

Command: Do not slaughter a blemished animal as a sacrifice
Summary: The command: Do not slaughter a blemished animal as a sacrifice (Leviticus 22:22). A blemished animal might not be slaughtered as a sacrifice, even if its fat was not burned.
Commandment: Do not slaughter a blemished animal as a sacrifice.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: a blemished animal was not acceptable as the bread of God (Leviticus 22:22).

Command: Do not burn the fat of a blemished animal
Summary: The command: Do not burn the fat of a blemished animal (Leviticus 22:22). The fat of a blemished beast might not be burned on the altar as an offering made by fire.
Commandment: Do not burn the fat of a blemished animal.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: the fat of a blemished beast was not an acceptable offering made by fire (Leviticus 22:22).

Command: Do not leave sacrifices past the time allowed for eating them
Summary: The command: Do not leave sacrifices past the time allowed for eating them (Leviticus 22:30). Each offering had its appointed eating time; what remained beyond it was not to be eaten.
Commandment: Do not leave sacrifices past the time allowed for eating them.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: an offering eaten beyond its appointed day was not accepted (Leviticus 22:30; Leviticus 19:7-8).

Command: The court shall count seven sabbaths of years
Summary: The court counts seven sabbaths of years — seven times seven years, forty-nine years — to fix the Jubilee.
Commandment: The court shall count seven sabbaths of years.
Application: Jubilee is not guessed at but counted: the court's count of seven sabbaths of years makes the fiftieth year a public, dated fact, proclaimed to all. Orderly counting keeps release from depending on anyone's memory or favour.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). The counting of seven sabbaths of years fixes the Jubilee as a public date, not a private guess.

Command: Do not compel a Hebrew servant to do slave labour
Summary: A Hebrew who has sold himself to you because of poverty must not be compelled to do the labour of a slave; he serves as a hired servant and sojourner.
Commandment: Do not compel a Hebrew servant to do slave labour.
Application: The distinction mattered: a Hebrew servant was a brother in hardship, not chattel, and his work was bounded accordingly. The laws regulated an ancient institution rather than endorsing it, and the institution has ended.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint forbids slave labour for a Hebrew servant.

Command: Do not allow a foreigner to rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour
Summary: A foreign master must not be allowed to rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour in your sight; the community bears responsibility for a brother sold outside it.
Commandment: Do not allow a foreigner to rule over a Hebrew servant with rigour.
Application: Responsibility does not end at the community's edge: Israel was to watch over a brother even under a foreign master, and not stand by while he was crushed. The institution has ended, but the duty not to look away from a brother's oppression has not.
Purpose: To regulate and restrain an ancient institution: six-year release, provision, no ruthless rule (Exodus 21; Deuteronomy 15). Here that restraint extends to a Hebrew under a foreign master.

Command: Do not bow down on smooth stone
Summary: Leviticus 26:1 forbids bowing down on a figured or smooth stone set up for worship: 'neither shall ye set up any image of stone in your land, to bow down unto it: for I am the LORD your God.' The stone need not be a statue to be an idol's furniture.
Commandment: Do not bow down on smooth or figured stone set up for worship.
Application: Worship is not made lawful by a humble object: a stone slab used as an idol's place is as forbidden as a golden calf. God alone receives bowing worship.
Purpose: Scripture's stated seal: for I am the LORD your God (Leviticus 26:1).

Command: Estimate the value of consecrated animals
Summary: The command: Estimate the value of consecrated animals (Leviticus 27:12). A beast vowed to the LORD was set before the priest, who estimated its value, and that estimation stood.
Commandment: Estimate the value of consecrated animals, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:12.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: Estimate the value of consecrated houses
Summary: The command: Estimate the value of consecrated houses (Leviticus 27:14). A house sanctified to the LORD was valued by the priest, and his estimation stood.
Commandment: Estimate the value of consecrated houses, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:14.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Command: Do not eat sacrifices offered with improper intention
Summary: The command: Do not eat sacrifices offered with improper intention (Leviticus 7:18). An offering eaten with the intention of eating it beyond its appointed day was an abomination and brought iniquity on the eater.
Commandment: Do not eat sacrifices offered with improper intention.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Burn sacrifices that became impure
Summary: The command: Burn sacrifices that became impure (Leviticus 7:19). Flesh that touched any unclean thing was burned with fire, not eaten.
Commandment: Burn sacrifices that became impure, as prescribed in Leviticus 7:19.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: A priest shall not serve with torn garments
Summary: The command: A priest shall not serve with torn garments (Leviticus 10:6). Aaron and his sons were not to tear their garments in mourning while the anointing oil was upon them.
Commandment: A priest shall not serve with torn garments.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Do not have relations with your father's brother
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not have relations with your father's brother. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not have relations with your father's brother
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Do not have relations with your father
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not have relations with your father. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not have relations with your father
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Do not have relations with your daughter
Summary: One of the boundaries of Leviticus 18: do not have relations with your daughter. The chapter forbids these unions as defiling, and warns that the land itself would spew out a people who practised them (Leviticus 18:24-28).
Commandment: Do not have relations with your daughter
Application: Leviticus 18 marks God's people as holy and distinct, and the New Testament reaffirms sexual purity, honouring the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20; Hebrews 13:4).
Purpose: To mark God's people as holy and distinct (Leviticus 18) and, in the New Testament, to honor the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Command: Do not reap the corner of your field
Summary: The corner of the field is not to be reaped wholly; a corner is left standing for the poor.
Commandment: Do not reap the corner of your field.
Application: Leaving the corner unreaped is deliberate incompleteness: the owner stops short of his full harvest so that the landless have a field to glean. The corner is not an accident of farming but a provision of law.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the field, that care takes the form of an unreaped corner.

Command: Do not gather the gleanings of your harvest
Summary: When reaping the harvest, the gleanings — what the reapers drop or leave — are not to be gathered up by the owner.
Commandment: Do not gather the gleanings of your harvest.
Application: The harvester's dropped sheaf is not waste to be recovered but provision left in the field. Gleaning law builds charity into the harvest itself, so the poor gather with dignity rather than begging for a dole.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the harvest, that care takes the form of leaving the gleanings ungathered.

Command: Do not gather the gleanings of your vineyard
Summary: After the vintage, the gleanings of the vineyard — the grapes left behind — are not to be gathered by the owner.
Commandment: Do not gather the gleanings of your vineyard.
Application: The vineyard owner takes his harvest and leaves the remainder where the poor and the stranger can find it. Gleaning law turns the edge of the field into a table for those without land of their own.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the vineyard, that care takes the form of leaving the gleanings ungathered.

Command: Leave the unformed clusters of grapes for the poor and stranger
Summary: The unformed clusters of grapes are left for the poor and the stranger, not stripped by the owner after the vintage.
Commandment: Leave the unformed clusters of grapes for the poor and stranger.
Application: What the owner might dismiss as not worth picking is another family's food. The law dignifies the small remainder: provision for the poor includes the imperfect clusters, not only the full harvest.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the vineyard, that care takes the form of leaving the unformed clusters for the poor and stranger.

Command: Do not pick the unformed clusters of grapes
Summary: The small, unformed clusters of grapes — the imperfect bunches left on the vine — are not to be picked clean by the owner.
Commandment: Do not pick the unformed clusters of grapes.
Application: Even the imperfect fruit counts as provision: the owner does not strip the vine bare but leaves the small clusters for those who come after the harvest. Generosity is measured by what is left, not only by what is given.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). In the vineyard, that care takes the form of leaving the unformed clusters unpicked.

Command: Do not steal stealthily
Summary: Do not steal by stealth — quietly taking what is not yours, even where no force is used.
Commandment: Do not steal stealthily.
Application: Stealth does not soften theft; it is theft's ordinary form, the quiet taking that hopes nobody will notice. The command names the secret taking alongside open robbery, so that no thief can plead that he took gently.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: taking by stealth is theft no less than taking by force, and is forbidden as such (Leviticus 19:11).

Command: Do not shame or embarrass your neighbour
Summary: One of the neighbour-laws of Leviticus 19:17-18: do not shame or embarrass your neighbour, part of the passage that ends in 'thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.'
Commandment: Do not shame or embarrass your neighbour
Application: Jesus joins this neighbour rule to love of God as the hinge of the Law (Matthew 22:39-40); love of neighbour is the measure of love of God in practice.
Purpose: Leviticus 19:18 states the neighbor rule; Jesus joins it to love of God as the hinge of the Law (Matthew 22:39-40).

Command: Men must not destroy the corners of the beard
Summary: One of the appearance laws of Leviticus 19:27: men must not destroy the corners of the beard.
Commandment: Men must not destroy the corners of the beard
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the corners marked Israel's consecration and separated its mourning and appearance from neighbouring pagan customs. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the corners marked Israel's consecration and separated its mourning and appearance from neighbouring pagan customs. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Leviticus 19:27).

Command: Do not tattoo marks on the skin
Summary: One of the mourning marks forbidden in Leviticus 19:28: do not tattoo marks on the skin.
Commandment: Do not tattoo marks on the skin
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: cuttings and marks were the visible rites of pagan mourning and idolatrous devotion; Israel's grief was not to take those forms. Debated: whether the prohibition covers all permanent marks today, or only marks made for the dead and for idolatry, is a genuine difference of reading — this row does not settle it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: cuttings and marks were the visible rites of pagan mourning and idolatrous devotion; Israel's grief was not to take those forms. Scripture states the prohibition with the qualifier 'for the dead' (Leviticus 19:28).

Command: A priest shall not marry a zonah
Summary: The command: A priest shall not marry a zonah (Leviticus 21:7). A priest might not marry a zonah, a woman of unchaste profession.
Commandment: A priest shall not marry a zonah.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The marriage rules guarded the priesthood's public holiness in a world where priests were public figures; they are not Christian marriage law, which is governed by creation and by the New Testament household commands (Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:22-33). The high priest's stricter rule — a virgin of his own people — is included here as the second half of the same law.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8).

Command: A priest shall not marry a chalalah
Summary: The command: A priest shall not marry a chalalah (Leviticus 21:7). A priest might not marry a woman profaned by a forbidden union, a chalalah, whose status would profane his seed.
Commandment: A priest shall not marry a chalalah.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The marriage rules guarded the priesthood's public holiness in a world where priests were public figures; they are not Christian marriage law, which is governed by creation and by the New Testament household commands (Matthew 19:3-9; Ephesians 5:22-33). The high priest's stricter rule — a virgin of his own people — is included here as the second half of the same law.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he is holy unto his God (Leviticus 21:7-8).

Command: A priest with a temporary blemish shall not serve
Summary: The command: A priest with a temporary blemish shall not serve (Leviticus 21:17). Even a passing blemish barred a priest from offering while it lasted, until he was whole again.
Commandment: A priest with a temporary blemish shall not serve.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The blemish did not make the priest unclean or unwelcome: he still ate the bread of his God, most holy and holy (Leviticus 21:22). He was barred only from approaching to offer — a visible picture that the offering itself must be unblemished, pointing to the unblemished Lamb (1 Peter 1:19).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: he shall not profane my sanctuaries, for I the LORD do sanctify them (Leviticus 21:23).

Command: Offer only unblemished animals
Summary: The command: Offer only unblemished animals (Leviticus 22:21). Every offering brought to the altar was to be perfect, without blemish, that it might be accepted.
Commandment: Offer only unblemished animals, as prescribed in Leviticus 22:21.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: it shall be perfect to be accepted (Leviticus 22:21).

Command: Do not inflict a wound on a dedicated animal
Summary: The command: Do not inflict a wound on a dedicated animal (Leviticus 22:21). An animal dedicated to the LORD was not to be wounded or marred, since only the unblemished was acceptable.
Commandment: Do not inflict a wound on a dedicated animal.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: only an unblemished gift was fitting for the LORD; marring a dedicated animal dishonoured the offering.

Command: Do not sprinkle the blood of a blemished animal
Summary: The command: Do not sprinkle the blood of a blemished animal (Leviticus 22:22). The blood of a blemished animal might not be sprinkled on the altar.
Commandment: Do not sprinkle the blood of a blemished animal.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated ground: blood sprinkled from a blemished animal could not make an acceptable offering (Leviticus 22:22).

Command: Do not eat parched grain from the new crop before the sheaf offering
Summary: No parched grain of the new harvest may be eaten until the sheaf of firstfruits has been waved before the LORD.
Commandment: Eat no parched corn from the new crop until the day the sheaf offering is brought.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The first sheaf went to God before Israel ate of the harvest: firstfruits first, then the table. The New Testament keeps the principle in a new key — Christ is the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the confession itself gives the reason — 'a Syrian ready to perish was my father,' and God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them this land (Deuteronomy 26:5-10).

Command: Do not eat green ears from the new crop before the sheaf offering
Summary: No green ears of the new grain harvest may be eaten until the sheaf of firstfruits has been waved before the LORD.
Commandment: Eat no green ears from the new crop until the day the sheaf offering is brought.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The first sheaf went to God before Israel ate of the harvest: firstfruits first, then the table. The New Testament keeps the principle in a new key — Christ is the firstfruits of them that slept (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the confession itself gives the reason — 'a Syrian ready to perish was my father,' and God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them this land (Deuteronomy 26:5-10).

Command: Do not prune in the sabbatical year
Summary: In the seventh year the vineyard is not pruned: the land keeps a sabbath to the LORD, and the vine is left untrimmed.
Commandment: Do not prune in the sabbatical year.
Application: Pruning is the farmer's care for next year's crop; forbearing it for a year is a visible act of trust. The sabbatical year interrupted the ordinary cycle of work, teaching Israel that the land — and its people — rest by God's command, not by exhaustion.
Purpose: To prevent permanent destitution and permanent debt in Israel (Leviticus 25; Deuteronomy 15). In the sabbatical year, that purpose takes the form of a land left to rest, unpruned.

Command: The substituted animal also retains consecration
Summary: The command: The substituted animal also retains consecration (Leviticus 27:10). If an exchange was made anyway, both the original animal and its substitute were holy.
Commandment: The substituted animal also retains consecration, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:10.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: A devoted thing shall not be redeemed
Summary: The command: A devoted thing shall not be redeemed (Leviticus 27:28). A thing devoted under the ban, whether man, beast, or field, could not be redeemed at any price.
Commandment: A devoted thing shall not be redeemed.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: Destroy all leaven on the fourteenth of Nisan
Summary: On the fourteenth day of Nisan, all leaven must be put away from Israel's houses before the Passover meal.
Commandment: On the fourteenth day of Nisan, put away all leaven from your houses.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The removal of leaven pictured leaving Egypt in haste, with no time for bread to rise, and a clean break from the old life there. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not eat any mixture containing leaven during Passover
Summary: Nothing containing leaven — no leavened mixture of any kind — may be eaten during the Passover feast.
Commandment: Eat nothing containing leaven during the seven days of Unleavened Bread.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The rule closed every loophole: leaven was excluded not only as bread but in any mixture. Debated: some see the commanded observance fulfilled as shadow (Colossians 2:16-17); others keep feasts voluntarily as memorial, not as binding command. The site does not settle whether observance continues.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Do not make figures of human beings
Summary: Exodus 20:23 forbids making gods of silver and gods of gold alongside the LORD — in the traditional reading, figures fashioned in human form for worship. The verse follows the ban on other gods and graven images, closing off the most dignified form of idolatry: an image that looks like a person.
Commandment: Do not make figures of human beings as gods, whether of silver or of gold, to set beside the LORD.
Application: Idolatry is not excused by fine materials or lifelike form. Worship belongs to the unseen God alone, who cannot be contained in any figure his creatures make.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the prohibition guards the second commandment — no image, however noble its form, may stand beside or represent the LORD (Exodus 20:4-5, 23).

Command: Do not withhold food, clothing, or conjugal rights from a wife
Summary: Exodus 21:10 protects a wife whose husband takes another wife: 'her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish.' A second marriage may not impoverish the first wife.
Commandment: Do not diminish a wife's food, clothing, or conjugal rights.
Application: The law restrained a practice it did not commend, protecting the first wife's standing. Its form belonged to ancient Israel's household law; its principle — a wife's provision and honour are not to be cut back — endures.
Purpose: To protect a wife's standing when her husband takes another wife: her food, clothing, and marital rights are not to be diminished (Exodus 21:10).

Command: Do not benefit from the flesh of an ox condemned to stoning
Summary: The flesh of an ox that has been condemned to stoning for killing a person is not to be eaten or otherwise turned to profit.
Commandment: Do not benefit from the flesh of an ox condemned to stoning.
Application: A death that the Law treated as a judgment was not to become somebody's dinner or profit. The rule guards against turning a solemn sentence into gain.
Purpose: To keep a court sentence solemn: what the Law condemned was not to be converted into private benefit.

Command: Court shall judge damages by a goring ox
Summary: When an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox is to be stoned and the owner judged according to the case — acquitted if the ox had not been known to gore, liable if it had.
Commandment: The court shall judge damages by a goring ox according to whether the animal was known to be dangerous.
Application: Liability follows knowledge: an owner who knew his animal was dangerous and did not restrain it bears a heavier guilt than one taken by surprise. The same rule of known risk still shapes fair judgments about negligence today.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the owner answers for the damage his animal causes, in proportion to what he knew and failed to prevent.

Command: Court shall carry out the laws of plaintiff, admitter, and denier
Summary: In a dispute over goods, where one claims a deposit and the other denies or admits part, the court carries out the laws of plaintiff, admitter, and denier — including oath and double payment where the Law assigns them.
Commandment: The court shall carry out the laws of plaintiff, admitter, and denier.
Application: Disputes are not settled by who shouts loudest but by the Law's procedures: claim, admission, denial, and oath each have their consequence. Orderly procedure protects both the claimant and the accused from arbitrary judgment.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: disputed deposits are settled by the Law's fixed procedures for plaintiff, admitter, and denier.

Command: Leave sabbatical-year produce free for the poor
Summary: In the sabbatical year, what the land produces of itself is left free: the poor of the people and the beasts of the field may eat of it.
Commandment: Leave sabbatical-year produce free for the poor.
Application: The sabbatical year taught dependence: for one year in seven the land was not worked, and its unaided produce belonged to whoever needed it. The calendar system belonged to Israel's land order, but the lesson — provision for the poor is built into the rhythm of work, not left to leftovers — endures.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the sabbatical year rested the land and fed the poor from its unaided produce, so that need was met without the poor having to beg for it.

Command: A non-priest shall not eat sacrificial meat
Summary: The command: A non-priest shall not eat sacrificial meat (Exodus 29:33). The flesh of the consecration offerings belonged to Aaron and his sons alone.
Commandment: A non-priest shall not eat sacrificial meat.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Prepare the holy anointing oil
Summary: The command: Prepare the holy anointing oil (Exodus 30:31). The holy anointing oil, compounded of choice spices and olive oil, consecrated the tabernacle, its vessels, and the priests.
Commandment: Prepare the holy anointing oil, as prescribed in Exodus 30:31.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Do not eat meat cooked with milk
Summary: Meat cooked with milk may not be eaten; the mixture is forbidden at Israel's table.
Commandment: Do not eat meat cooked with milk.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The threefold form — not to cook, not to eat, not to benefit — closes every use of the mixture. The New Testament records the food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the prohibition keeps what gives life (milk) from being mixed with what takes life (meat) in cooking and eating, and keeps Israel's table distinct; Scripture states no reason for this rule.

Command: Confess wrongdoing and repent
Summary: Numbers 5:7 requires confession where wrong has been done: 'then they shall confess their sin which they have done: and he shall recompense his trespass with the principal thereof, and add unto it the fifth part thereof.' Confession here is joined to restitution, not offered instead of it.
Commandment: Confess the sin you have done, and make recompense for it.
Application: Confession without repayment is only half the command, and repayment without confession hides the wrong. The church keeps both together: confess, and put right what can be put right.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: confession precedes recompense in the trespass procedure (Numbers 5:6-7).

Command: Do not put oil on a sotah meal offering
Summary: The command: Do not put oil on a sotah meal offering (Numbers 5:15). The jealousy offering was barley meal without oil, an offering of memorial, not of tribute.
Commandment: Do not put oil on a sotah meal offering.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. This procedure belongs entirely to Israel's theocratic court: it was a public ordeal for a case no witness could settle, and it has no Christian counterpart — the New Testament settles suspected adultery by witness, confession, and church discipline (Matthew 18:15-17; John 8:3-11, where Jesus refuses a trap trial).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the procedure gave a suspected wife a public, God-decided vindication instead of a husband's private vengeance. Scripture states the procedure without a stated reason beyond the spirit of jealousy coming upon the husband (Numbers 5:14,30).

Command: Do not put frankincense on a sotah meal offering
Summary: The command: Do not put frankincense on a sotah meal offering (Numbers 5:15). The jealousy offering of barley meal carried no oil and no frankincense, for it was an offering of memorial bringing iniquity to remembrance.
Commandment: Do not put frankincense on a sotah meal offering.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. This procedure belongs entirely to Israel's theocratic court: it was a public ordeal for a case no witness could settle, and it has no Christian counterpart — the New Testament settles suspected adultery by witness, confession, and church discipline (Matthew 18:15-17; John 8:3-11, where Jesus refuses a trap trial).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the procedure gave a suspected wife a public, God-decided vindication instead of a husband's private vengeance. Scripture states the procedure without a stated reason beyond the spirit of jealousy coming upon the husband (Numbers 5:14,30).

Command: Levites shall carry the ark on their shoulders
Summary: The command: Levites shall carry the ark on their shoulders (Numbers 7:9). The sons of Kohath bore the ark and the holy vessels on their shoulders, not on a cart, when the camp set forward.
Commandment: Levites shall carry the ark on their shoulders, as prescribed in Numbers 7:9.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the ark, the throne of God's presence, was borne by consecrated hands on shoulders, not hauled as common freight.

Command: Do not break a bone of the second Passover lamb
Summary: No bone of the second Passover lamb may be broken, as with the first Passover; all its ordinances are kept.
Commandment: Do not break any bone of the second Passover lamb.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The unbroken-bone detail carries over whole to the second date, as do all the ordinances. John 19:36 applies the detail to Jesus.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the men defiled by a dead body asked why they should be kept back from offering the LORD's offering — and God answered with a second date, not a refusal (Numbers 9:6-11).

Command: Do not leave second Passover meat until morning
Summary: None of the second Passover lamb may be left until morning; what remains is dealt with as the ordinance prescribes.
Commandment: Leave none of the second Passover lamb until the morning.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The same-night rule carries over whole to the second date, as do all the ordinances of the Passover.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the men defiled by a dead body asked why they should be kept back from offering the LORD's offering — and God answered with a second date, not a refusal (Numbers 9:6-11).

Command: Do not leave the sanctuary unguarded
Summary: The command: Do not leave the sanctuary unguarded (Numbers 18:5). Aaron and his sons kept the charge of the sanctuary and the altar, that wrath would not come upon Israel.
Commandment: Do not leave the sanctuary unguarded.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that there be no wrath upon the congregation of Israel (Numbers 18:5).

Command: Observe the laws of corpse impurity
Summary: Whoever touches a dead body, a bone, a slain man, or a grave, or enters the tent of the dead, is unclean seven days and is purified with the water of separation on the third and seventh days.
Commandment: Whoever touches a dead body is unclean seven days, and shall purify himself with the water of separation on the third and seventh days.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Death was the gravest defilement in the Law, which is why its cleansing took seven days and the strangest rite. The New Testament answers it directly: Christ touches the dead and they live (1 Corinthians 15:26).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the law of the dead body defiles tent, vessels, and persons (Numbers 19:14-16); the water of separation is the appointed cleansing (Numbers 19:17-19).

Command: Offer the Shemini Atzeret additional offering
Summary: On the eighth day, the solemn assembly after Tabernacles, the appointed burnt offering and sin offering are brought as its own additional offering.
Commandment: Offer the appointed offerings of the eighth day, the solemn assembly.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: Carry out the laws of annulling vows
Summary: The laws of annulling vows are carried out as the Law sets them: a father may annul his young daughter's vow on the day he hears it, and a husband his wife's, with the stated consequences.
Commandment: Carry out the laws of annulling vows.
Application: Annulling a vow is not casual release but a household procedure: the father or husband who hears the vow may disallow it the same day, and the LORD forgives her. The procedure protected the household from rash vows while keeping every vow solemn.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: vows bind, so release from a vow must itself follow a fixed procedure — the father's or husband's same-day annulment — rather than private disregard.

Command: Do not kill a murderer before he stands trial
Summary: A manslayer must not be killed before he stands before the congregation in judgment: the avenger of blood may not strike before trial.
Commandment: Do not kill a murderer before he stands trial.
Application: Trial before punishment is the cities-of-refuge law's first guard: even the avenger waits for a hearing, because intent must be judged, not assumed. The cities belonged to Israel's land system and no longer function; the fair-trial principle they embodied endures as justice wisdom.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance forbids killing before trial.

Command: Court shall send an accidental manslayer to a city of refuge
Summary: When the congregation judges an unintentional manslayer, the court sends him to his city of refuge, where he remains until the death of the high priest.
Commandment: Court shall send an accidental manslayer to a city of refuge.
Application: The city was both prison and protection: the manslayer lived there, safe from the avenger, until the high priest's death released him. Intent, not only outcome, determined his fate — and the city gave intent a place to be judged.
Purpose: To balance life's sacredness with intent: the unintentional killer fled to a city and stood trial, safe from vengeance (Numbers 35). Here that balance takes the form of the court's sentence to a city of refuge.

Command: An apostate shall not eat the Passover
Summary: One who has turned away from the LORD's covenant may not eat the Passover meal.
Commandment: No apostate shall eat the Passover.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The Passover table was for those within the covenant; turning away from it meant exclusion from its memorial meal.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the meal is eaten in haste on the night of deliverance from Egypt, ready to depart (Exodus 12:11).

Command: Break the neck of an unredeemed firstborn donkey
Summary: The command: Break the neck of an unredeemed firstborn donkey (Exodus 13:13). An unclean animal could not be offered, so if its owner would not redeem it with a lamb, its neck was broken instead.
Commandment: Break the neck of an unredeemed firstborn donkey, as prescribed in Exodus 13:13.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Redemption of the firstborn remembered that God spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt. The New Testament speaks of Jesus as the firstborn and of believers as redeemed, but does not continue the redemption payment as a Christian rite (Colossians 1:15-18; 1 Peter 1:18-19).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: because the LORD slew all the firstborn in Egypt and spared Israel's, therefore the firstborn are his (Exodus 13:14-15).

Command: Betroth a Hebrew maidservant
Summary: Exodus 21:8-9 requires that a master who takes a maidservant deal with her as a wife: if he betroths her to himself or to his son, she is treated as a daughter, with a wife's standing, not a servant's.
Commandment: Betroth a Hebrew maidservant taken for a wife, and treat her with a wife's standing.
Application: The law restrained an ancient institution by giving the maidservant a protected standing in the household. The institution has ended; the protection of the vulnerable party remains the lesson.
Purpose: To give a maidservant a protected standing in the household: the master who takes her must treat her as a wife, not as property to be discarded (Exodus 21:8-9).

Command: Allow redemption of a Hebrew maidservant
Summary: Exodus 21:8 provides for a maidservant taken for a wife and then not pleasing her master: she may be redeemed, and he has no power to sell her to a strange nation. Her future is not closed by his refusal.
Commandment: Allow a Hebrew maidservant to be redeemed if her master does not take her as wife.
Application: The law restrained an ancient institution by keeping a door open for the maidservant. The institution has ended; the restraint — no person treated as mere property to be discarded — points past regulation to brotherhood (Philemon 16).
Purpose: To keep a maidservant's future from being closed off: if her master does not take her as wife, she may be redeemed rather than sold to strangers (Exodus 21:8).

Command: Do not cheat a convert monetarily
Summary: One of the protections for the vulnerable in Exodus 22: do not cheat a convert monetarily.
Commandment: Do not cheat a convert monetarily
Application: God's care for those without a defender is carried by James into the church as pure religion: visiting orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27).

Command: Do not wrong a convert with words
Summary: One of the protections for the vulnerable in Exodus 22: do not wrong a convert with words.
Commandment: Do not wrong a convert with words
Application: God's care for those without a defender is carried by James into the church as pure religion: visiting orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27).

Command: Do not press a debtor for payment when he cannot pay
Summary: A creditor must not press a debtor for payment like an exactor when the debtor cannot pay; the law forbids treating a poor borrower as a thing to be squeezed.
Commandment: Do not press a debtor for payment when he cannot pay.
Application: Collection has a limit set by mercy: the creditor's right to be repaid does not licence harassment of a man who has nothing. Patience with the genuinely unable is part of justice, not a softening of it.
Purpose: To protect the poor debtor: the creditor's claim does not extend to pressing a man who cannot pay.

Command: Do not intermediate, guarantee, witness, or write a note for an interest loan
Summary: No one may act as intermediary, guarantor, witness, or scribe of a note for a loan on interest between brothers — the whole apparatus of usury is forbidden, not only the lender's hand.
Commandment: Do not intermediate, guarantee, witness, or write a note for an interest loan between brothers.
Application: The ban reaches everyone who would make an unlawful loan work: the middleman, the guarantor, the witness, and the clerk. A wrong is not made right by doing only a small part of it.
Purpose: To make wrongs right: the prohibition on interest to a brother binds every party who enables the loan, not only the lender.

Command: Judges shall not hear one party in the absence of the other
Summary: A judge must not hear one party in the absence of the other; both sides are heard before judgment is given.
Commandment: Judges shall not hear one party in the absence of the other.
Application: Secret hearings breed suspicion and favouritism. A fair court hears both parties together, so that each can answer the other's claim before any judgment falls.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: just judgment requires both parties to be heard; hearing one side alone prejudges the cause.

Command: Court shall decide by majority
Summary: The court decides by majority: after deliberation, the verdict follows the greater number of judges.
Commandment: The court shall decide by majority.
Application: Deliberation without decision is paralysis, so the Law gives the court a way to conclude: the majority decides. Majority rule settles the verdict; it does not by itself make the verdict just, which is why the surrounding laws guard against following a multitude to do evil.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: a court must be able to reach a verdict, and the majority decides — while the companion laws guard the majority itself against following a multitude to do evil (Exodus 23:2).

Command: Court shall not execute on a majority of one in a capital case
Summary: In a capital case the court must not execute on a majority of one; a death sentence requires a stronger majority than a single vote.
Commandment: The court shall not execute on a majority of one in a capital case.
Application: Life is weighed more heavily than other verdicts: a bare majority is not enough to put a man to death. The extra margin is a deliberate brake on irreversible judgment.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: because a death sentence cannot be undone, a majority of one is insufficient to execute in a capital case. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 23:2).

Command: A judge who argued for acquittal shall not argue for conviction in a capital case
Summary: In a capital case, a judge who argued for acquittal must not later turn and argue for conviction on the same case.
Commandment: A judge who argued for acquittal shall not argue for conviction in a capital case.
Application: The rule leans the court toward life: once a judge has seen a ground for acquittal, he may not reverse himself to seek a death sentence. In capital cases, the court is guarded against its own momentum toward condemnation.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: in a capital case the court is guarded against turning toward death, so a judge who argued for acquittal may not argue for conviction. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 23:2).

Command: A judge shall not base his opinion on another judge's opinion
Summary: A judge must not form his opinion merely by following another judge's opinion; each judge judges on the evidence before him.
Commandment: A judge shall not base his opinion on another judge's opinion.
Application: Deference is not judgment. A judge who merely echoes a colleague has not judged the case, and a court of echoes cannot be trusted to find the truth.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the multitude can carry a court away from the truth, and the law guards the lone witness and the unpopular party against that pressure. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 23:2).

Command: Court shall not inflict punishment on the Sabbath
Summary: No judicial punishment is to be inflicted on the Sabbath day; the day of rest is not a day of penalties.
Commandment: Let no punishment be inflicted by the court on the Sabbath day.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Even the work of justice paused, so that the Sabbath was wholly a day of rest. Debated: some Christians keep the Sabbath day as a binding command; others see its rest fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 4; Colossians 2:16-17). The site does not settle the question.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Sabbath is the LORD's day of rest, kept holy in remembrance of creation and of deliverance from Egypt (Exodus 20:8-11; Deuteronomy 5:12-15).

Command: A Nazirite shall let his hair grow
Summary: One component of the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6: a Nazirite shall let his hair grow. The Nazirite separated himself unto the LORD for a set time, marked by abstinence, uncut hair, and avoidance of corpses.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall let his hair grow
Application: The vow was voluntary and temporary by design, ending with offerings at the tabernacle (Numbers 6:13-21); its abstinences marked consecration, not a standing rule for all believers.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, hair uncut as the visible sign, and corpse-avoidance as the priest-like holiness of the vow.

Command: A Nazirite shall not eat raisins
Summary: One component of the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6: a Nazirite shall not eat raisins. The Nazirite separated himself unto the LORD for a set time, marked by abstinence, uncut hair, and avoidance of corpses.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall not eat raisins
Application: The vow was voluntary and temporary by design, ending with offerings at the tabernacle (Numbers 6:13-21); its abstinences marked consecration, not a standing rule for all believers.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, hair uncut as the visible sign, and corpse-avoidance as the priest-like holiness of the vow.

Command: A Nazirite shall not eat grape husks
Summary: One component of the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6: a Nazirite shall not eat grape husks. The Nazirite separated himself unto the LORD for a set time, marked by abstinence, uncut hair, and avoidance of corpses.
Commandment: A Nazirite shall not eat grape husks
Application: The vow was voluntary and temporary by design, ending with offerings at the tabernacle (Numbers 6:13-21); its abstinences marked consecration, not a standing rule for all believers.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Nazirite separates himself unto the LORD (Numbers 6:2,5-6); no further reason is given, so the components' purposes are traditional — wine abstained from as a mark of consecration, hair uncut as the visible sign, and corpse-avoidance as the priest-like holiness of the vow.

Command: Eat the second Passover lamb
Summary: At the second Passover, the lamb is eaten roast with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, keeping all the ordinances of the Passover.
Commandment: Eat the second Passover lamb roast with fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The second date kept no one excluded for a year: uncleanness or a journey meant a month's delay, not refusal. The Passover ritual itself is fulfilled in Christ (1 Corinthians 5:7).
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the men defiled by a dead body asked why they should be kept back from offering the LORD's offering — and God answered with a second date, not a refusal (Numbers 9:6-11).

Command: A non-priest shall not perform priestly service
Summary: The command: A non-priest shall not perform priestly service (Numbers 18:7). The office of the priesthood belonged to Aaron and his sons alone; a stranger who came near was put to death.
Commandment: A non-priest shall not perform priestly service.
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the priest's office was given as a gift of service to Aaron and his sons alone (Numbers 18:7).

Command: Carry out the laws of tzara'at
Summary: The whole tzara'at procedure is carried out as Leviticus 13–14 prescribes: the priest examines skin and house, the unclean cries 'Unclean, unclean,' the house is purified, the cleansed person shaves, washes, and brings offerings.
Commandment: Carry out the laws of tzara'at as prescribed: priestly examination, separation while unclean, and the offerings of cleansing.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The procedure kept the camp holy and gave the afflicted a road back to worship. Jesus healed the leper and sent him to the priest with the Mosaic offering (Mark 1:40-45), showing mercy reaching where ritual could only separate.
Purpose: To order who could approach worship while ceremonially unclean and how they were restored. TRADITIONAL reading: with the temple order ended, these washings no longer bind believers; Jesus' touch restored those the laws isolated (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48).

Command: Redeem a dedicated field by adding a fifth
Summary: The command: Redeem a dedicated field by adding a fifth (Leviticus 27:19). One who redeemed a sanctified field paid the valuation plus a fifth part; unredeemed, it became the priest's at the jubile.
Commandment: Redeem a dedicated field by adding a fifth, as prescribed in Leviticus 27:19.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Valuations and redemptions priced devotion in a fixed, public way, so that a vow could not be quietly abandoned or quietly inflated. The whole system of dedicated things ended with the temple system; Christians give freely and cheerfully, not by valuation tables (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: fixed valuations kept vows honest and public, preventing both evasion and extravagant self-pricing. Scripture states the scale without a separate reason (Leviticus 27:1-29).

Command: Do not offer honey on the altar
Summary: The command: Do not offer honey on the altar (Leviticus 2:11). No honey might be burned as an offering made by fire on the altar.
Commandment: Do not offer honey on the altar.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches these sacrifices could never perfect the worshiper; they pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering, which is why they ceased with the new covenant.
Purpose: To provide atonement, thanksgiving, and fellowship under the old covenant. Hebrews teaches these pointed forward to Christ's once-for-all offering (Hebrews 10:1-14), so the system ceased.

Command: A priest shall not drink wine or strong drink when entering the sanctuary
Summary: The command: A priest shall not drink wine or strong drink when entering the sanctuary (Leviticus 10:9). Priests on duty were to drink no wine or strong drink when they went into the tent of meeting.
Commandment: A priest shall not drink wine or strong drink when entering the sanctuary.
Application: This row narrows the parent group command to this one mitzvah. The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Hebrews teaches the earthly tabernacle was a copy of the heavenly one, and Christ now serves as high priest in the true tabernacle.
Purpose: To give Israel a mediated approach to God through the tabernacle pattern (Exodus 25:40). Hebrews teaches the earthly copy gave way to Christ's priesthood in the true tabernacle (Hebrews 8:1-6).

Command: Do not benefit from meat cooked with milk
Summary: No benefit may be taken from meat cooked with milk: the mixture may not be used, sold, or turned to any gain.
Commandment: Take no benefit from meat cooked with milk.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The threefold form — not to cook, not to eat, not to benefit — closes every use of the mixture. The New Testament records the food distinctions set aside (Mark 7:19; Acts 10).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the prohibition keeps what gives life (milk) from being mixed with what takes life (meat) in cooking and eating, and keeps Israel's table distinct; Scripture states no reason for this rule.

Command: Do not revile a judge
Summary: A judge is not to be reviled — spoken of with contempt — even by one who believes the judgment wrong.
Commandment: Do not revile a judge.
Application: Cursing invokes evil; reviling heaps contempt. This mitzvah covers the contemptuous word itself, guarding the dignity of judgment even when a litigant is aggrieved. Disagreement is pursued by appeal and argument, not by reviling.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the judge's office bears God-given authority, so reviling him dishonours the order God set. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Exodus 22:28).

Command: Do not pervert the judgment of the stranger or fatherless
Summary: Do not pervert the judgment of the stranger or of the fatherless: each one's cause is judged on its merits, without bending toward the stronger party.
Commandment: Do not pervert the judgment of the stranger or fatherless.
Application: This mitzvah names the stranger and the fatherless expressly, apart from the widow: two of the defenceless, whose causes a court is most tempted to bend toward a native or a patron. Their judgment is not to be wrested for any reason.
Purpose: God's stated care for those without a defender — widow, orphan, stranger — carried by James into the church as pure religion (James 1:27). Here that care forbids perverting the judgment of stranger or fatherless.

Command: The Sinew That Shrank
Summary: Because Jacob's hip was struck as he wrestled, Israel does not eat the sinew on the hollow of the thigh. The verse states this as an explanation of an existing practice, not as a direct imperative — see flags.
Commandment: Do not eat the sinew which shrank, on the hollow of the thigh.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. This is a memorial custom rooted in Jacob's wrestling: the practice remembers that night. Jewish tradition still observes it (nikkur, the removal of the sinew); Christians generally read dietary customs of this kind as covenant-bound rather than continuing obligations.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: it memorializes Jacob's wrestling, in which the hollow of his thigh was touched (Genesis 32:31-32).

Command: Tell Your Children the Passover Story
Summary: When children ask what the Passover service means, parents are to tell them: it is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, who passed over Israel's houses in Egypt. This is the telling, distinct from the feast observance itself.
Commandment: When your children ask, tell them what the Passover means and what God did in Egypt.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The Passover telling is the model for passing faith to children by story: Christians keep the same instinct — remembering deliverance — in the Lord's Supper (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:26), without treating the Passover ritual itself as a Christian obligation.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: so that the next generation knows what God did — 'by strength of hand the LORD brought us out from Egypt' (Exodus 13:14).

Command: Mezuzah: Write the Words on Your Doorposts
Summary: God's words are to be written upon the posts of the house and on the gates. Rabbinic tradition reads this literally as the mezuzah; the Christian reading has generally been that the household itself is to be marked by God's word. The obligation question is debated — see debated_mappings.
Commandment: Write God's words upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Views differ: Jewish observance affixes a mezuzah literally; many Christians read the verse as a picture of a home governed by God's word, and do not treat the object as a continuing Christian obligation. Either way, the point stands: God's word belongs at the threshold of daily life, not only in the place of worship.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the home is marked as belonging to the LORD, so that God's word meets everyone entering and leaving. Scripture states the act, not a separate reason beyond the Shema context (Deuteronomy 6:4-9).

Command: Bless God After You Have Eaten and Are Full
Summary: When you have eaten and are full, bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you. This is the biblical root of grace after meals, distinct from any live row.
Commandment: After eating and being full, bless the LORD your God for what he has given.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Thanksgiving for food is continued in the New Testament as a Christian practice: food is received with thanksgiving and sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4-5). The form — a blessing after the meal — is the traditional Jewish Birkat Hamazon; the gratitude itself is universal.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: gratitude for the good land which the LORD has given (Deuteronomy 8:10).

Command: Do Not Mention the Names of Other Gods
Summary: In all that God has said, Israel is to be circumspect — and make no mention of the name of other gods, neither let it be heard out of their mouths. This is distinct from worshipping idols (live row No Idols): it governs speech and invocation.
Commandment: Do not invoke or make mention of the names of other gods.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament carries the same instinct: flee idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14), and let speech be governed by loyalty to Christ alone. The verse does not forbid historical discussion of other religions; it forbids invoking other gods as gods.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: speech that invokes another god already gives it a place that belongs to the LORD alone. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason beyond the call to be circumspect in all God has said (Exodus 23:13).

Command: Destroy Idolatrous Places of Worship
Summary: When Israel enters the land, the places where the nations served their gods — on high mountains, hills, and under green trees — are to be utterly destroyed, with their altars, images, and groves broken down. This is the conquest-era removal command, distinct from the live No Idols row (personal idolatry) and from the Warfare row (Deuteronomy 20).
Commandment: Destroy the places of idolatrous worship in the land, breaking down their altars, images, and groves.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. This was a conquest-era command to Israel entering the land, not a standing mandate for Christians: the New Testament never commands believers to destroy other religions' places of worship, but it does command believers themselves to flee idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:14) and to pull down arguments raised against God (2 Corinthians 10:5). The procedure is temporary; the refusal of idolatry endures.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the land is given to Israel, and its idolatrous worship must not remain alongside the LORD's worship there (Deuteronomy 12:2-4).

Command: Do Not Plant an Asherah by the Altar
Summary: No grove of trees — an Asherah, the wooden symbol of the goddess — is to be planted near the altar of the LORD. True worship must not be mixed with Canaanite symbols, even as decoration.
Commandment: Do not plant a grove of trees near the altar of the LORD your God.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The altar belonged to the LORD alone; importing a neighbouring religion's symbol beside it was already a compromise. The New Testament parallel is not about trees but about mixture: worship is not to be blended with idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:14-16).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the grove was the visible sign of Asherah worship, and its presence beside the LORD's altar mixed two worships. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Deuteronomy 16:21).

Command: Do Not Set Up a Sacred Pillar
Summary: Israel shall not set up any image — in context, a standing stone pillar of the kind used in Canaanite worship — which the LORD hates. This is a distinct mitzvah from the Asherah verse beside it, and from the live No Idols row.
Commandment: Do not set up a sacred pillar, which the LORD your God hates.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral.
