The pillar was a rival worship object, not a mere monument: Jacob's pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28) was a memorial before this law, and the law draws the line at pillars used as objects of worship. The enduring principle is that worship objects borrowed from idolatry are refused, whatever their form.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: the LORD thy God hateth it (Deuteronomy 16:22).

Command: Do Not Intermarry with Idolatrous Nations
Summary: Israel shall not make marriages with the seven nations of the land — giving daughters to their sons or taking their daughters for sons. The verse itself gives the reason: they will turn your children away to serve other gods. The scope of this today is debated — see debated_mappings.
Commandment: Do not intermarry with the idolatrous nations of the land.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Views differ today: some read the command by its stated reason — faith, not ethnicity — and point to Ruth and to Moses' own household, where foreigners who joined Israel's faith were welcomed; others read it as a standing ethnic separation for Israel. The New Testament parallel most often cited is not being unequally yoked with unbelievers (2 Corinthians 6:14), which is about shared faith, not ancestry.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for they will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other gods (Deuteronomy 7:4).

Command: Do Not Worship God in Pagan Ways
Summary: When God cuts off the nations before Israel, Israel must not inquire how those nations served their gods and then serve the LORD the same way — including the abominations those nations did, such as burning children. Worshipping the true God with pagan practices is itself forbidden.
Commandment: Do not learn the worship of the nations and then worship the LORD in that way.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament carries the same warning: God is not worshipped acceptably by methods borrowed from idolatry, however sincere (1 Corinthians 10:20-21; Colossians 2:23 warns against self-made religion). Sincerity does not sanctify a pagan practice.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: every abomination to the LORD, which he hateth, have they done unto their gods (Deuteronomy 12:31).

Command: Do Not Blaspheme the Name of the LORD
Summary: Whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death — the whole congregation stones him. The command itself is distinct from the live Do Not Misuse God's Name row (Exodus 20:7, vain use); this is direct cursing and reviling of God's name, given after the blasphemer's case in Leviticus 24.
Commandment: Do not blaspheme — curse or revile — the name of the LORD.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The penalty belonged to Israel's theocratic court and is not carried into Christian church discipline, which answers blasphemy with witness and, where needed, exclusion from fellowship — but the prohibition itself is repeated: blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is the one sin Jesus says will not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31-32), and reverence for God's name remains the first petition of the Lord's Prayer.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the name is God's own self-disclosure, so cursing it strikes at God himself, not merely at a word. Scripture states the prohibition and penalty without a separate reason (Leviticus 24:16).

Command: Do Not Go About as a Talebearer
Summary: Do not go up and down as a talebearer among your people. This is the gossip prohibition of Leviticus 19:16a, distinct from the live Love Your Neighbor row, whose range (Leviticus 19:17-18) does not include verse 16.
Commandment: Do not spread tales about your neighbours among the people.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament lists gossip and whispering among the sins that mark a disordered community (Romans 1:29; 2 Corinthians 12:20), and James warns that the tongue, though small, sets great things on fire (James 3:5-6). Repeating what harms a neighbour, even if true, breaks the same love that forbids bearing false witness.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: tale-bearing destroys the trust on which neighbourly life depends, and the verse pairs it with standing against a neighbour's blood — speech that harms and silence that harms. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Leviticus 19:16).

Command: Do Not Stand Idly By Your Neighbour's Blood
Summary: Neither shalt thou stand against the blood of thy neighbour. This is Leviticus 19:16b — the duty to intervene, warn, or rescue when a neighbour's life is at stake — distinct from the tale-bearing clause in the same verse, drafted separately.
Commandment: Do not stand idly by while your neighbour's life is in danger.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament gives the same principle in story form: the priest and Levite who passed by on the other side failed exactly this command (Luke 10:30-37), and John makes it concrete — whoever has this world's goods and shuts his heart against a brother in need, how does God's love abide in him (1 John 3:17-18)?
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the verse pairs tale-bearing with standing against a neighbour's blood because both are ways of letting a neighbour be destroyed — one by speech, one by silence. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Leviticus 19:16).

Command: Do Not Plow with Ox and Donkey Together
Summary: Thou shalt not plow with an ox and an ass together. The third of the kilayim mixture laws — the team, not the seed or the garment.
Commandment: Do not plow with an ox and a donkey yoked together.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The traditional reading also notes a practical wisdom — two unlike animals pull unevenly and the weaker suffers — but Scripture states no reason, so that reading is labeled traditional, not scriptural. It is not a New Testament obligation.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: unlike animals yoked together pull unevenly, to the suffering of the weaker; the law guards both order and mercy to animals. Scripture states the prohibition without a reason (Deuteronomy 22:10).

Command: A Parapet for a New House Roof
Summary: When thou buildest a new house, then thou shalt make a battlement for thy roof, that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence. This is the biblical root of the duty of care for safety in building.
Commandment: When you build a new house, make a parapet for your roof, so you do not bring bloodguilt on your house.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The form is ancient — a flat roof used as living space needed a guard — but the duty is timeless: whoever builds something others will use must guard against foreseeable harm, and bears bloodguilt if they do not. Modern building safety law is the same duty in new forms.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that thou bring not blood upon thine house, if any man fall from thence (Deuteronomy 22:8).

Command: Do Not Move Your Neighbour's Landmark
Summary: Thou shalt not remove thy neighbour's landmark, which they of old time have set in thine inheritance. This is the boundary-stone law, distinct from the live Inheritance row, whose Numbers and Deuteronomy 21 ranges do not include Deuteronomy 19:14.
Commandment: Do not remove your neighbour's ancient landmark in the inheritance God has given.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. Boundaries are property made visible: moving one is theft that no one can see at once, because the field itself looks unchanged. The New Testament does not restate boundary stones, but it does restate the theft they guard against (Ephesians 4:28).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the landmark is the inherited boundary set by former generations, and moving it steals land by stealth. Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Deuteronomy 19:14).

Command: No Millstone Taken as a Pledge
Summary: No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge. This is the pledge law's hardest case, drafted separately from the entry-and-return rules that follow it.
Commandment: No one shall take the upper or nether millstone as a pledge.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The millstone was not ordinary collateral: it was the tool by which a household made its daily bread. Taking it was taking life itself, which is why Scripture says so in those words. The procedure belongs to Israel's civil law, but the principle — never secure a debt by taking what a person needs to live — is the mercy the New Testament still expects (James 2:15-16).
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: for he taketh a man's life to pledge (Deuteronomy 24:6).

Command: Do Not Muzzle the Ox
Summary: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn. This is distinct from the live Just Treatment of Workers row, whose ranges (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15) do not include Deuteronomy 25:4.
Commandment: Do not muzzle the ox while it treads out the corn.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. Paul quotes this verse directly and applies it: God says it not for oxen only — the labourer is worthy of his reward, and ministers of the gospel should live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:9-14; 1 Timothy 5:18). The principle outlives the threshing floor: do not starve the worker while he produces your gain.
Purpose: Scripture states the prohibition without a separate reason (Deuteronomy 25:4); the New Testament supplies its application to workers (1 Corinthians 9:9).

Command: Slaughter and Sacrifice Only at the Sanctuary
Summary: What man soever killeth an ox, lamb, or goat in the camp and bringeth it not to the tabernacle door is cut off — and they shall no more offer their sacrifices unto devils. This Leviticus 17 centralization law is outside every live row's range (Sacrifices covers Leviticus 1-7; Priesthood covers Leviticus 8-10).
Commandment: Do not slaughter sacrificial animals in the open field or sacrifice to goat-demons; bring every offering to the tabernacle door.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The New Testament gives the reason the centralization ended: the one sacrifice of Christ replaced the many, and worship is no longer bound to one place (John 4:21-24; Hebrews 10:11-14). Sacrifices to goat-demons and private altars were the exact rivals this law excluded.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that they may no more offer their sacrifices unto devils, after whom they have gone a whoring (Leviticus 17:7).

Command: Do Not Kill Mother and Young on the Same Day
Summary: And whether it be cow or ewe, ye shall not kill it and her young both in one day. This is distinct from the live Sacrifices row, whose Leviticus range ends at chapter 7.
Commandment: Do not kill a cow or ewe and her young both on one day.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The companion law is the mother bird (Deuteronomy 22:6-7, drafted separately): in both cases the next generation is not taken together with the parent. Mercy to animals is a thread of the Law, not an afterthought — the righteous man regards the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10).
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: the pairing of mother and young on one day offends the compassion the Law elsewhere commands toward animals; Scripture states the prohibition without a reason (Leviticus 22:28).

Command: Remove the Unclean from the Camp
Summary: Command the children of Israel, that they put out of the camp every leper, and every one that hath an issue, and whosoever is defiled by the dead — male and female alike. This Numbers 5 camp rule is distinct from the live Purity row, whose range is Leviticus 12-15.
Commandment: Put outside the camp every leper, everyone with a discharge, and everyone defiled by the dead, until cleansed.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The camp was where God dwelt among his people, so uncleanness was kept outside it until cleansed. The New Testament reverses the direction: Jesus touches the leper and the unclean are brought in, not sent out (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 8:43-48, both cited on the live Purity row) — which is why this camp rule is temporary, not continuing.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that they defile not their camps, in the midst whereof I dwell (Numbers 5:3).

Command: Levites: Consecration and Years of Service
Summary: The Levites are sprinkled with the water of purifying, shaved, washed, and offered as an offering before the LORD; from twenty and five years old and upward they go in to wait upon the service of the tabernacle, and from fifty years old they cease waiting upon the service and minister with their brethren in keeping the charge, but do no service. This Numbers 8 law is outside the live Priesthood row's ranges.
Commandment: The Levites are cleansed, offered, and set apart for tabernacle service from twenty-five years old, retiring from the work at fifty while still assisting.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The Levites were Israel's substitute for the firstborn (Numbers 3:12,41), given to Aaron and his sons for the service of the tabernacle. With the temple gone and the priesthood fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 7), the Levitical service ages and consecration rite are not Christian obligations; the pattern — set-apart service, with seasons of work and seasons of stepping back — remains instructive for ministry.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: the Levites are given to Aaron and his sons to do the service of the tabernacle in place of the firstborn (Numbers 3:12; 8:19).

Command: The Silver Trumpets
Summary: Make thee two trumpets of silver; of a whole piece shalt thou make them, that thou mayest use them for the calling of the assembly, and for the journeying of the camps — and if ye go to war, ye shall blow an alarm with the trumpets, and ye shall be remembered before the LORD; also in the day of gladness, and in solemn days, and in the beginnings of months, ye shall blow with the trumpets over burnt offerings and peace offerings.
Commandment: Make two silver trumpets, to call the assembly, to order the camps' journeys, to sound the alarm in war, and to sound over offerings and feasts.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The trumpets gathered, ordered, and warned: one instrument did the work of assembly, march, war-cry, and festival. The New Testament keeps the trumpet as the sound of gathering and of the last day (1 Thessalonians 4:16; 1 Corinthians 15:52), but the silver trumpets of the camp are not a Christian liturgical requirement.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that ye may be remembered before the LORD your God (Numbers 10:9-10) — the trumpet sound in war and in joy is a memorial before God.

Command: The King Writes a Copy of the Law
Summary: And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites: and it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life. This royal-copy law is in no live row.
Commandment: When the king sits on his throne, he shall write for himself a copy of this law from the priests' book, keep it with him, and read it all the days of his life.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as civil. The picture is deliberately humbling: the king is not above the law but under it, reading it all his life. The New Testament universalizes the instinct — rulers are God's servants under God's law (Romans 13:4) — without continuing the royal copy rite.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them — that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren (Deuteronomy 17:19-20).

Command: Do not refuse a loan because the release year approaches
Summary: In the sabbatical cycle, debts were released every seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:1-2); this law forbids letting the approaching release year harden the heart against lending to a poor brother.
Commandment: Do not refuse a loan to your poor brother because the seventh year, the year of release, is at hand.
Application: The release year was no excuse for a closed hand: the poor brother's need, not the calendar, was to govern lending, and the LORD promised blessing on open-handed giving.
Purpose: Lest the poor brother cry to the LORD and it be sin, and because the LORD blesses open-handed giving (Deuteronomy 15:9-10).

Command: Listen to the Prophet Like Moses
Summary: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken. And whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him. This is the true-prophet promise, distinct from the false-prophet test drafted next.
Commandment: Listen to the prophet whom the LORD raises up like Moses; whoever will not listen shall answer for it.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as moral. The New Testament applies the promise directly to Jesus: Moses said, 'A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear' — and Peter and Stephen both quote it of Christ (Acts 3:22-23; 7:37). Listening to the prophet like Moses therefore continues, fulfilled in listening to Christ.
Purpose: Scripture's stated context: God answers Israel's fear at Horeb — 'let me not hear the voice of the LORD my God any more' — by promising a mediator-prophet they can hear (Deuteronomy 18:15-19).

Command: The Public Reading Every Seventh Year
Summary: And Moses commanded them, saying, At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles, when all Israel is come to appear before the LORD thy God in the place which he shall choose, thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing — gathering men, women, children, and the stranger within the gates. This Hakhel reading is in no live row.
Commandment: At the end of every seven years, at the Feast of Tabernacles in the year of release, read this law before all Israel, men, women, children, and strangers.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. The seventh-year public reading kept the whole law audible to the whole people, including children and strangers — no one was left to learn the covenant by rumour. The New Testament keeps the practice in a new form: give attendance to reading (1 Timothy 4:13), so that the whole church hears the whole word, not only its favourite parts.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear the LORD your God, and observe to do all the words of this law — and that their children, which have not known any thing, may hear, and learn to fear the LORD (Deuteronomy 31:12-13).

Command: Write This Song and Teach It
Summary: Now therefore write ye this song for you, and teach it the children of Israel: put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel. The verse's plain command is the Song; the Torah-scroll mitzvah traditionally derived from it is stated as a derivation, not as the verse's wording.
Commandment: Write this song for yourselves, teach it to the children of Israel, and put it in their mouths, that it may be a witness against them.
Application: The moral/ceremonial/civil division is a traditional classification, not Scripture's own division; this law is traditionally classed as ceremonial. Views differ on what the verse commands: the plain reading commands writing and teaching this Song (the Song of Moses, Deuteronomy 32), as a witness against Israel; rabbinic tradition derives from it the mitzvah for every person to write a Torah scroll for himself (or have one written). The derivation is traditional, not the verse's plain sense, and this draft says so rather than presenting the scroll mitzvah as the verse's direct command — see debated_mappings and flags.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:19).

Command: Do not leave any of the thanksgiving offering until morning
Summary: The thanksgiving peace offering was a shared holy meal; unlike other peace offerings, its flesh had to be eaten the same day, with nothing kept overnight.
Commandment: The flesh of the thanksgiving offering shall be eaten on the day it is offered; none of it shall be left until morning.
Application: Thanksgiving was not to be deferred or drawn out: the meal of gratitude belonged to the day of the offering, and holy food left overnight was not to be treated as common.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: thanksgiving was to be completed promptly, the holy meal eaten the same day rather than left to spoil or treated as common.

Command: An impure priest shall not eat holy food
Summary: The holy gifts (terumah) belonged to the priests, but a priest in impurity — from leprosy, a discharge, or touching uncleanness — was barred from eating them until cleansed (Leviticus 22:4-7).
Commandment: A priest unclean by leprosy, a discharge, or contact with uncleanness shall not eat of the holy things until he is clean.
Application: Holiness and impurity did not mix at the LORD's table: the priest's own cleansing came before his portion, and eating holy food in impurity profaned the holy name.
Purpose: Holy food was not to be eaten in impurity, keeping what is holy to the LORD distinct from uncleanness (Leviticus 22:2-4).

Command: Do Not Put God to the Test
Summary: The testing ban: do not test the LORD your God as Israel tested him at Massah, demanding proof before obedience. Doubt: Distinct imperative, but closely tied to the Shema passage and the Massah narrative; could fold into Love God Wholeheartedly rather than standing alone.
Commandment: Do not put the LORD your God to the test.
Application: Jesus quotes this against Satan's invitation to force God's hand. Testing God means demanding he prove himself on our terms before we trust him.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: Israel tested the LORD at Massah, demanding proof before obedience (Deuteronomy 6:16); Jesus quotes the ban against Satan's invitation to force God's hand (Matthew 4:7).

Command: Be Holy
Summary: The holiness call: be holy, for the LORD your God is holy — the summons that opens the holiness code. Doubt: Umbrella call rather than a distinct command: it introduces the whole holiness code and could fold into the moral laws as a group instead of standing alone.
Commandment: Be holy, for the LORD your God is holy.
Application: Peter carries the same call into the church: as obedient children, be holy in all your conduct. Holiness here is both a gift and a command.
Purpose: Scripture's stated reason: because the LORD your God is holy (Leviticus 19:2); Peter reissues the same call to the church (1 Peter 1:15-16).

Command: Love Your Enemies and Pray for Your Persecutors
Summary: Jesus' command to love beyond friends: love enemies, bless cursers, do good to haters, and pray for persecutors.
Commandment: Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute you.
Application: The command reverses the old slogan 'hate your enemy'. Its measure is God's own kindness to the evil and the good.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven' (Matthew 5:45).

Command: Turn the Other Cheek and Go the Second Mile
Summary: Jesus' non-retaliation command: do not repay evil for evil; offer the other cheek, give the cloak as well, and walk the second mile.
Commandment: Do not resist evil with retaliation: if struck on one cheek, turn the other; if sued for your coat, give your cloak also; if compelled one mile, go two.
Application: Each example refuses the cycle of revenge while still naming the wrong. It is personal non-retaliation, not a ban on lawful justice or on protecting others.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to break the cycle of revenge and display the character of the kingdom rather than the honour code of the world.

Command: Give to Everyone Who Asks
Summary: Jesus' open-handed command: give to the one who asks, and do not turn away the one who would borrow.
Commandment: Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.
Application: The command checks a closed fist. Wisdom still governs how a gift helps best, but the default posture is generosity, not refusal.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to imitate a giving Father and to refuse the love of possessions that shuts out a neighbour in need.

Command: Be Reconciled to Your Brother First
Summary: Jesus' priority command: before bringing your gift to the altar, first go and be reconciled to a brother who has something against you.
Commandment: If your brother has anything against you, leave your gift, first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.
Application: Worship is not a cover for an unmended breach. The command is urgent — agree with your adversary quickly — because unresolved wrong hardens into judgment.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason in context: lest the adversary deliver you to the judge (Matthew 5:25).

Command: Let Your Yes Be Yes
Summary: Jesus' truth-speaking command: do not swear oaths to shore up your word; let a plain yes be yes and a plain no be no.
Commandment: Do not swear at all; let your communication be Yes, yes and No, no, for whatever is more than these comes from evil.
Application: Oath-taking was being used to grade truthfulness. Jesus calls for speech so truthful that no oath is needed to believe it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: what goes beyond plain yes and no 'cometh of evil' (Matthew 5:37).

Command: Give, Pray, and Fast in Secret
Summary: Jesus' secrecy command for devotion: do alms, prayer, and fasting before the Father in secret, not to be seen by people.
Commandment: When you give alms, pray, or fast, do it in secret before your Father, not sounding a trumpet or disfiguring your face to be seen by men.
Application: The acts themselves are assumed — giving, praying, fasting — but their audience is changed from the crowd to the Father, who sees in secret and rewards openly.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: the Father 'which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly' (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18).

Command: Do Not Serve God and Money
Summary: Jesus' loyalty command: no one can serve two masters; lay up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, where moth and rust corrupt.
Commandment: Lay not up treasures on earth, but lay up treasures in heaven; no man can serve God and mammon.
Application: Where treasure goes, the heart follows. The command exposes divided loyalty: wealth is a rival master, not a neutral tool, when it commands obedience.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'where your treasure is, there will your heart be also' (Matthew 6:21).

Command: Ask, Seek, and Knock
Summary: Jesus' persistence command in prayer: ask and it will be given, seek and you will find, knock and the door will be opened.
Commandment: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
Application: Distinct from the Lord's Prayer pattern (live row), this is the manner of praying: persistent, childlike asking of a Father who gives good gifts, above all the Holy Spirit.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: an earthly father gives bread, not a stone, to a child who asks — how much more the heavenly Father (Matthew 7:9-11).

Command: Enter by the Narrow Gate
Summary: Jesus' gate command: enter through the strait gate, for wide is the gate and broad the way that leads to destruction.
Commandment: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life.
Application: The command warns against following the crowd. The narrow way is not narrow because God is stingy, but because it is the way of his commands rather than self-chosen religion.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to press hearers to choose the costly way of obedience over the easy way of the majority.

Command: Beware of False Prophets
Summary: Jesus' discernment command: beware of false prophets in sheep's clothing, and know them by their fruits.
Commandment: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves; ye shall know them by their fruits.
Application: The test is fruit, not polish: a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruit. The command guards the flock without licensing suspicion of every teacher.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: inwardly they are ravening wolves, whatever their outward dress (Matthew 7:15).

Command: Do to Others as You Would Have Them Do to You
Summary: The Golden Rule: whatever you would want others to do to you, do the same to them — Jesus' summary of the Law and the Prophets in action.
Commandment: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
Application: Distinct from the love commands as a practical rule: put yourself in the other's place before you act, and treat them as you would wish to be treated.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for this is the law and the prophets' (Matthew 7:12).

Command: Do Not Give Holy Things to Dogs
Summary: Jesus' discernment command about holy things: do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine, lest they trample them and turn on you.
Commandment: Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
Application: The command is not contempt for outsiders but stewardship of holy truth: some hearers, for now, will only trample what they are offered, and persistence then harms both.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to guard sacred truth from contemptuous handling while still loving the hearer — timing and readiness matter.

Command: Deny Yourself, Take Up Your Cross, and Follow Me
Summary: Jesus' discipleship command: whoever would come after him must deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow him.
Commandment: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.
Application: The cross here is not a burden in general but a death sentence carried willingly: following Christ costs self-rule. Whoever saves his life loses it; whoever loses it for Christ's sake finds it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to state the cost of discipleship plainly, so no one follows expecting ease.

Command: Sell All and Give to the Poor
Summary: Jesus' word to one rich man: sell all you have, give to the poor, and come follow me. HELD ITEM, drafted on its merits: the borderline doubt is carried here, not resolved — spoken to one rich man in one conversation, whether it is a universal command or a personal call exposing that man's idol is debated.
Commandment: Sell all you have, give to the poor, and come follow Christ.
Application: The man went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. The story exposes wealth as a rival god, and the call to follow as costlier than rule-keeping. As a held item it is published here as a person-specific word whose universal scope is debated (see Duration), not as a settled universal law.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to expose the one idol that kept this man from following — though whether every believer must literally sell all is the debated point, and this row does not settle it.

Command: Foot Washing
Summary: The basin and towel: Jesus washed his disciples' feet and told them to do as he had done to them. HELD ITEM, drafted on its merits: the borderline doubt is carried here, not resolved — some churches practice foot washing as an ordinance, most treat it as a model of humble service.
Commandment: Wash one another's feet, just as Christ has washed yours.
Application: Jesus says 'ye also ought to wash one another's feet' and 'ye should do as I have done to you'. The example is certain; its standing as a required rite is the debate, and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you' (John 13:15).

Command: Watch and Pray; Be Ready
Summary: Jesus' watchfulness command: watch and pray lest you enter temptation, and be ready, for the Son of man comes at an hour you do not expect.
Commandment: Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come. Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.
Application: Watchfulness is readiness, not date-setting: lamps burning, loins girded, prayer kept up when the flesh is weak. The command spans Gethsemane and the return of Christ.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to keep disciples ready for trial and for the Master's return, since neither hour is known.

Command: Let the Little Children Come to Me
Summary: Jesus' welcome command: suffer the little children to come unto him and forbid them not, for of such is the kingdom of God.
Commandment: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
Application: The disciples were rebuking the children as an interruption; Jesus rebukes the rebukers. Receiving the kingdom as a little child — trust without status — is the condition of entering it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for of such is the kingdom of God' (Mark 10:14).

Command: Go and Do Likewise
Summary: Jesus' closing command to the parable of the Good Samaritan, stated as a command and not merely a moral: go, and do thou likewise.
Commandment: Go, and do thou likewise.
Application: The lawyer asked who his neighbour was; Jesus reverses the question into action. The Samaritan's mercy — binding wounds, paying the cost — becomes the hearer's assignment. This row is included because Jesus states it as a command, not because a parable's moral was assumed to be one.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to turn neighbour-love from a definition into costly action toward whoever lies wounded in the road.

Command: Confront a Brother Privately First
Summary: Jesus' church-discipline command: if your brother trespasses against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone, before taking witnesses or telling the church.
Commandment: Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
Application: Distinct from the forgiveness command (live row), which governs the heart toward an offender, this governs the process: private first, then witnesses, then the church — gaining the brother, not winning the case.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother' (Matthew 18:15).

Command: Feed My Sheep
Summary: The risen Christ's charge to Peter: if you love me, feed my lambs, tend my sheep, feed my sheep. Drafted on its merits with its scope stated: addressed to Peter in his restoration, and read by many as the pattern for all pastoral care.
Commandment: Feed my lambs; tend my sheep; feed my sheep.
Application: Three times asked, three times charged — Peter's denial is undone by a commission. Whether the charge belongs to Peter alone as apostle or extends as the pattern of all shepherding is debated, and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: love for Christ is proved by feeding his flock (John 21:15-17).

Command: Do Not Fear Those Who Kill the Body
Summary: Jesus' fear command: do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
Commandment: Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Application: The command reorders fear itself: persecutors have the lesser power. Right fear of God frees disciples from the fear of men.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to free witnesses from the fear of persecutors by setting the greater judgment of God before them.

Command: Confess Christ Before Men
Summary: Jesus' confession command: whoever confesses him before men, him will he confess before his Father; whoever denies him, him will he deny.
Commandment: Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven. But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father.
Application: Confession here is public allegiance under pressure, not private belief alone. The promise and the warning are joined: the confessor is owned, the denier disowned.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: Christ will confess the confessor before his Father (Matthew 10:32).

Command: The Twelve's Mission Charge
Summary: Jesus' charge to the Twelve on their first mission: preach that the kingdom is at hand, heal the sick, cleanse lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils, freely give — wise as serpents, harmless as doves, shaking dust from unwelcoming towns.
Commandment: Go, preach, saying, The kingdom of heaven is at hand. Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils: freely ye have received, freely give.
Application: Grouped as one mission charge because it was given as one sending. Whether its details (no bag, no staff, shaking dust) bind later missions or belonged to that sending is debated; its preaching, healing, and freely-giving heart is the enduring pattern churches draw from it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'freely ye have received, freely give' (Matthew 10:8).

Command: Wait for the Promise of the Father
Summary: The risen Christ's one-time command to the apostles: tarry in Jerusalem until you are endued with power from on high. Drafted with its scope stated: a specific waiting, completed at Pentecost.
Commandment: Tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high.
Application: The apostles obeyed and waited in Jerusalem; the promise came at Pentecost (live story). It is not a standing command to wait in a city, but the historical hinge between the resurrection and the church's mission.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you' (Acts 1:8, given with the command).

Command: Render to Caesar and to God
Summary: Jesus' tribute command: render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.
Commandment: Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things which are God's.
Application: The trap — endorse Rome or defy it — is sidestepped by a division that still subordinates Caesar: coin bears Caesar's image, but people bear God's, and what bears God's image belongs to God.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to refuse both rebellion for its own sake and worship of the state, giving each realm its due.

Command: Beware the Leaven of the Pharisees
Summary: Jesus' warning command: beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy — the teaching that says one thing and lives another.
Commandment: Beware ye of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
Application: Leaven spreads quietly through the whole lump; so does hypocrisy. The command guards disciples against a religion of outward performance hiding inward corruption.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason in Luke: 'for there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed' (Luke 12:2).

Command: Call No Man Father or Master
Summary: Jesus' title command: be not called Rabbi, call no man your father on earth, neither be called masters, for one is your Master, even Christ, and all ye are brethren.
Commandment: Be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
Application: Spoken against titles used to claim spiritual superiority. How literally it forbids religious titles today is debated across traditions — some read it as an absolute ban on honorifics, others as a ban on the status-seeking it rebuked — and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to forbid spiritual status-seeking, since all disciples are brethren under one Master and one Father.

Command: Humble Yourself
Summary: Jesus' exaltation reversal: whoever exalts himself shall be abased, and he that humbles himself shall be exalted.
Commandment: Whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
Application: The command runs through the banquet and the Pharisee's prayer alike: the seat you take for yourself will be taken from you, but the low place is where God lifts.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make humility the posture of the kingdom, reversing the world's climb for honour.

Command: Come, Take My Yoke, and Learn from Me
Summary: Jesus' invitation-command to the weary: come unto me, take my yoke upon you, and learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart.
Commandment: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart.
Application: Distinct from the repent-and-believe row as a discipleship word: the yoke is not removed but exchanged — his yoke is easy, his burden light — and learning happens under it, from a meek Master.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light' (Matthew 11:29-30).

Command: Go and Sin No More
Summary: Jesus' word to individuals — the man healed at Bethesda and the woman taken in adultery: go, and sin no more. Drafted on its merits with scope stated: spoken to individuals in the moment, and read by many as the general call that pardon carries a changed life.
Commandment: Go, and sin no more.
Application: In both cases pardon or healing is joined to a command, not left bare: grace does not leave the life as it found it. Whether these two personal words form a standing law row or remain narrative pardons is debated, and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to join forgiveness to amendment of life, so that pardon is not taken as licence.

Command: Sell Your Possessions and Give Alms
Summary: Jesus' general command to his disciples, distinct from the rich ruler's personal word: sell what you have, give alms, and provide treasure in heaven that does not fail.
Commandment: Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not.
Application: Unlike the rich ruler's one-man word (separate row), this is spoken to disciples generally. How literally it requires selling possessions, versus requiring a generosity that loosens their grip, is debated, and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also' (Luke 12:34).

Command: Be Perfect and Merciful as Your Father
Summary: Jesus' perfection command in its two Gospel forms: be perfect as your Father in heaven is perfect, and be merciful as your Father is merciful.
Commandment: Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect. Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful.
Application: Matthew's 'perfect' and Luke's 'merciful' are parallel forms of one command, merged here rather than split: the Father's indiscriminate kindness — sun and rain on just and unjust — is the standard, not mere rule-keeping.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: the Father 'maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good' (Matthew 5:45).

Command: Hold Fast and Be Faithful unto Death
Summary: The risen Christ's command in the Revelation letters: hold fast what you have, be faithful unto death, and receive the crown of life.
Commandment: Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. Hold that fast which thou hast, that no man take thy crown.
Application: Spoken to Smyrna, Thyatira, and Philadelphia under pressure, merged here as one command because the wording and the charge are the same: endurance that does not let go under persecution.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that no man take thy crown' (Revelation 3:11).

Command: Do Not Let Your Heart Be Troubled
Summary: Jesus' farewell command: let not your heart be troubled; believe in God, believe also in me.
Commandment: Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me.
Application: Distinct from the repent-and-believe row as a command to troubled disciples on the night of departure: troubled hearts are steadied not by explanations but by trust in the Father and the Son.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason in context: 'In my Father's house are many mansions' (John 14:2).

Command: Head Coverings
Summary: Paul's instruction on head coverings in worship: men uncovered, women covered, in the Corinthian assembly. HELD ITEM, drafted on its merits: the borderline doubt is carried here, not resolved — whether the covering is a transcultural command or a first-century cultural expression is disputed.
Commandment: In worship, let men pray uncovered and women pray covered, as a sign of the created order.
Application: Paul grounds the practice in creation, nature, and the angels — yet its cultural expression varies widely across churches today, and this row does not settle which reading is right.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to display the created order in worship — though whether the covering itself or only the order it signified endures is the debated point.

Command: Greet with a Holy Kiss
Summary: The greeting command: greet one another with a holy kiss, a warm and pure sign of fellowship. HELD ITEM, drafted on its merits: the borderline doubt is carried here, not resolved — the kiss itself is culturally conditioned and most churches greet differently.
Commandment: Greet one another with a holy kiss.
Application: The kiss was the ordinary warm greeting of the ancient world, made holy by the fellowship it expressed. The underlying warmth is clear; the form is the debate.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to greet fellow believers with a warm, holy affection that marks them as one family.

Command: Food Sacrificed to Idols
Summary: The idol-food instruction: do not eat food sacrificed to idols in a way that betrays conscience — your own or a brother's. HELD ITEM, drafted on its merits: the borderline doubt is carried here, not resolved — a situational instruction for a first-century problem, whose scope beyond idol-food settings is debated.
Commandment: Do not eat food sacrificed to idols where it would defile conscience or cause a brother to stumble.
Application: Paul balances knowledge (an idol is nothing) with love (knowledge puffs up, love builds up): liberty yields to a brother's conscience. Eating in an idol's temple as worship is condemned outright; eating marketplace meat is a conscience question.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth' (1 Corinthians 8:13).

Command: Abstain from Blood, Strangled Things, and Fornication
Summary: The Jerusalem decree: the council asks Gentile believers to abstain from meats offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. Drafted beside the idol-food row because its blood and strangled clauses are distinct, and its scope is debated.
Commandment: Abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication.
Application: The decree settled the Gentile question — no circumcision required — while asking for these abstentions for fellowship's sake. Fornication's ban is enduring moral law; whether the food clauses bind all churches for all time or eased Jewish-Gentile table fellowship is debated, and this row does not settle it.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things' (Acts 15:28).

Command: Put Off the Old Self and Put On the New
Summary: Paul's renewal command: put off the old man corrupted by deceitful lusts, be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man created in righteousness and true holiness.
Commandment: Put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and put on the new man.
Application: The old and new selves are not improved and un-improved versions of the same life but two garments: one is taken off because it belongs to a former conversation, the other put on because it is created after God's image.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make sanctification a daily change of clothing, not a single past event.

Command: Speak Truth; Let No Corrupt Talk Come Out
Summary: Paul's speech command: put away lying and speak truth to your neighbour, and let no corrupt communication proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for edifying.
Commandment: Putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another. Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying.
Application: Truth-telling is grounded in membership: we are members of one another, so a lie wounds the body. Edifying speech is the positive half — words that build up and minister grace to hearers.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for we are members one of another' (Ephesians 4:25).

Command: Put Away Anger, Bitterness, and Malice
Summary: Paul's anger command: be angry and sin not, let not the sun go down on your wrath, and put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, evil speaking, and malice, being kind and tenderhearted instead.
Commandment: Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice.
Application: Anger itself is not simply condemned — 'be angry and sin not' — but anger nursed overnight gives the devil a foothold, and the whole family of bitter speech must be put away, replaced by kindness and forgiveness.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'neither give place to the devil' (Ephesians 4:27).

Command: Do Not Grieve the Holy Spirit
Summary: Paul's grief command: grieve not the Holy Spirit of God, whereby you are sealed unto the day of redemption.
Commandment: And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.
Application: Set between the speech and anger commands, this names whom corrupt words wound: the Spirit who seals believers is a person who can be grieved, not a force to be used.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: the Spirit is the seal 'unto the day of redemption' (Ephesians 4:30).

Command: Imitate God and Walk in Love
Summary: Paul's imitation command: be followers of God as dear children, and walk in love, as Christ has loved us and given himself for us.
Commandment: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children; and walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God.
Application: Imitation here is a child's copying of a Father, measured by Christ's self-giving. It frames the whole Ephesian ethic: love is not a feeling but a walk patterned on sacrifice.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: Christ 'hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God' (Ephesians 5:2).

Command: Redeem the Time; Walk Wisely
Summary: Paul's wisdom command: walk circumspectly, not as fools but as wise, redeeming the time because the days are evil — and walk in wisdom toward outsiders.
Commandment: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.
Application: Time is bought back from waste because the days are evil, not because the calendar is full. Toward outsiders the same wisdom governs: conduct that makes the gospel credible.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'because the days are evil' (Ephesians 5:16).

Command: Be Filled with the Spirit; Sing Psalms and Hymns
Summary: Paul's filling command: be not drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, and letting the word of Christ dwell richly.
Commandment: Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.
Application: The contrast is control: wine controls toward excess, the Spirit toward song and thanksgiving. The filling is corporate — 'speaking to yourselves' — not a private ecstasy.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to replace intoxication's control with the Spirit's, expressed in shared song and thanksgiving.

Command: Submit to One Another
Summary: Paul's mutual-submission command: submit yourselves one to another in the fear of God — the heading under which the household code itself is given.
Commandment: Submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God.
Application: Distinct from the household row (live), which spells out wives, husbands, children, parents, servants, and masters: this is the mutual posture that precedes and frames all of them, owed by every believer to every other.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make deference mutual in the body, not a one-way duty of the weaker party.

Command: Put On the Whole Armour of God
Summary: Paul's armour command: put on the whole armour of God, that you may stand against the wiles of the devil, and having done all, stand.
Commandment: Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Application: The armour is God's own, piece by piece — truth, righteousness, gospel peace, faith, salvation, the word — and the posture is standing, not advancing by human strength. Prayer on all occasions closes the list.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for we wrestle not against flesh and blood' (Ephesians 6:12).

Command: Think on These Things
Summary: Paul's thought command: whatever things are true, honest, just, pure, lovely, and of good report — think on these things.
Commandment: Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
Application: The mind is given a menu, not a vacuum: attention is itself obedience. What is dwelt on becomes what is done, which is why the verse follows 'those things do'.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to train attention, since thought is the seedbed of action.

Command: Do All Things Without Murmuring
Summary: Paul's shining command: do all things without murmurings and disputings, that you may be blameless and shine as lights in a crooked generation.
Commandment: Do all things without murmurings and disputings: that ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world.
Application: Murmuring is Israel's wilderness sin in miniature. Its absence makes the community visible: lights are seen against darkness precisely because they do not complain like the world.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'among whom ye shine as lights in the world' (Philippians 2:15).

Command: Work Out Your Salvation with Fear and Trembling
Summary: Paul's working-out command: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you both to will and to do.
Commandment: Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
Application: The paradox is the point: human working-out rests on divine working-in. Fear and trembling are reverence before a holy God, not anxiety about whether grace will hold.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for it is God which worketh in you' (Philippians 2:13).

Command: Stand Fast, Watch, and Be Strong
Summary: Paul's steadfastness command: watch, stand fast in the faith, quit yourselves like men, be strong, and let all your things be done with charity.
Commandment: Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Application: A soldier's closing charge, repeated across letters: watchfulness, unmoved faith, courage, strength. The Philippians and Thessalonians parallels show it as a standing apostolic charge, not a one-letter flourish.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to hold the line of faith under pressure rather than drift with it.

Command: Admonish the Idle, Encourage the Fainthearted, Help the Weak
Summary: Paul's pastoral-care command: warn the unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, and be patient toward all.
Commandment: Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
Application: One community, three different treatments: the idle need warning, the fainthearted comfort, the weak support — and all of it needs patience. Undifferentiated care misfires; this command differentiates.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to fit the care to the condition, as a physician fits the remedy.

Command: Prove All Things; Hold Fast the Good
Summary: Paul's testing command: prove all things, hold fast that which is good, and abstain from all appearance of evil.
Commandment: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Abstain from all appearance of evil.
Application: Testing is commanded, not forbidden: claims — including prophetic ones — are weighed, the good kept, and even the appearance of evil avoided, because witness depends on it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to combine open examination with firm retention of what proves true.

Command: Quench Not the Spirit; Despise Not Prophesyings
Summary: Paul's Spirit command: quench not the Spirit, and despise not prophesyings — the counterweight to the testing command, which follows it.
Commandment: Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings.
Application: Testing (the next verses) must not become suppression: the Spirit's work through prophecy is not to be snuffed out because discernment is required. Both commands stand together.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to keep the church open to the Spirit's gifts while still testing them.

Command: Comfort and Edify One Another
Summary: Paul's comfort command: comfort one another with the hope of resurrection, and edify one another, even as you do.
Commandment: Wherefore comfort one another with these words. Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
Application: Comfort here is doctrine applied: the return of Christ and the resurrection of the dead are not speculation but words for grieving believers to speak to each other.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope' (1 Thessalonians 4:13, the passage's opening).

Command: Honour All People; Love the Brotherhood; Fear God
Summary: Peter's honour command: honour all men, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the king.
Commandment: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Application: Distinct from the submission-to-authorities row (live), which governs obedience to rulers: this governs honour itself — universal to all people, special to the brotherhood, reverent to God, and due even to the king.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to order honour rightly — wide to all, deep to the church, highest to God.

Command: Be Sober and Watchful unto Prayer
Summary: Peter's sobriety command: the end of all things is at hand, so be sober and watch unto prayer; be sober, be vigilant, because your adversary the devil walks about seeking whom he may devour.
Commandment: But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer. Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour.
Application: Sobriety here is clear-headedness, not merely abstinence: a clouded mind cannot pray or stand guard. The devil's prowl is the reason given for vigilance.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour' (1 Peter 5:8).

Command: Cast All Your Care upon Him
Summary: Peter's care command: cast all your care upon him, for he cares for you.
Commandment: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
Application: The command follows humbling under God's hand: care is not carried by willpower but transferred — cast, thrown — onto one who cares. It is the practical side of humility.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for he careth for you' (1 Peter 5:7).

Command: Humble Yourselves, Draw Near to God, and Resist the Devil
Summary: James's and Peter's joined command: humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, draw nigh to God and he will draw nigh to you, cleanse your hands, and resist the devil steadfast in the faith.
Commandment: Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up. Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Application: James and Peter give the same sequence from two angles: humility first, nearness second, resistance third. Cleansed hands and purified hearts belong to the double-minded made single, not to a ritual.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'he shall lift you up' and 'he will flee from you' (James 4:7, 10).

Command: Do Not Speak Evil of One Another
Summary: James's speech command: speak not evil one of another, brethren; he that speaks evil of his brother judges the law.
Commandment: Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law.
Application: Distinct from the live judgment row, which governs hypocritical condemnation: this governs slanderous speech about a brother, which usurps the one Lawgiver who alone can save and destroy.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'there is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy' (James 4:12).

Command: Be Doers of the Word
Summary: James's hearing command: be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Commandment: But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Application: The hearer-only is pictured as a man who looks in a mirror and forgets his face: hearing without doing is self-deception, not partial obedience.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: the hearer-only 'deceiveth his own self' (James 1:22), like one who forgets his face (James 1:24).

Command: Be Swift to Hear, Slow to Speak, Slow to Wrath
Summary: James's temper command: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath, for the wrath of man works not the righteousness of God.
Commandment: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
Application: The order matters: listening first slows both tongue and temper. Human wrath, however righteous it feels, does not produce God's righteousness.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God' (James 1:20).

Command: Bridle the Tongue
Summary: James's tongue command: if any man seems religious and bridles not his tongue, his religion is vain; the tongue is a fire that no man can tame.
Commandment: If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain.
Application: Distinct from the swift/slow row, which governs temper in listening: this governs the tongue's ongoing power to bless and curse from the same mouth, to set whole courses of life on fire.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to expose unbridled speech as proof of vain religion, not a small fault.

Command: Confess Your Faults and Pray for One Another
Summary: James's confession command: confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that you may be healed.
Commandment: Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed.
Application: Confession here is mutual, not sacramental in form: faults spoken to a brother, prayer offered by a brother, healing as the fruit. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that ye may be healed' (James 5:16).

Command: Call the Elders and Pray Over the Sick
Summary: James's sickness command: if any is sick, let him call for the elders of the church, let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.
Commandment: Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.
Application: The sick person takes the initiative, the elders pray, oil is the sign, and the Lord raises up: the prayer of faith is the instrument named, and forgiveness is joined to healing where sin is involved.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'the prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up' (James 5:15).

Command: Restore the One Who Wanders
Summary: James's restoration command: if any err from the truth and one convert him, let him know that he who converts the sinner from the error of his way saves a soul from death.
Commandment: Brethren, if any of you do err from the truth, and one convert him; let him know, that he which converteth the sinner from the error of his way shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins.
Application: Distinct from the burden-bearing row's gentle restoration (Galatians 6:1, noted there): this is the wandering believer pursued, not the fallen brother restored — the rescue of a soul from death, covering a multitude of sins.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: he 'shall save a soul from death, and shall hide a multitude of sins' (James 5:20).

Command: Test the Spirits
Summary: John's testing command: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God, because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Commandment: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
Application: The test is confessional: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God. Openness to spiritual claims without testing is credulity, not faith.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'many false prophets are gone out into the world' (1 John 4:1).

Command: Do Not Love the World
Summary: John's world command: love not the world, neither the things in the world; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
Commandment: Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him.
Application: 'The world' here is the ordered system of lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and pride of life — all passing away — set against doing the will of God, which abides forever.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever' (1 John 2:17).

Command: Obey and Remember Those Who Rule Over You
Summary: Hebrews' leadership command: remember those who have the rule over you and follow their faith, and obey them that have the rule over you and submit, for they watch for your souls.
Commandment: Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation. Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls.
Application: Distinct from submission to civil rulers (live row): this is submission to church leaders who teach the word and watch over souls, given that they must give account — with joy, not grief.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account' (Hebrews 13:17).

Command: Offer the Sacrifice of Praise Continually
Summary: Hebrews' praise command: by him let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, the fruit of lips giving thanks to his name.
Commandment: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
Application: With the temple sacrifices ended, praise itself becomes the continual offering — lips confessing his name — joined in the next verse to doing good and sharing, which are also sacrifices well pleasing to God.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to replace ended animal sacrifice with continual praise as the church's offering.

Command: Do Not Forget to Entertain Strangers
Summary: Hebrews' hospitality command: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Commandment: Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
Application: Hospitality is commanded as remembrance, not convenience: strangers are easily forgotten, and the precedent is Abraham's tent. The 'angels unawares' is the motive, not a promise of reward for every guest.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for thereby some have entertained angels unawares' (Hebrews 13:2).

Command: Remember Those in Bonds
Summary: Hebrews' prisoner command: remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them, and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Commandment: Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Application: Remembrance here is identification: bound with them, as if in the same body. It is the prison-visiting command in its most inward form — sympathy that puts itself in the cell.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'as bound with them' and 'as being yourselves also in the body' (Hebrews 13:3).

Command: Do Not Be Carried Away by Strange Teachings
Summary: Hebrews' doctrine command: be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines, for it is good that the heart be established with grace.
Commandment: Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines: for it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein.
Application: The strange doctrines in view are food-rules as a way of standing with God. The heart established by grace does not need dietary religion to be secure, and drifting teaching must not carry it away.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace' (Hebrews 13:9).

Command: Women in Worship: Learn Quietly
Summary: Paul's worship-order instruction: let women learn in silence with all subjection, and let women keep silence in the churches where the law's order is in view. Drafted neutrally and without settling the debate: some traditions read this as a transcultural order for worship, others as a first-century Corinthian and Ephesian correction whose application varies — this row does not settle it.
Commandment: Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
Application: The two passages are grouped as one row because both address women's speech in the gathered assembly, and both are debated together. Paul's stated ground is the created order (1 Timothy 2:13-14); the application churches draw from it differs widely, and this row reports the texts without adjudicating.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason as stated: 'For Adam was first formed, then Eve' (1 Timothy 2:13).

Command: Adorn with Modesty and Good Works
Summary: Paul's and Peter's adornment instruction: women should adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly array, but with good works. Whether the specific adornments are a transcultural ban or a first-century cultural expression of the enduring modesty command is debated, and this row does not settle it.
Commandment: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; but with good works.
Application: The positive half is the point both writers stress: the hidden person of the heart, a meek and quiet spirit, and good works as the true ornament. The specific items named are the debated cultural form; modesty itself is the enduring substance churches agree on.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make character and good works, not display, the adornment — with the named items' literal scope debated.

Command: Flee Youthful Lusts; Pursue Righteousness
Summary: Paul's fleeing command to Timothy, given as a general charge: flee youthful lusts, and follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
Commandment: Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
Application: Fleeing is active, not passive: lusts are not debated with but fled from, and the pursuit that replaces them is corporate — 'with them that call on the Lord'. Addressed to Timothy, it is drafted because its wording is a general charge to the young in faith.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to replace forbidden desire with pursued righteousness in company, not alone.

Command: Shun Profane and Vain Babblings
Summary: Paul's shunning command: shun profane and vain babblings, for they will increase unto more ungodliness, and guard the deposit committed to you against oppositions of science falsely so called.
Commandment: But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings.
Application: Empty talk is not harmless noise: it spreads like gangrene (the next verse names Hymenaeus and Philetus). Guarding the deposit and shunning babble are two sides of the same stewardship.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for they will increase unto more ungodliness' (2 Timothy 2:16).

Command: Avoid Foolish Questions and Strife
Summary: Paul's avoidance command: avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions, and strivings about the law, for they are unprofitable and vain — and the servant of the Lord must not strive.
Commandment: But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes.
Application: Not every question deserves an answer: questions bred to produce strife are avoided, while the Lord's servant answers with gentleness and instruction those who can be recovered.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for they are unprofitable and vain' and 'they do gender strifes' (Titus 3:9; 2 Timothy 2:23).

Command: Be an Example to Believers
Summary: Paul's example command to Timothy, drafted as a general charge: let no man despise your youth, but be an example of the believers in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Commandment: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
Application: Authority for the young leader is earned by example, not claimed by office: six spheres are named, from speech to purity. Addressed to Timothy, it is drafted because young believers in every generation face the same despising.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make a life the credential where age cannot yet be one.

Command: Do All Things Decently and in Order
Summary: Paul's order command for worship: let all things be done decently and in order.
Commandment: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Application: The closing rule of the long worship-order chapter: God is not the author of confusion but of peace. Decency and order are the frame within which gifts — tongues, prophecy, singing — are exercised, not a ban on them.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace' (1 Corinthians 14:33).

Command: Do All to the Glory of God
Summary: Paul's glory command: whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Commandment: Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
Application: Set at the end of the idol-food discussion, this lifts the whole question beyond permission: the test of any act, even eating and drinking, is whether God is glorified by it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make God's glory the final test of ordinary acts, not only of religious ones.

Command: Give No Offence
Summary: Paul's offence command: give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God.
Commandment: Give none offence, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God.
Application: Distinct from the idol-food row, which governs conscience at table: this governs public witness to three audiences at once — outsider Jews, outsider Gentiles, and the church itself — none of whom should be needlessly stumbled.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to guard the gospel's reputation with outsiders and its unity within.

Command: Follow My Example as I Follow Christ
Summary: Paul's imitation command: be followers of me, even as I also am of Christ — and mark those who walk after the same pattern.
Commandment: Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ.
