Application: Imitation is conditional and mediated: Paul offers himself only insofar as he follows Christ, and points to a pattern others also walk in. It authorises example-based discipleship without making any man the standard.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make mature example a legitimate, if subordinate, guide for newer believers.

Command: Present Your Bodies a Living Sacrifice
Summary: Paul's presentation command: present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Commandment: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Application: With sacrifices ended, the body itself becomes the offering — living, not slain; holy, not blemished; daily, not annual. The mercies of God in Romans 1-11 are the ground: 'therefore' carries the whole gospel into the body.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'by the mercies of God' (Romans 12:1).

Command: Be Not Conformed to the World; Be Transformed
Summary: Paul's transformation command: be not conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, that you may prove the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God.
Commandment: And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
Application: Conformity is passive pressure; transformation is the mind renewed until God's will can be discerned and proved by living it. The two verbs are the negative and positive of one command.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God' (Romans 12:2).

Command: Rejoice with Those Who Rejoice; Weep with Those Who Weep
Summary: Paul's sympathy command: rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Commandment: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
Application: Sympathy is commanded in both directions, and rejoicing is often the harder: envy resists another's joy, while weeping only asks for presence. Both require entering the other's feeling rather than correcting it.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to make the body's shared feeling the proof of its shared life.

Command: Live Peaceably with All People
Summary: Paul's peace command: if it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Commandment: If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Application: The qualifiers are part of the command, not an escape from it: 'if possible' admits that some will refuse peace, and 'as much as lieth in you' places the whole of your share on you.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to pursue peace to the limit of one's own power, without guaranteeing the other's response.

Command: Owe Nothing but Love
Summary: Paul's debt command: owe no man anything, but to love one another; for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
Commandment: Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law.
Application: Debts are to be cleared, not carried; the one debt that is never cleared is love, because it is due perpetually. Love here fulfils the law's neighbour-commands in a single obligation.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law' (Romans 13:8).

Command: Put On the Lord Jesus Christ
Summary: Paul's clothing command: put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
Commandment: But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.
Application: The night is far spent and the day at hand: the works of darkness are cast off, and Christ himself is put on like a garment. Making provision for the flesh — planning for indulgence — is the thing forbidden.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'the night is far spent, the day is at hand' (Romans 13:12).

Command: Receive the Weak in Faith; Do Not Judge a Brother's Conscience
Summary: Paul's reception command: receive him that is weak in the faith, but not to doubtful disputations; let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not, and let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Commandment: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
Application: The weak brother is received, not cross-examined: food days and holy days are conscience matters where each stands before his own Master. The strong bear, the weak are not despised, and judgment of a brother's servant is forbidden.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to keep conscience questions from breaking fellowship, with each believer answerable to God.

Command: Stand Fast in the Liberty of Christ
Summary: Paul's liberty command: stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Commandment: Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Application: Liberty is not licence but freedom from law-keeping as the way of standing with God. Returning to circumcision as a requirement would entangle the Galatians again — Christ would profit them nothing on those terms.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage' (Galatians 5:1).

Command: Be Not Weary in Well Doing
Summary: Paul's endurance command: be not weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Commandment: And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Application: Weariness is the slow enemy of good: not a dramatic fall but a tired stopping. The harvest image gives the remedy — due season, not immediate season, is when reaping comes.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not' (Galatians 6:9).

Command: Do Good to All, Especially the Household of Faith
Summary: Paul's doing-good command: as we have opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Commandment: As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.
Application: The circle is wide — all men — with a centre — the household of faith. Opportunity is the occasion: good is done as doors open, not postponed until a grander occasion arrives.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to order generosity outward from the church without confining it there.

Command: Seek the Things Above
Summary: Paul's upward command: if you are risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God, and set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Commandment: If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.
Application: Seeking above is grounded in a risen life already given, not in contempt for earth: affections follow the risen Christ, and earthly things are then handled without being worshipped.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God' (Colossians 3:1).

Command: Let the Peace of Christ Rule in Your Hearts
Summary: Paul's peace command: let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to which also you are called in one body, and be thankful.
Commandment: And let the peace of God rule in your hearts, to the which also ye are called in one body; and be ye thankful.
Application: Peace here is an umpire: where competing claims clash, Christ's peace arbitrates. It rules in hearts called into one body, so its decisions are corporate, not merely private calm.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to let Christ's peace arbitrate disputes rather than pride or fear.

Command: Let Your Speech Be Seasoned with Salt
Summary: Paul's gracious-speech command: let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer every man.
Commandment: Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
Application: Grace is the flavour, salt the preservative and bite: speech to outsiders must be neither flattering nor caustic, but seasoned so that it preserves truth and answers each person fittingly.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man' (Colossians 4:6).

Command: Esteem Others Better Than Yourselves
Summary: Paul's humility command: let nothing be done through strife or vainglory, but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves, with the mind that was in Christ Jesus.
Commandment: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.
Application: The mind of Christ is then spelled out in self-emptying: form of God, form of servant, death on a cross. Esteeming others better is not flattery but the mind that took the lowest place.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: Christ 'made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7).

Command: Let Your Moderation Be Known
Summary: Paul's gentleness command: let your moderation be known unto all men, for the Lord is at hand.
Commandment: Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand.
Application: Moderation here is gentle forbearance, publicly known — not a private virtue but a reputation. Its ground is the Lord's nearness: the judge is at hand, so believers need not enforce their own rights.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'The Lord is at hand' (Philippians 4:5).

Command: Purge Out the Old Leaven; Put Away the Wicked Person
Summary: Paul's church-purity command: purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, and put away from among yourselves that wicked person.
Commandment: Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.
Application: Leaven spreads through the whole lump: tolerated sin in Corinth — a man with his father's wife — corrupts the feast, which must be kept in sincerity and truth. Discipline here is purging, not vengeance, and it belongs to the church, not outsiders.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump' (1 Corinthians 5:6).

Command: Come Out, Be Separate, and Cleanse Yourselves
Summary: Paul's separation command: come out from among them and be separate, touch not the unclean thing, and cleanse yourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
Commandment: Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you. Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
Application: Separation here is from unequal fellowship with idolatry, not from contact with unbelievers (Paul elsewhere commands the opposite). The promise — 'I will receive you, and be a Father unto you' — is the ground of the cleansing, not its reward.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'I will receive you, and will be a Father unto you' (2 Corinthians 6:17-18).

Command: Bring Every Thought into Captivity to Christ
Summary: Paul's thought-warfare command: casting down imaginations and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.
Commandment: Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.
Application: The warfare is not carnal but argumentative: strongholds are reasonings. Thoughts are not merely managed but captured — taken prisoner and brought under Christ's obedience.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: to treat rebellious reasoning as a stronghold to be demolished, not entertained.

Command: Examine Yourselves; Be of One Mind and Live in Peace
Summary: Paul's closing command to Corinth: examine yourselves whether you are in the faith, prove your own selves — and finally, be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace.
Commandment: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace.
Application: Self-examination precedes the farewell blessing: the Corinthians who demanded proof of Christ in Paul are told to prove themselves. Unity and peace are the closing notes — the God of love and peace will be with a church that lives them.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'the God of love and peace shall be with you' (2 Corinthians 13:11).

Command: Be Not Unequally Yoked
Summary: Paul's yoking command: be not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, for what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness, or light with darkness?
Commandment: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
Application: Applied by many churches to marriage and binding partnerships, and by others more narrowly to the idolatrous fellowship of its context; the command's breadth is debated, and this row does not settle it — but the pairing image (two animals under one yoke, pulling one way) is the point in either reading.
Purpose: Scripture's own reason: 'what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness?' (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Command: Have Dominion Over Creation
Summary: The creation mandate to subdue the earth and rule over its living creatures as God's stewards.
Commandment: Subdue the earth and have dominion over every living creature.
Application: Dominion here is stewardship under God, not exploitation: the same chapter that gives the mandate gives humanity plants for food and calls the world good. It is the standing counterpart to the multiply mandate in the same verse, rowed separately because it commands a different act (rule and care, not increase).
Purpose: To order and care for the earth as God's appointed rulers within it, reflecting his own rule; Genesis 1:28 states the mandate without a stated expiry.

Command: Work and Keep the Garden
Summary: Adam's Eden task: to dress and keep the garden God planted.
Commandment: Dress and keep the garden of Eden.
Application: Work precedes the Fall in this account: tending is part of humanity's original calling, not a curse. The specific garden task ended with the expulsion (Genesis 3:23-24); the work ethic it embodies is carried elsewhere, but this row covers the Eden task itself, not work in general.
Purpose: To tend the garden God planted as humanity's first appointed work; the task belongs to Eden and ended when Adam and Eve were sent out.

Command: Do Not Eat from the Tree of Knowledge
Summary: The one prohibition in Eden: every tree may be eaten from except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death.
Commandment: Do not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for in the day you eat of it you shall surely die.
Application: This is the test command of Eden: abundance (every tree) joined to one boundary, with the consequence stated in the command itself. It was broken at the Fall and the tree became inaccessible (Genesis 3:22-24); it does not bind anyone today as an Eden prohibition, though its lesson about boundaries and trust is preached from it.
Purpose: To test trust and obedience within abundance: one stated boundary, with death as the stated consequence (Genesis 2:17).

Command: Do Not Eat Flesh with Its Blood
Summary: The Noahic food prohibition: flesh with its lifeblood still in it must not be eaten.
Commandment: Do not eat flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof.
Application: Given to Noah and his sons as part of the post-flood order, before Sinai and before any Jewish identity existed. Debated: some hold this Noahic prohibition still binds all humanity and note the Jerusalem council's abstain-from-blood instruction (Acts 15:29); others hold it belonged to the pre-Mosaic order and passed with the old covenant's food laws. The site does not settle this.
Purpose: To honor life as residing in the blood; Genesis 9:4 states the prohibition without a stated expiry, which is why its duration is debated rather than settled here.

Command: Do Not Shed Human Blood
Summary: The Noahic life law: whoever sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, because man is made in God's image.
Commandment: Do not shed human blood; the shedder's blood is required in return.
Application: Distinct from the live Sinai row (Do Not Murder): this is the earlier, pre-Mosaic command, given to all Noah's descendants, not only to Israel. Its stated ground is the image of God, and that ground is why the prohibition is treated as enduring even though its penalty procedure belonged to the ancient order.
Purpose: To guard human life on the stated ground that man is made in the image of God (Genesis 9:6).

Command: Walk Before God and Be Blameless
Summary: The covenant walk command to Abram: walk before God and be perfect, given as the covenant of circumcision is established.
Commandment: Walk before me, and be thou perfect.
Application: A broad covenant call rather than a single act, and it should be read that way: it is the posture under which the circumcision covenant (rowed separately) was given. Kept as its own row because Genesis 17:1 states it as a distinct imperative and it is echoed across Scripture as the walk of faith, but the parent may fold it into the circumcision row if umbrella rows are cut.
Purpose: To live the covenant life openly before God in integrity; Genesis 17:1 makes it the condition and character of the covenant that follows, not an optional extra.

Command: Build the Ark
Summary: God's command to Noah: make an ark of gopher wood, with rooms, pitched within and without, to the dimensions and pattern given.
Commandment: Make thee an ark of gopher wood, with rooms, pitched within and without with pitch.
Application: The user's own example of a one-time command: temporary, completed, never repeated. Noah did according to all God commanded him (Genesis 6:22). Rowed separately from entering and leaving the ark, which are distinct imperatives at distinct moments.
Purpose: To preserve Noah, his family, and the living creatures through the flood judgment God had announced (Genesis 6:17-18).

Command: Enter the Ark
Summary: God's command to Noah when the ark was ready: come, with all his house, into the ark.
Commandment: Come thou and all thy house into the ark.
Application: A distinct imperative from building the ark: construction complete, the household is commanded inside, with the stated reason that Noah was seen righteous before God in his generation. Merge candidate: the parent may fold enter/leave into the build row as one ark episode; kept separate here under the one-row-per-distinct-command rule.
Purpose: To bring the righteous household inside the prepared vessel before the flood waters came (Genesis 7:1, 7:4).

Command: Leave the Ark
Summary: God's command after the waters dried: go forth from the ark, with family and every living thing.
Commandment: Go forth of the ark, thou, and thy wife, and thy sons, and thy sons' wives with thee; bring forth every living thing with thee.
Application: Noah did not leave on his own timing: he waited for the spoken command even after the ground was dry. Distinct moment from entering; same merge caveat as the enter row.
Purpose: To repopulate the cleansed earth from the ark's household and creatures, opening the post-flood order (Genesis 8:17; 9:1).

Command: Rule Over Sin
Summary: God's word to Cain before the murder: sin lies at the door, and Cain must rule over it.
Commandment: Do thou rule over sin that lies at your door.
Application: A genuine imperative spoken to one man at one moment of temptation, not a general law text: Cain was warned before he acted and did not obey. Its principle is preached universally, but the command as given was Cain's, at that door, on that day — hence One-time here, with the universal principle noted rather than used to reclass it.
Purpose: To turn Cain from anger and a fallen face toward doing well before sin mastered him (Genesis 4:6-7).

Command: Leave Your Country
Summary: God's call command to Abram: get out of his country, kindred, and father's house to a land God would show him.
Commandment: Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee.
Application: The founding migration command of the patriarchal story: one man, one departure, with promises attached (a great nation, blessing to all families of the earth). Completed when Abram departed as commanded (Genesis 12:4); never reissued as a standing law.
Purpose: To separate Abram for the covenant people and the promised land from which blessing would reach all families of the earth (Genesis 12:2-3).

Command: Bring the Covenant Animals
Summary: God's command to Abram in the covenant ceremony: take a heifer, she goat, ram, turtledove, and young pigeon.
Commandment: Take me an heifer of three years old, and a she goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon.
Application: A one-time ritual act: Abram brought and divided the animals, and God passed between the pieces (Genesis 15:17). No story title matches this ceremony, so RelatedEvents is left empty rather than linked to a wrong story.
Purpose: To furnish the covenant-making rite by which God bound himself to give Abram's seed the land (Genesis 15:17-18).

Command: Offer Isaac on Moriah
Summary: God's command to Abraham: take Isaac, his only son, to Moriah and offer him as a burnt offering.
Commandment: Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of.
Application: The hardest one-time command in Genesis, completed by obedience and then stayed: the angel's counter-word, lay not thine hand upon the lad (Genesis 22:12), belongs to this same episode and is covered here rather than rowed as a second command. God provided the ram instead (Genesis 22:13).
Purpose: To test whether Abraham feared God and withheld nothing, even his promised son (Genesis 22:12 states the test's point after the stay).

Command: Return to Your Mistress
Summary: The angel's command to the runaway Hagar: return to Sarai and submit under her hands.
Commandment: Return to thy mistress, and submit thyself under her hands.
Application: A genuine divine command to a person in flight, with a promise attached (a multiplied seed, Genesis 16:10). Small in scale but unambiguous in form, and therefore included rather than passed over as mere narrative.
Purpose: To send Hagar back under Sarai's hand with the promise of a multiplied seed through Ishmael (Genesis 16:10).

Command: Dwell in Gerar, Do Not Go to Egypt
Summary: God's command to Isaac in famine: do not go down to Egypt; dwell in the land God would tell him of.
Commandment: Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of.
Application: A person-specific redirection: Isaac, unlike his father in an earlier famine, was told to stay. He dwelt in Gerar (Genesis 26:6). The covenant promises to Abraham were restated to him in the same speech.
Purpose: To keep Isaac in the promised land through famine so the Abrahamic covenant would be established with him there (Genesis 26:3-4).

Command: Escape Sodom, Do Not Look Back
Summary: The angels' command to Lot as Sodom's judgment fell: escape for your life, do not look behind, do not stay in the plain, escape to the mountain.
Commandment: Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain.
Application: One moment, one household, one road out. Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26) — the warning inside the command, fulfilled in the same chapter. Lot's plea for Zoar (Genesis 19:20) does not change the command's form.
Purpose: To rescue Lot's household alive from a judgment already falling, with no delay and no backward glance (Genesis 19:17).

Command: Return to Your Kindred
Summary: God's command to Jacob after twenty years with Laban: return to the land of his fathers and his kindred.
Commandment: Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred; and I will be with thee.
Application: Parallels merged: the Genesis 31:3 command and the 31:13 repetition (arise, get thee out from this land) are one return journey commanded twice, not two returns. Jacob obeyed, and Laban pursued and then covenanted with him (Genesis 31:43-54).
Purpose: To bring Jacob back to the promised land with God's promised presence, ending his exile with Laban (Genesis 31:3).

Command: Go Up to Bethel
Summary: God's command to Jacob: arise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar to the God who appeared when he fled from Esau.
Commandment: Arise, go up to Beth-el, and dwell there: and make there an altar unto God.
Application: A return to the place of the dream (Genesis 28) now commanded as an act of worship: Jacob first put away his household's strange gods (Genesis 35:2 — Jacob's own household order, not a separate divine command, and not rowed separately). God blessed him at Bethel and renamed the ground of the promise (Genesis 35:9-15).
Purpose: To bring Jacob back to Bethel in worship, fulfilling the vow-ground of his first flight and re-establishing the covenant there (Genesis 35:1, 35:9-12).

Command: Go Down to Egypt Without Fear
Summary: God's command to Jacob at Beersheba: fear not to go down into Egypt, for God would make him a great nation there and bring him up again.
Commandment: Fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation.
Application: Jacob was already on the road to Joseph when God spoke; the command removed the fear of leaving the promised land by promising both presence in Egypt and return. No story title matches Jacob's descent itself (Joseph and His Brothers is Joseph's story), so RelatedEvents is left empty.
Purpose: To authorize Jacob's descent to Joseph in Egypt with the promise of nationhood there and eventual return (Genesis 46:3-4).

Command: Stretch Out the Rod for the Plagues
Summary: God's repeated command through the plagues: Moses (and Aaron with the rod) must stretch out hand and rod over Egypt for each sign.
Commandment: Take thy rod, and stretch out thine hand upon the waters of Egypt, and over the signs that follow.
Scripture: Exodus 7:19; Exodus 8:5; Exodus 8:16; Exodus 9:22; Exodus 10:12; Exodus 10:21
Application: A merged row under the one-row-per-distinct-command rule: the rod is stretched out for blood (Exodus 7:19), frogs (8:5), lice (8:16), hail (9:22), locusts (10:12), and darkness (10:21) — one repeated commanded act across the plague series, not six separate laws. The Red Sea stretching is rowed separately because it is a different act with a different outcome. Parent may split per plague if finer granularity is wanted.
Purpose: To bring each plague as a sign against Pharaoh and the gods of Egypt until Israel was let go (Exodus 7:17; 8:10).

Command: Stretch Out Your Hand Over the Sea
Summary: God's command at the Red Sea: speak that Israel go forward, lift the rod, and stretch out the hand over the sea to divide it.
Commandment: Lift thou up thy rod, and stretch out thine hand over the sea, and divide it, that the children of Israel shall go on dry ground through the midst of the sea.
Application: Two utterances, one event: lift the rod and stretch out the hand (Exodus 14:16), then stretch it out again to close the sea (14:26). Moses is also told to speak to Israel that they go forward (14:15) — covered here as part of the same crossing command, not a separate row.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea
Purpose: To divide the sea for Israel's escape and to close it on Pharaoh's army, showing that the LORD fought for Israel (Exodus 14:25, 14:30-31).

Command: Strike the Rock at Rephidim
Summary: God's command at Rephidim: smite the rock in Horeb, and water will come out for the people.
Commandment: Thou shalt smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it, that the people may drink.
Application: Distinct from the Meribah rock row: different place (Rephidim/Horeb, not Meribah), different verb (smite, not speak), different occasion. The two rocks must not be merged — Moses' later error was treating the second like the first.
Purpose: To give water to a thirsting, murmuring people at Rephidim, proving God's presence among them (Exodus 17:7).

Command: Speak to the Rock at Meribah
Summary: God's command at Meribah: speak to the rock before the assembly, and it will give forth water.
Commandment: Take the rod, gather the assembly, and speak ye unto the rock before their eyes, and it shall give forth his water.
Application: The command Moses broke: told to speak, he struck (Numbers 20:11), and for that he was barred from leading Israel into the land (20:12). Rowed separately from Rephidim precisely because the difference between the two commands is the point of the story.
Purpose: To give water to the congregation and their beasts at Meribah, and to sanctify God before Israel by exact obedience (Numbers 20:12).

Command: Send Spies into Canaan
Summary: God's command to Moses in the wilderness of Paran: send men to search the land of Canaan.
Commandment: Send thou men, that they may search the land of Canaan, which I give unto the children of Israel.
Application: One sending, twelve men, one land. The spies' bad report and Israel's unbelief followed (Numbers 13:31-14:4), but the sending itself was commanded, not a human initiative — which is why it belongs here and not as mere narrative.
RelatedEvents: The Twelve Spies and Israel's Unbelief
Purpose: To search the promised land before Israel's entry, as God gave it to them (Numbers 13:2).

Command: Make the Bronze Serpent
Summary: God's command in the wilderness: make a fiery serpent, set it on a pole, and everyone bitten who looks upon it shall live.
Commandment: Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.
Application: A one-time commanded object, not a standing idol: the serpent was for looking and living in that plague, and centuries later Hezekiah broke it in pieces precisely because it had become an object of worship (2 Kings 18:4). Jesus himself takes it up as the picture of his lifting up (John 3:14-15).
Purpose: To give bitten Israelites life by looking, after their complaint brought fiery serpents (Numbers 21:6-7).

Command: Number the People
Summary: God's command to Moses, given twice for two generations: take the sum of the congregation of Israel.
Commandment: Take ye the sum of all the congregation of the children of Israel, by their families and fathers' houses.
Application: Administrative, not moral — included because the brief is every distinct command, and these are explicit imperatives. Merged row: the Numbers 1 census (Sinai) and the Numbers 26 census (plains of Moab, a new generation) are two censuses under one command type; parent may split into two rows if each census is wanted separately.
Purpose: To count Israel by tribe and family for camp order, service, and war (Numbers 1:3; 26:2).

Command: Go, But Speak Only My Word
Summary: God's command to Balaam: he may go with Balak's men, but only the word God speaks may he speak.
Commandment: If the men come to call thee, rise up, and go with them; but yet the word which I shall say unto thee, that shalt thou do.
Application: A conditional permission framed as command: Balaam might go, but only the word God gave him might he speak (repeated in Numbers 22:35). Balaam's later counsel against Israel (Numbers 31:16) shows the leash, not the license, was the point.
Purpose: To let Balaam go to Balak while keeping his mouth wholly under God's word, so blessing, not curse, came to Israel (Numbers 23:20).

Command: Make Atonement with the Censer
Summary: Moses' command to Aaron in the plague: take a censer with altar fire and incense, go quickly, and make atonement for the congregation.
Commandment: Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them.
Application: Source flag for the parent: the immediate speaker is Moses to Aaron (Numbers 16:46), acting on God's instruction in the plague crisis, not a direct divine speech formula. Kept because the act (censer atonement) stopped the plague (16:48) and is presented as commanded obedience, but drop it if the parent requires direct divine-speech commands only.
Purpose: To make atonement for the congregation and stop the plague after Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:46-48).

Command: Arise, Go Over the Jordan
Summary: God's commission to Joshua after Moses' death: arise, go over the Jordan with all the people into the promised land.
Commandment: Arise, go over this Jordan, thou, and all this people, unto the land which I do give to them.
Application: The commission that opens Joshua: Moses dead, Jordan ahead, land promised. Joshua obeyed within three days (Joshua 1:11; 3:1-2).
Purpose: To lead Israel across the Jordan into the land promised to their fathers (Joshua 1:2-4).

Command: Circumcise the People Again
Summary: God's command to Joshua at Gilgal: make sharp knives and circumcise the children of Israel the second time.
Commandment: Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time.
Application: A second circumcision because the wilderness generation had not been circumcised on the way (Joshua 5:4-7). Distinct from the Abrahamic covenant row: that row is the standing covenant sign; this is the one-time renewal act at Gilgal. RelatedEvents left empty: no story title matches the Gilgal circumcision, and Crossing the Jordan covers chapters 3-4, not this act.
Purpose: To renew the covenant sign in the new generation before they took the land, rolling away the reproach of Egypt (Joshua 5:9).

Command: March Around Jericho
Summary: God's command for Jericho: compass the city once a day for six days, seven times on the seventh, with trumpets and a shout.
Commandment: Ye shall compass the city, all ye men of war, and go round about the city once. Thus shalt thou do six days; and on the seventh day ye shall compass the city seven times.
Application: Six days of single circuits, seven on the seventh day, trumpets and a shout (Joshua 6:4-5). The walls fell flat (6:20). A tactical absurdity commanded as obedience, and therefore the classic one-time command of the conquest.
Purpose: To take Jericho by obedient procession and shout rather than by siege craft, showing the LORD gave the city (Joshua 6:2, 6:16).

Command: Go in This Your Might
Summary: The LORD's commission to Gideon: go in this your might and save Israel from the Midianites.
Commandment: Go in this thy might, and thou shalt save Israel from the hand of the Midianites: have not I sent thee?
Application: Gideon's commission, given at the winepress where he threshed wheat in hiding (Judges 6:11). The fleece episodes (6:36-40) are deliberately NOT rowed: they are Gideon's tests of God, not God's commands to Gideon.
Purpose: To deliver Israel from seven years of Midianite oppression through a reluctant judge God had sent (Judges 6:1, 6:14).

Command: Tear Down Baal's Altar
Summary: The LORD's night command to Gideon: throw down his father's Baal altar, cut down the grove, build an altar to the LORD, and offer the bullock.
Commandment: Throw down the altar of Baal that thy father hath, and cut down the grove that is by it; and build an altar unto the LORD thy God, and offer the second bullock.
Application: The night work before the campaign: tear down the family Baal altar, cut the grove, build an altar to the LORD, and offer the bullock (Judges 6:26). Gideon did it by night for fear (6:27) — obedience, not eagerness, is the note.
Purpose: To purge idolatry from Gideon's own household before God used him against Midian, putting the LORD's altar where Baal's had stood (Judges 6:25-26).

Command: Separate the Army at the Water
Summary: God's command to Gideon: bring the people to the water and separate them by how they drink, keeping only the 300.
Commandment: Bring the people down unto the water, and I will try them for thee there; every one that lappeth of the water with his tongue, as a dog lappeth, him shalt thou set by himself.
Application: A selection command, not a battle plan: the army was reduced from 32,000 to 10,000 to 300 by the water test (Judges 7:2-7), so that Israel could not claim its own hand had saved it. Kept as its own row because the imperative (bring them down to the water) is distinct from the go command; parent may fold it into the go row.
Purpose: To reduce Gideon's army to 300 so Israel would know the LORD, not numbers, gave the victory (Judges 7:2, 7:7).

Command: Arise, Go to Nineveh
Summary: God's command to Jonah, given twice: arise, go to Nineveh, and cry against it.
Commandment: Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.
Application: Parallels merged: the Jonah 1:2 commission and the Jonah 3:2 recommission are one command given twice (after the fish), not two missions. Jonah's flight is disobedience to this row, and his second going is obedience to it.
Purpose: To warn Nineveh of judgment so the city might repent — and it did, from king to cattle (Jonah 3:5-10).

Command: Show Yourself to Ahab
Summary: God's command to Elijah in the third year of drought: go, show yourself to Ahab, and God will send rain.
Commandment: Go, shew thyself unto Ahab; and I will send rain upon the earth.
Application: The drought-ending summons: after three years without rain, Elijah is told to show himself to the king who sought his life. The Carmel contest (1 Kings 18:17-40) follows from this showing, and the story title Elijah on Mount Carmel is the containing story.
Purpose: To end the drought by a public confrontation: Elijah before Ahab, then rain on the earth (1 Kings 18:1, 18:41-45).

Command: Hide at Cherith, Go to Zarephath
Summary: God's drought-exile commands to Elijah: hide by the brook Cherith, then go to Zarephath and dwell there.
Commandment: Get thee hence, and turn thee eastward, and hide thyself by the brook Cherith; then arise, get thee to Zarephath, and dwell there.
Application: Merged row: two moves under one itinerant commission — hide by Cherith (1 Kings 17:3, ravens fed him) then go to Zarephath (17:9, the widow sustained him). Parent may split into two rows; kept merged because both are stages of the same drought exile, not two missions.
Purpose: To hide and sustain Elijah through the drought God had announced — by ravens at Cherith, by a widow at Zarephath (1 Kings 17:4-6, 17:9).

Command: Anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha
Summary: God's command to Elijah at Horeb: return by the wilderness of Damascus and anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha.
Commandment: Go, return on thy way to the wilderness of Damascus: and when thou comest, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria, and Jehu to be king over Israel, and Elisha to be prophet in thy room.
Application: One commission, three anointings: Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel, Elisha as prophet in Elijah's room (1 Kings 19:16). Elijah anointed Elisha directly (19:19-21); Hazael and Jehu were anointed through Elisha's ministry (2 Kings 8:13; 9:3, 6). Rowed as one commission because it is one speech.
Purpose: To raise the instruments of judgment and succession after Carmel and Horeb: kings who would cut down Baal's house, and a prophet to follow Elijah (1 Kings 19:17-18).

Command: Anoint Saul as King
Summary: God's command to Samuel: anoint Saul to be captain over Israel against the Philistines.
Commandment: Thou shalt anoint Saul to be captain over my people Israel, that he may save my people out of the hand of the Philistines.
Application: Saul was anointed privately (1 Samuel 10:1) and then chosen publicly by lot (10:20-24). This row covers the command to anoint, not Saul's later reign or his Amalek disobedience (that command is the held Remember Amalek item, not duplicated here).
Purpose: To give Israel the king they demanded as a captain to save them from the Philistines, while God heard their cry (1 Samuel 9:16).

Command: Anoint David as King
Summary: God's command to Samuel: go to Jesse at Bethlehem, and anoint the son God shows him.
Commandment: Fill thine horn with oil, and go, I will send thee to Jesse the Bethlehemite: for I have provided me a king among his sons. Arise, anoint him: for this is he.
Application: Samuel was sent to Bethlehem while Saul still reigned, to a son of Jesse God had provided (1 Samuel 16:1). David was anointed in the midst of his brethren, and the Spirit came upon him from that day (16:13). RelatedEvents left empty: David Becomes King covers his later reign, not this secret anointing.
Purpose: To provide Israel a king after God's own heart from Jesse's house while Saul was rejected (1 Samuel 16:1, 16:7).

Command: Go Up to Hebron
Summary: God's answer to David's enquiry after Saul's death: go up to Hebron in Judah.
Commandment: Go up into one of the cities of Judah — unto Hebron.
Application: David enquired and God answered with a single direction; David went up to Hebron and was anointed king over Judah there (2 Samuel 2:4). A small command with a large consequence: the first step of David's kingship.
Purpose: To move David from exile into Judah, where he was anointed king over the house of Judah (2 Samuel 2:4).

Command: Keep the Nazirite Rule for Samson
Summary: The angel's command to Samson's mother before his birth: keep the Nazirite rule for the child from the womb.
Commandment: Beware, and drink not wine nor strong drink, and eat not any unclean thing; for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb.
Application: The command was given to Manoah's wife before Samson's birth (Judges 13:4-5, repeated 13:7): no wine or strong drink, no unclean thing, no razor on the child's head, because the child would be a Nazarite from the womb. Included because the imperative form is explicit and person-specific, even though its recipient is Samson's mother and its subject is Samson.
Purpose: To set Samson apart from the womb as a Nazarite who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines (Judges 13:5).

Command: Take a Wife of Whoredoms
Summary: God's command to Hosea: take a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms as a sign of Israel's whoredom.
Commandment: Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.
Application: A prophetic sign-act command, deliberately shocking: Hosea's marriage pictured Israel's whoredom against the LORD (Hosea 1:2 states the reason). Rowed separately from the chapter 3 command because it is a different marriage act at a different time; parent may merge both Hosea rows into one sign-act row.
Purpose: To enact in Hosea's own marriage the LORD's charge against Israel's unfaithfulness (Hosea 1:2).

Command: Go, Love Again
Summary: God's second marriage command to Hosea: go yet, love a woman beloved yet adulterous, as the LORD loves Israel.
Commandment: Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel.
Application: The second Hosea marriage command (Hosea 3:1): love again a woman beloved yet adulterous, according to the LORD's love for Israel though they look to other gods. Same merge caveat as the chapter 1 row.
Purpose: To enact the LORD's redeeming love for an unfaithful Israel, bought back and kept (Hosea 3:2-3).

Command: Go to the Potter's House
Summary: God's command to Jeremiah: arise, go down to the potter's house, and there hear God's words.
Commandment: Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words.
Application: A deed-commission, not a speech alone: Jeremiah must go to the place before he hears the word, and the potter's vessel becomes the sermon (Jeremiah 18:3-10). Generic prophetic 'speak to this people' commissions are not separately rowed (see notes); this one is included because the commanded journey and object lesson are a distinct act.
Purpose: To show Jeremiah, in the potter's work, that Israel is clay in the LORD's hand — to be remade or ruined as he speaks (Jeremiah 18:6-10).

Command: Eat the Scroll
Summary: God's command to Ezekiel: eat the roll he is given, and go speak to the house of Israel.
Commandment: Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel.
Application: A sign-act command at Ezekiel's commission: eat the roll, then go speak to Israel (Ezekiel 3:1, 3:4). The eating is the distinctive commanded deed, which is why it is rowed while generic 'prophesy' commissions are not.
Purpose: To internalize God's word before speaking it — sweet as honey in the mouth (Ezekiel 3:3) — so the prophet speaks from within, not from outside.

Command: Seal the Book
Summary: God's command to Daniel at the end of his visions: shut up the words and seal the book to the time of the end.
Commandment: Shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end.
Application: A closing command to the aged prophet: seal the book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4, repeated in 12:9). Its time limit is part of the command itself — sealed, not suppressed forever, with knowledge to increase at the end.
Purpose: To preserve Daniel's vision sealed for the time of the end, when many shall run to and fro and knowledge shall be increased (Daniel 12:4).

Command: Write What You See
Summary: The risen Christ's command to John on Patmos: write what you see in a book and send it to the seven churches.
Commandment: What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia.
Application: The writing commission of Revelation: what John sees, he must write in a book and send to the seven churches (Revelation 1:11), and write the things which are, and which shall be hereafter (1:19). The seven letters (chapters 2-3) are applications of this one commission, not seven separate commands, and are not separately rowed.
Purpose: To preserve the revelation of Jesus Christ in written form for the seven churches and, through them, the church (Revelation 1:1-3).

Command: The Greatest Commandments
Summary: Jesus' summary of the whole Law: love God with everything you are, and love your neighbor as yourself.
Commandment: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself.
Application: Jesus says all the Law and the Prophets hang on these two. Every other command in this collection is an unfolding of one of them.
Purpose: Jesus' own summary: all the Law and the Prophets hang on these two (Matthew 22:40).

Command: The New Commandment: Love One Another
Summary: The command Jesus gave on the night before the cross: love one another as he has loved — a love measured by his own self-giving.
Commandment: Love one another just as Christ has loved you; let this love mark you as his disciples.
Application: The commandment is called new not because love was new, but because its measure is new: as I have loved you, even to laying down life for friends.
Purpose: Measured by Christ's own self-giving love (John 13:34); the mark of discipleship (John 13:35).

Command: The Great Commission
Summary: The risen Christ's charge to his church: go, make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them everything he commanded.
Commandment: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything Christ commanded.
Application: The commission carries Christ's own authority — all authority in heaven and on earth — and his own promise: I am with you always, to the end of the age.
Purpose: Given with all authority and the promise of Christ's presence to the end of the age (Matthew 28:18-20).

Command: Repent and Believe the Gospel
Summary: Jesus' opening proclamation: the kingdom of God is at hand, so turn from sin and trust the good news.
Commandment: Repent and believe the gospel, for the kingdom of God is at hand.
Application: Peter preaches the same command at Pentecost: repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins. Repentance and faith are the door into the kingdom, not works added to it.
Purpose: The door into the kingdom: Jesus' opening proclamation (Mark 1:15), preached at Pentecost (Acts 2:38).

Command: The Lord's Supper: Do This in Remembrance
Summary: The meal Christ instituted on the night he was betrayed: bread as his body, cup as the new covenant in his blood, eaten in remembrance until he comes.
Commandment: Eat the bread and drink the cup in remembrance of Christ, proclaiming his death until he comes.
Application: Paul delivers the same institution to Corinth and adds its rhythm: as often as you eat and drink, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes.
Purpose: Remembrance and proclamation until he comes (1 Corinthians 11:26): a standing meal, not a one-time act.

Command: Forgive as You Have Been Forgiven
Summary: The forgiveness command: forgive those who wrong you, as freely as God in Christ has forgiven you.
Commandment: Forgive those who sin against you, as your Father has forgiven you.
Application: Jesus ties our forgiveness to God's with unsettling directness, and the unforgiving servant shows what happens when a forgiven person refuses to forgive.
Purpose: Forgiveness received must become forgiveness given (Matthew 6:14-15; Colossians 3:13).

Command: Judge Righteously, Not Hypocritically
Summary: The judgment command: do not condemn others while blind to your own faults; judge with right judgment.
Commandment: Do not judge hypocritically; first take the plank from your own eye, then judge with right judgment.
Application: The command does not forbid all judgment — John 7:24 commands right judgment — but it forbids the hypocrite's judgment, which condemns in others what it excuses in itself.
Purpose: To forbid hypocritical condemnation while commanding right judgment (John 7:24).

Command: Pray: The Lord's Prayer
Summary: The prayer Christ taught his disciples: a pattern for prayer that begins with God's name and kingdom before turning to daily needs.
Commandment: Pray like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name; your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as in heaven.
Application: The prayer is both a text to pray and a pattern to follow: God's glory first, then daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from evil.
Purpose: The pattern Jesus taught for prayer: God's glory first, then daily needs, forgiveness, and deliverance (Matthew 6:9-13).

Command: Seek First the Kingdom
Summary: The priority command: put God's kingdom and righteousness before food, clothing, and worry, and trust him for the rest.
Commandment: Seek first God's kingdom and his righteousness, and do not be anxious about food and clothing.
Application: The command reorders anxiety itself: worry is answered not by more provision but by a prior loyalty — the kingdom first, and all these things added.
Purpose: To reorder anxiety by prior loyalty: kingdom first, and all these things added (Matthew 6:33).

Command: Abide in Christ
Summary: The vine command: remain in Christ as a branch remains in the vine, or you can do nothing.
Commandment: Abide in me as I abide in you; apart from me you can do nothing.
Application: Abiding is not a feeling but a staying: keep his words, keep his commands, and let his life flow through you into fruit.
Purpose: Fruitfulness depends on remaining in Christ as branch in vine (John 15:4-5); apart from him, nothing.

Command: Walk by the Spirit
Summary: Paul's central command for Christian conduct: live by the Spirit's leading, and the works of the flesh lose their power.
Commandment: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh; bear the Spirit's fruit instead.
Application: The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control — is the character the Law aimed at but could not produce.
Purpose: The Spirit produces the character the Law aimed at but could not (Galatians 5:22-25).

Command: Bear One Another's Burdens
Summary: The burden-bearing command: carry the weight of a brother's failure, sorrow, and need, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Commandment: Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Application: Paul names this the law of Christ: strength exists to carry weakness, not to admire itself. The strong restore the fallen gently, watching themselves.
Purpose: Paul names this the law of Christ (Galatians 6:2): strength exists to carry weakness.

Command: Do Not Forsake Meeting Together
Summary: The gathering command: keep assembling with God's people for encouragement, especially as the Day draws near.
Commandment: Do not neglect meeting together, but encourage one another all the more as you see the Day approaching.
Application: The early church's pattern was daily fellowship, teaching, breaking of bread, and prayer. Gathering is not an optional extra but the place encouragement happens.
Purpose: Gathering as the place of encouragement, especially as the Day approaches (Hebrews 10:25).

Command: Submit to Governing Authorities
Summary: The authority command: submit to the governing powers, which God has instituted, and honor those in office.
Commandment: Submit to the governing authorities and honor those in office, for authority is instituted by God.
Application: Submission has its limit, which Scripture itself shows: where rulers command disobedience to God, believers obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). The command is submission, not worship of the state.
Purpose: Authority is instituted by God (Romans 13:1), limited where rulers command disobedience to God (Acts 5:29).

Command: Household Commands
Summary: The household code: wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters — each with duties shaped by Christ's own pattern.
Commandment: Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord; husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church; children, obey your parents; parents, do not provoke your children.
Application: The code's most radical stroke is its address to the powerful: husbands must love as Christ loved — giving himself up — and masters must remember they too have a Master in heaven.
Purpose: Household duties shaped by Christ's pattern (Ephesians 5-6). Debated: churches differ on how the wives/husbands, children/parents, servants/masters instructions apply today — as enduring order, or as a first-century household code whose Christ-shaped mutuality (husbands loving as Christ loved) governs application. The site does not settle this.

Command: Pray Without Ceasing, Give Thanks in Everything
Summary: The unceasing-prayer command: rejoice always, pray continually, and give thanks in every circumstance.
Commandment: Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all circumstances, for this is God's will for you in Christ Jesus.
Application: Thanksgiving in all circumstances is not denial of suffering but trust inside it — the peace of God guarding hearts that bring everything to him in prayer.
Purpose: God's stated will for believers in Christ Jesus (1 Thessalonians 5:18): rejoicing, continual prayer, thanks in all circumstances.

Command: Guard and Proclaim the Teaching
Summary: The stewardship command: hold fast the apostolic teaching, preach the word in season and out, and pass it to faithful people who will teach others.
Commandment: Preach the word in season and out of season, hold fast the pattern of sound words, and entrust it to faithful people who will teach others also.
Application: The teaching is a deposit to be guarded, not an invention to be improved. Each generation receives it, keeps it, and hands it on intact.
Purpose: The apostolic deposit to be guarded and handed on intact to faithful teachers (2 Timothy 2:2).

Command: Pure Religion: Care for Widows and Orphans
Summary: The pure-religion command: true devotion shows itself in visiting orphans and widows in their affliction and keeping unstained by the world.
Commandment: Visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and keep yourself unstained from the world.
Application: James makes care for the defenseless the test of real religion, not its decoration. Paul's instructions to Timothy organize that care in the church, honoring widows who are truly widows.
Purpose: James makes care for the defenseless the test of real religion (James 1:27).

Command: Do Not Show Partiality
Summary: The impartiality command: do not favor the rich over the poor in the assembly or in judgment, for God shows no partiality.
Commandment: Do not show favoritism: treat the poor man in shabby clothes with the same honor as the rich man in fine clothes.
Application: James calls favoritism sin, plainly: it judges with evil thoughts and breaks the royal law of loving your neighbor. In Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
Purpose: Favoritism is sin that breaks the royal law of neighbor-love (James 2:8-9); God shows no partiality.

Command: Work Quietly and Provide for Your Household
Summary: The work command: earn your own living quietly, provide for your household, and do not live as a burden on others.
Commandment: Work quietly, earn your own living, and provide for your own household; if anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.
Application: Work is given dignity here: honest labor supports a family, funds generosity, and silences busybodies. Refusing to provide for one's own household is called a denial of the faith.
Purpose: Honest labor supporting family and funding generosity (Ephesians 4:28); refusing to provide for one's household is called denial of the faith (1 Timothy 5:8).

Command: Do not graft trees of diverse kinds
Summary: One of the mixture laws of Leviticus 19:19: do not graft trees of diverse kinds. The verse as written forbids mingled seed in the field; the tradition counts grafting of diverse trees as a distinct mixture law under the same verse. Doubt: whether grafting stands as a separate enumeration distinct from the field-seed mixture law is debated in the tradition, and the verse itself speaks of mingled seed rather than grafting by name.
Commandment: Do not graft trees of diverse kinds
Application: TRADITIONAL reading: the mixture law is classed among the chukim, statutes whose reason Scripture does not state; like the other mixture laws of Leviticus 19:19 it belonged to Israel's land law under the Sinai covenant.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: no reason is stated in Scripture; the mixture law is classed among the chukim. Duration Temporary because it is a Mosaic land law bound to Israel under the Sinai covenant, of the same kind as the other mixture laws of Leviticus 19:19, which the collection files as Temporary.

Command: Do not retain a captive woman in servitude after letting her go
Summary: One of the family laws of Deuteronomy 21-25: do not retain a captive woman in servitude after letting her go. If a man has no delight in her, he must let her go where she will; he may not keep her in servitude or make merchandise of her. This row covers retaining her in servitude; the companion row do-not-sell-a-captive-woman covers selling her.
Commandment: Do not retain a captive woman in servitude after letting her go
Application: These civil provisions belonged to ancient Israel's family law and have passed with it; the protection of the weaker party they aimed at remains the lesson.
Purpose: To protect a captive woman once let go: she is not to be kept in servitude or made merchandise of after being humbled (Deuteronomy 21:14). Duration Temporary because it is a Mosaic war-and-family law bound to Israel under the Sinai covenant, of the same kind as the companion sell row, which the collection files as Temporary.

Command: Do not use second-tithe money for an unclean purpose
Summary: The command: Do not use second-tithe money for an unclean purpose (Deuteronomy 26:14). The tithe confession declared that none of it had been taken away for any unclean use. This row covers spending tithe money for an unclean purpose; the companion row do-not-eat-the-tithe-in-mourning-in-uncleanness-or-for-the-dead covers the eating clauses of the same verse.
Commandment: Do not use second-tithe money for an unclean purpose
Application: It cannot be practised as written without the standing temple and Aaronic priesthood; its enduring lesson is God's holiness, the cost of atonement, and worship offered exactly as God appoints.
Purpose: TRADITIONAL reading: holy gifts were not to be diverted to unclean purposes, keeping what was consecrated to the LORD distinct from impurity. Duration Debated: the scope of 'unclean use' in this verse — spending tithe money versus the eating clauses — is the debated point, so the collection files it Debated rather than settling it.

Command: The 613 Mitzvot: A Rabbinic Enumeration
Summary: The tradition that the Torah contains 613 commandments — 248 positive and 365 negative — first systematized by medieval rabbis, not stated anywhere in Scripture itself.
Commandment: The Torah's commandments are traditionally counted as 613 in total.
Application: Scripture never gives a count of its own commandments; the 613 figure comes from rabbinic tradition (traced to Rabbi Simlai and codified by Maimonides), and different rabbinic lists disagree on details. It is a study aid, not a biblical census. Christians also differ on how the Mosaic law applies today — fulfilled in Christ, yet its moral substance enduring — which is why this collection treats the traditional moral/ceremonial/civil division as traditional, not as Scripture's own. A full 613-entry draft is a separate future decision, not attempted here.
Purpose: Not a command at all but a study aid: the rabbinic tradition counting the Torah's commandments as 613 (248 positive, 365 negative), traced to Rabbi Simlai and codified by Maimonides. Scripture itself gives no count. See notes for the proposed handling: this row should NOT receive a Duration value.
